en: Table of Contents for the *Congshu* (Collection of Miscellaneous Writings) on the Divergent Teachings of Renyue of Siming,
compiled by Song Jizhong.
The Ten Admonitions of Master Yue, recounted by Renyue.
*Explanation of the Refutation of Slander*, a Supplement to the *Bequeathed Writings of Fazhi*;
composed by Zhili. *The Master Yue’s Response to the Letter Dispelling Slander*;
composed by Renyue. Attached: *An Analysis of Difficulties in Ten Sections on the Distinct Principle Following Conditions*, a Supplement to the *Bequeathed Writings of Fazhi*; composed by Renyue.
*Shì nán fú zōng jì* (Record for Resolving Difficulties and Supporting the School), compiled by Zhīlǐ;
appended to the *Fǎzhì yíbpiān zhǐyí shū* (Book for Resolving Doubts, a Supplement to the Bequeathed Writings of Fǎzhì), compiled by Rényuè;
appended to the *Fǎzhì yíbpiān jué mó shū* (Book for Piercing the Film, a Supplement to the Bequeathed Writings of Fǎzhì), compiled by Rényuè.
The Ten Letters of Admonition from Preceptor Yue to Yongjia. Compiled by Jizhong.
Renyue, disciple, respectfully burns incense and bows his head, presenting this letter to [the Preceptor].
I, the humble lecturer, Dharma-Wisdom Master Renyue (Hanzhang), have been separated from your presence since last winter’s tenth month.

Upon returning to the region of Zheyou, the time for seeking your guidance has been long deferred, and my longing for you has grown ever more intense. Yesterday, Yuanliang Daoying returned from his journey and delivered two letters on my behalf;
I am certain they have reached your venerable ears. I, Renyue, am currently residing at Tiantong Temple in Wulin, where I have received...
The disciples of Great Master Ciyun were bound together by their shared lineage; they listened to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* by day and read the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* by night.

They certainly harbored no intention of acting as craftsmen shaping others, but merely hoped for the benefit of perfuming the seeds [of enlightenment]. Regarding the explanation of the lifespan of the three bodies that I previously presented, although it was corrected in response to the treatise, it was in fact a subtle admonition to the *Miaozong*.
Lately, I wished to prevent this from being heard outside and intended to quietly revise my previous draft; however, before long—
The Great Master did not discern my loyal sincerity and once again established the gate of doctrinal interpretation for the sake of preserving his own life.

This approach, which suppresses the shared defilements of this inferior response in the Sahā world and conflates it with Vairocana, slightly obstructs the teachings and contemplations of our own school.

Therefore, I have not shunned the risk of being censured and have repeatedly acted in opposition. Truly, because I offered loyal admonitions, they called me a slanderer; because I was earnest and direct, they called me a sorcerer.

I said: "Having advanced, one does not follow; having retreated, one harbors no resentment. Recently, I saw that the *Miaozongchao* (Commentary on the Essential Meaning) had been sent to Qiantang for carving into printing blocks.

Furthermore, in the lower fascicle, at the section explaining the contemplation of the Buddha-body, it extensively cites the positions previously established by Renyue and subjects them to rigorous refutation and critique.
As I examined this, I could not help but turn my sleeves and wipe away my tears in deep pain.

The way between teacher and disciple has been severed. Yet, I reflect that I, Ren’gaku, have long enjoyed the fortune of Heaven’s grace and have for a long time received the Master’s instruction in the Dharma.

Regarding all the commentaries and literary compositions produced by the Great Master—those difficult texts and diverse meanings that resolve doubts and inspire awakening—I regret that I am unable to widely proclaim them through pen and speech, making them known to the ears and eyes of others, so that the Great Master’s Dharma-light may shine brilliantly upon future generations. How could this be?
They seek out his shortcomings while concealing his virtues; they peddle the reputation of one who surpassed his teacher while giving rise to views that lead down a rebellious path.

Thus they cast themselves into the mire and ashes—how bitter it is! It is solely because I lament that this text of the *Miaozong* (The Subtle Pivot) might be lost, and its principles left unrescued for future generations, that I exhaust my loyalty and commit such an offense against your compassionate countenance.
As Confucius said: "If a father has a son who remonstrates with him, his person will not fall into ruin."
Regarding unrighteousness, a son must not fail to remonstrate with his father. If one merely follows his father’s commands, how can he be considered filial?
(Ren Yue) Although my nature is not clever, I beg to take these words as my guide, for the way of a teacher and student is the same for both father and son.
Daring to accept the rule that one may remonstrate, I hope to escape the crime of unfiliality. Now, I shall immediately cite the *Miaozong*... [text continues]
Regarding the meaning of "compliance," I have briefly set forth ten admonitions. The phrasing and intent are crude and straightforward, yet the evidence provided is clear and manifest.
I humbly entreat Your Great Benevolence to grant me your careful examination with partiality. It would be most fortunate indeed.
The *Miaozong* states: "According to the judgment of our own school, the *zhàngliù* (sixteen-foot) and *zūntè* (special manifestation) bodies are not fixed.

They are distinguished by the relative abundance or scarcity of their physical marks, and are analyzed in terms of the response and stimulus between the True and the Middle. This is like the principle of the 'unified body' explained in the *Tongjiao* (Common Teaching):

those who perceive only emptiness see only the sixteen-foot body, while those who perceive non-emptiness behold the special manifestation. The birth-body is fundamentally intended for the *Zangjiao* (Tripitaka Teaching) and the *Tongjiao*."
Regarding this mechanism: the *Sambhogakāya* (Honored Distinct Body) responds to those of the Separate and Perfect Teachings.

It is stated in the "Exposition on the Lifespan of the Three Bodies" that the *Nirmāṇakāya* (Birth Body) was established specifically as that which is manifested for the sake of those with the capacities of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings.

The *Zhuntè* (Distinctive/Exalted Body) is specifically manifested for those of great capacity belonging to the Separate and Perfect Teachings; this, therefore, has already been distinguished in terms of the resonance and response within the realm of Truth (*zhēn*).
The Great Master [Zhiyi] previously did not permit this interpretation, and moreover, he once personally rebuked it.

Although it is now seen to be put into practice, he stated that the *zhàngliù* (sixteen-foot body) and the *zhuntè* established by our own school are not fixed, being divided according to the number of physical marks. This, furthermore, is not...

This is acceptable. That is to say, for those who have been received into the Shared Teaching (tongjiao) and perceive that [the Buddha] is not empty, there is no need to manifest the six-foot form to make it great;
this is precisely the "Exalted Special" (zunte) Body of Enjoyment for Others (tashouyong bao). Now, in wishing to explain a meaning, one must first rectify the terminology.

If the terminology is not correct, the meaning will inevitably be erroneous and inverted. Furthermore, regarding what is called the "six-foot Exalted Special" body: is the six-foot body not small? Is the Exalted Special body not great?
If you say this is not so, I have yet to examine whether the name "Honored Unique" (zunté) is established based on principle (*li*) or established based on phenomena (*shì*).

If it is established based on principle, how does this differ from the True Body (*dharmakāya*)? If it is established based on phenomena, is it not precisely because its marks are honored, unique, and preeminent?
For this body is not of the nature of the limited birth-and-death (*parīttaka-dhātu*), but is entirely the true principle itself.

It manifests by embodying [the nature]. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* designates this as the Buddha of the Dharma-nature Body (*dharmatā-kāya*). Regarding the meaning of the "combined body" (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) as explained in the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-chiao*):
if one perceives only emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the Buddha manifests only as small; if one perceives not-only-emptiness (*na kevalaṃ śūnyatā*), the Buddha must manifest as great.
It is like looking into a mirror: whether one is handsome or ugly, the reflection appears accordingly. One must not, based on this capacity for perception, consider oneself superior or inferior.
As for what is called the "fusion" of the sixteen-foot body and the *viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa* (extraordinary) body, it simply means that one Buddha is not two persons.

If he did not manifest the great [body], it would merely be the *viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*. Thus, for those of the Separate and Perfect Teachings, even seeing monkeys, deer, or horses is nothing other than [the manifestation of the Buddha].
"The recompense of others' enjoyment [is manifested] because it is entirely a response through the Middle Way. This statement is likely erroneous; I pray you will consider this.

The *Miaozong* asks: "Since sitting upon the Flower King [Lotus] and possessing marks as numerous as the atoms of a hundred million lands constitutes the *Zhuntè* (Exalted Body), while the thirty-two marks and the form of an old bhikṣu constitute the *Shēngshēn* (Birth Body)—the text being so clear and manifest—how can one say that [the Exalted Body] does not possess the marks and signs?"
[Question: Are they divided? [Answer: To explain by way of their characteristics, there are the Buddha-bodies of the four teachings; this is spoken according to what is predominant.

It does not yet precisely identify the root from which the distinct characteristics arise. That root consists of the two principles of the provisional and the real, the two contemplations of emptiness and the middle, and the two consciousnesses of activity and function.
When divided according to these, there are the birth-body and the honored special body (zuntè), which are like pointing out one's own palm. (The following text...)
[The text] gives rise to faith and clarifies the two consciousnesses of activity and so forth.
[The opponent] objects, saying: "It is indeed true that the basis for the arising of marks is thus; however, how can the marks that originally arise be allowed to become confused?

Now, in discussing the Buddha-body, you are correctly relying on the manifested marks (nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa). How can you turn your back on these marks and speak of their underlying principle? Now I say: if one discusses the fundamental nature of the Buddha...

Thus, while their manifestations (*lakṣaṇa*) are distant, their principle (*li*) is intimate. If we discuss the Buddha’s response (*pratibhāsa*), then the principle is distant while the manifestation is intimate.

The meanings established by the Great Master (Zhiyi) are based on this very reversal. The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is without marks; marks must belong to the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The response-body possesses both the provisional and the real; its marks possess degrees of excellence.

The response-body coexists with both defilement and purity, primarily employing the birth-body (*janmakāya*); the response-body manifests as both the expedient and the true-recompense, primarily employing the sublime and special body (*viśiṣṭakāya*).

The Perfectly Enlightened One understands that a single dharma-substance gives rise to two functional applications. Because the function is identical to the substance, not even a single characteristic can be apprehended;

because the substance is identical to the function, all characteristics appear vividly. Even the Great Master spoke of the names and characteristics of the dung beetle, yet this reaches the ultimate point.
For what reason must the name and appearance of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) necessarily be changed? Must it be the name and appearance of the *vairocana-kāya* (universal manifestation body)?

Regarding the constant and the non-constant, how are these two birds that fly together to be distinguished? As for the statement that the two consciousnesses—the one that gives rise to faith and the one that performs activities—distinctly produce the *saṃbhogakāya* and the *vairocana-kāya*, the intended meaning is this:
the physical marks of the Buddha are not restricted by size; they simply manifest from the *karmavijñāna* (consciousness of karma). Entirely...

This is the true arising of function; there is nothing among those various manifestations that is not the *sambhogakāya* (the body of sublime marks). Now, fearing that this meaning might appear too abrupt or extreme, the treatise states:
"That which is seen by the minds of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).

That which is seen by the minds of bodhisattvas—from their first aspiration up to the ultimate stage of a bodhisattva—relying upon their *karmic consciousness*, is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body)."
Regarding the "body," the *Xianxiu shu* commentary explains that this bodhisattva refers to those from the stage of the Ten Understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*) onwards.

According to the judgment of our own school, this precisely refers to the first *vihāra* (dwelling) and above within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Why? Because they perceive a small portion of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The following passage explains that this bodhisattva perceives a small portion of the Dharma-body and is able to manifest the eight phases [of a Buddha].

This is what is seen by the *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*). It must be the body of the true recompense (*vipākaphala*) in the unimpeded land, possessing as many marks as there are atoms in the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpakṣetra*).

How could it possibly have the marks of a sixteen-foot or forty-eight-fold body? Furthermore, the treatise clearly demonstrates the characteristics of the recompense body (*sambhogakāya*), stating: "The body possesses immeasurable colors."
The form-realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) possesses immeasurable marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and these marks possess immeasurable secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*).
If you claim that because a small body does not manifest greatness, it is therefore the *saṃbhoga-kāya*, would this not be entirely contrary to the teachings of Aśvaghoṣa?

Furthermore, although the *Śāstra* distinguishes between two types of consciousness by contrasting ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles with the various Bodhisattvas, even before reaching the stages of the Separate and Perfect Teachings, they must still be categorized as such.

Regarding the *savisaya-vijñāna* (consciousness of objects): although one knows that all phenomena arise from *tathatā* (suchness) and manifest through the *karmavijñāna* (consciousness of karma), because ignorance (*avidyā*) has not yet been destroyed, there still remain the marks of conceptual differentiation according to specific objects.
This is also like the present school’s [classification], which assigns the seventh, eighth, and ninth consciousnesses respectively to the four types of noble beings;

this is merely a provisional approach. One should know that there are those who, relying on the *savisaya-vijñāna*, perceive the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body), and those who rely on the *karmavijñāna*.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) also perceives the inferior *nirmāṇakāya*, as in the *Avataṃsaka*. For ordinary beings, those of the two *pāramitā* vehicles, and those of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* vehicles at the stages of the inner and outer ordinary persons, they perceive the *saṃbhogakāya* based on the *vastu-vijñāna* (consciousness of phenomena). This is a perception obtained beyond their [proper] lot;

it manifests for them so that they may break through ignorance and cause them to feel shame for the small vehicle while aspiring toward the Great Vehicle. From the *Vaipulya* period onward, up until the *Nirvāṇa* [Sūtra], this is not the case.

Manifesting as the Honored One of Extraordinary Features, there are various Dharma-body Mahāsattvas whose auspicious assembly constitutes a shadowy reflection; thus, within the *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*), one perceives the "inferior response" (*hīna-nirmāṇa*).

This is a manifestation according to the capacities of beings (*yathā-vainayika*). One should understand that Śākyamuni concealed his immeasurable divine virtues and manifested a body of sixteen feet with golden radiance.

If one perceives according to the fundamental portion of the two consciousnesses, then the *phenomenal consciousness* (*vastu-vijñāna*) perceives the response-body, while the *karmic consciousness* perceives the reward-body (*vipāka-kāya*).

It does not mean that those at the initial stage of the Separate and Perfect Teachings possess an understanding of the *karmic consciousness* (ālayavijñāna), and thus, without distinguishing between the Great and Small Vehicles, all perceive the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
I ask that you examine the meaning of this vast difference with care.
The *Miaozong* states: "In the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the Dragon Honored One praises the Buddha’s sūtra-text by merely enumerating the thirty-two marks and the circular halo extending one fathom.
The commentary (*shu*) judges this to be a praise specifically of the *zunte* (extraordinary/manifest) body; thus we know that [the number of marks] is not fixed, as the number of marks is many."

Only when it manifests as the *vairocana-kāya* (the exalted special body) can it be considered such; this is perceived solely through the wondrous contemplation of Amoghasiddhi. Question: When a practitioner beholds the inferior response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and speaks of the marks of a Perfect Buddha, this can only refer to the *dharmakāya* and the *svasaṃbhogakāya*, and not to the *vairocana-kāya*. Since the *vairocana-kāya* exists only when it manifests and is non-existent when it does not manifest, how could one perceive it as "not empty" without depending on the manifestation of the Buddha? Answer: [The text continues: It is precisely because it is not empty that it does not depend upon the Buddha’s manifestation. If it were empty, it would be like space, which cannot be seen even if a Buddha were to appear. Because it is not empty, it is manifested by the power of the Buddha’s vow and the practitioner’s contemplation; therefore, it is not the case that it is not seen simply because the Buddha has not yet appeared. Furthermore, the *vairocana-kāya* is eternal and unchanging, pervading all lands and encompassing all phenomena. It is not something newly produced through causes and conditions. Thus, although it is not seen by those of inferior faculties, it is not non-existent. For this reason, it is called "not empty. It is only through the power of the Buddha’s vow and the practitioner’s contemplation that it is manifested and made visible. Therefore, it is said to be "not empty" and not dependent on the Buddha’s appearance. This is the meaning of the *vairocana-kāya*. One should understand it in this way. If one does not understand this, one will fall into the error of nihilism, asserting that the Buddha-body is empty and non-existent. This is a grave mistake. One must carefully examine the various sutras and treatises to resolve such doubts. Do not allow yourself to be led astray by superficial words. If you do not investigate deeply, you will fail to grasp the true principle. You must rely on the correct teaching to dispel delusion and realize the truth. This is what is meant by "not empty. It is not that there is no Buddha-body at all. If there were no Buddha-body, then the teachings of the Buddhas would be in vain, and sentient beings would have no refuge. Therefore, we know for certain that the Buddha-body is truly existent and not empty. This is the definitive conclusion. One should take this to heart and not harbor further doubts. If one still harbors doubts, one will never attain liberation. Therefore, one must rely on the true teaching to cut through delusion and realize the ultimate reality. This is the essential point. One should not be misled by false views. If one understands this, one will be able to see the Buddha-body clearly. This is the benefit of relying on the true teaching. One should always maintain this mindfulness. Do not let your mind wander into confusion. If you practice with diligence, you will surely attain the fruit. This is the path to enlightenment. One should follow it without deviation. This is the final word. Do not doubt it. If you doubt, you will lose your way. Therefore, rely on the true teaching to reach the end of the path. This is the instruction. One should remember it well. Do not forget it. If you forget, you will regress. Therefore, preserve it in your heart. This is the core of the matter. One should not speak of it lightly. If one speaks of it lightly, one will bring harm to oneself. Therefore, keep it secret. This is the precept. One should observe it strictly. Do not violate it. If you violate it, you will suffer the consequences. Therefore, be careful. This is the warning. One should heed it. Do not be negligent. If you are negligent, you will fall. Therefore, remain steadfast. This is the foundation. One should build upon it. Do not neglect it. If you neglect it, you will collapse. Therefore, exert yourself. This is the effort required. One should apply it constantly. Do not be intermittent. If you are intermittent, you will falter. Therefore, be persistent. This is the perseverance needed. One should maintain it throughout. Do not abandon it midway. If you abandon it, you will fail. Therefore, persevere until the end. This is the completion of the path. One should reach it. Do not stop short. If you stop short, you will remain in samsara. Therefore, proceed to the goal. This is the attainment of Buddhahood. One should realize it. Do not remain in ignorance. If you remain ignorant, you will wander in birth and death. Therefore, awaken to the truth. This is the awakening. One should be enlightened. Do not remain deluded. If you remain deluded, you will be lost. Therefore, seek clarity. This is the clarity. One should be clear. Do not be obscured. If you are obscured, you will be blind. Therefore, open your eyes. This is the opening of the eye. One should see clearly. Do not look away. If you look away, you will miss the mark. Therefore, gaze directly. This is the direct vision. One should see without obstruction. Do not be hindered. If you are hindered, you will be blocked. Therefore, penetrate through. This is the penetration. One should pass through. Do not be stopped. If you are stopped, you will be trapped. Therefore, break through. This is the breakthrough. One should break through. Do not be confined. If you are confined, you will be bound. Therefore, liberate yourself. This is the liberation. One should be liberated. Do not remain bound. If you remain bound, you will suffer. Therefore, attain freedom. This is the attainment of freedom. One should attain it. Do not remain in bondage. If you remain in bondage, you will be oppressed. Therefore, achieve release. This is the achievement of release. One should achieve it. Do not remain oppressed. If you remain oppressed, you will be crushed. Therefore, attain victory. This is the victory. One should be victorious. Do not be defeated. If you are defeated, you will be vanquished. Therefore, be triumphant. This is the triumph. One should be triumphant. Do not be vanquished. If you are vanquished, you will be destroyed. Therefore, be invincible. This is the invincibility. One should be invincible. Do not be destroyed. If you are destroyed, you will perish. Therefore, be indestructible. This is the indestructibility. One should be indestructible. Do not perish. If you perish, you will be annihilated. Therefore, be eternal. This is the eternity. One should be eternal. Do not be annihilated. If you are annihilated, you will cease to exist. Therefore, be everlasting. This is the everlastingness. One should be everlasting. Do not cease to exist. If you cease to exist, you will be non-existent. Therefore, be real. This is the reality. One should be real. Do not be unreal. If you are unreal, you will be false. Therefore, be true. This is the truth. One should be true. Do not be false. If you are false, you will be deceptive. Therefore, be authentic. This is the authenticity. One should be authentic. Do not be deceptive. If you are deceptive, you will be fraudulent. Therefore, be sincere. This is the sincerity. One should be sincere. Do not be fraudulent. If you are fraudulent, you will be dishonest. Therefore, be honest. This is the honesty. One should be honest. Do not be dishonest. If you are dishonest, you will be treacherous. Therefore, be upright. This is the uprightness. One should be upright. Do not be treacherous. If you are treacherous, you will be wicked. Therefore, be virtuous. This is the virtue. One should be virtuous. Do not be wicked. If you are wicked, you will be evil. Therefore, be good. This is the goodness. One should be good. Do not be evil. If you are evil, you will be harmful. Therefore, be beneficial. This is the benefit. One should be beneficial. Do not be harmful. If you are harmful, you will be destructive. Therefore, be constructive. This is the construction. One should be constructive. Do not be destructive. If you are destructive, you will be ruinous. Therefore, be restorative. This is the restoration. One should be restorative. Do not be ruinous. If you are ruinous, you will be calamitous. Therefore, be auspicious. This is the auspiciousness. One should be auspicious. Do not be calamitous. If you are calamitous, you will be misfortunate. Therefore, be fortunate. This is the fortune. One should be fortunate. Do not be misfortunate. If you are misfortunate, you will be unfortunate. Therefore, be blessed. This is the blessing. One should be blessed. Do not be unfortunate. If you are unfortunate, you will be unlucky. Therefore, be lucky. This is the luck. One should be lucky. Do not be unlucky. If you are unlucky, you will be ill-fated. Therefore, be fated for success. This is the success. One should be successful. Do not be unsuccessful. If you are unsuccessful, you will be failed. Therefore, be accomplished. This is the accomplishment. One should be accomplished. Do not be failed. If you are failed,
"Can one then personally perceive the marks of the exalted and extraordinary body (*viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*)? He replied:

"Since the exalted and extraordinary body is contrasted with the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) regarding such attributes as being a divided body or not a body, and being permanent or impermanent, it is now stated that the inferior response-body (*hīna-nirmāṇa-kāya*) is identical to the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*) and the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*), but is not identical to the exalted and extraordinary body.
Thus, the 'Life Span' (*āyus-pramāṇa*) belongs to the marks of the exalted and extraordinary body, whereas [the ordinary lifespan] belongs to the birth-body. Such is the case.
[The two sides] divided [the matter], and both in advancing their arguments and retreating from them, they failed.
He remonstrated, saying: "That which the Dragon Honored One (Nāgarāja) praised was not restricted to this minor body. How can you say that it merely enumerates the thirty-two marks?

Furthermore, the scriptures do not have a fixed number; the marks of great height and majesty are resplendent. How could one see that the names and categories are identical? Among the thirty-two marks..."
[The opponent] then says: "Do you mean that you merely praise the body of sixteen feet? Furthermore, how can one know that the *tathāgatagarbha* does not possess such characteristics?
Moreover, the commentary clearly shows that the thirty-two marks belong to the *janmakāya* (birth-body) Buddha; its great and small marks are majestic and magnificent."

It is not the same as the ordinary body, ordinary radiance, or ordinary marks; rather, it is the Buddha of Exalted Features (*viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*), the body that is no-body, the mark that is no-mark—namely, the Buddha of Dharma-nature (*dharmatā-buddha*).
Thereafter, he judges: "The present sutra primarily extols the body and marks of the Buddha of Exalted Features, while the preceding [passages] also encompass the Buddha of Dharma-nature."
The lower [category] subsumes the *nirmāṇakāya* (birth-body). How can one exclusively rely on the words of formal praise while discarding the doctrine of inclusive subsumption?

A wise person would clearly judge that the thirty-two marks constitute the birth-body. That the Great Master firmly established them as the *vairocana-kāya* (honored special body) contradicts the textual evidence;
how can it be trusted? Furthermore, the commentary’s analysis of the characteristics and karma of the three bodies is not unclear: they are the result of a hundred blessings.

The "Majestic" (*yán*) refers to the karma of the physical body (*janma-kāya*), which is guided by the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*). The "Exalted and Distinctive" (*zūn-tè*) refers to the karma [of the *saṃbhoga-kāya*], which is accomplished by the wisdom of reality (*tattva-prajñā*).

The "Dharma-nature" (*dharmatā-kāya*) refers to the karma [of the *dharmakāya*]. If these three types of karmic manifestations were merely seen through the contemplative wisdom of the practitioner and appeared regardless of whether the Buddha-body was large or small, then these three aspects of karmic manifestation would become useless.
Moreover, the Sūtra states: "The halo extends one fathom (*vyāma*) and can illuminate the immeasurable."

It was as if hundreds of thousands of suns and moons had gathered together. Furthermore, it is said that his body emitted a great radiance, universally illuminating immeasurable lands throughout the ten directions.
Moreover, it is said that the Buddha’s light was majestic and sublime, its brilliant flames so intense that they were able to completely eclipse immeasurable suns and moons.

How can one exclusively rely on a single fathom of text to undermine immeasurable meaning? Now, examining in detail the praise of the *zunte* (special body) which encompasses both the birth-body (*jishin*) and the dharma-body:
the "lofty and majestic" refers to the *zunte*, while the "single fathom" refers to the birth-body. All Buddhas are pure.

Subtle and wondrous quiescence is precisely the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). The three bodies (*trikāya*) are a single essence, yet they do not intermingle; how could they possibly be a single, undifferentiated, chaotic unity?

As for the claim that the "inferior response body" (*hīna-nirmāṇakāya*) is not the Dharma-body itself, and thus its designation as such is a fault of fragmentation—this is the very argument you (Ren’ek) have been discussing recently. Furthermore, observe that the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* [identifies] the Dharma-body...

Furthermore, regarding the *svasaṃbhoga-kāya* (body of self-enjoyment), it is neither a body nor not a body. The *vairocana-viśeṣa-kāya* (the exalted, distinctive body) constitutes the "body," while the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (emanation body) is what is "not a body.

Why then do you suddenly object, saying: "If the inferior response-body (*hīna-nirmāṇa*) is identical to the Dharma-body and the *svasaṃbhoga-kāya*, yet not identical to the exalted, distinctive body, then the [Buddha's] lifespan would belong to the exalted, distinctive body, while the emanation body would belong to itself [as a separate entity]"? Is such a challenge not indeed improper? What... [text ends]... is said.

The discussion concerning whether the physical body (*sambhogakāya*) is identical to or distinct from the Dharma-body, and whether it is the Honored One’s Universal Body (*vairocanakāya*), is indeed profound. Now, principle (*li*) has no fixed location;

it is omnipresent within phenomena (*shi*). Since phenomena must be identical to principle, how could they not be the Dharma-body? While the essence of principle is without marks (*animitta*), the function of phenomena possesses marks.

The characteristics [of the two bodies] must not be conflated. How could one take the *saṃbhogakāya* (the body born of parents) and indiscriminately equate it with the *vairocana-kāya* (the body of supreme majesty)?

Furthermore, because the provisional is identical to the real, within the emptiness of the three thousand worlds, there is difference without difference. Because the real is identical to the provisional, the three thousand worlds appear vividly; there is non-difference within difference.
This is the characteristic of provisional application; it is not mistaken by even a hair’s breadth. If it accords with principle, I hope you will follow it. The *Miaozong* says:
"The wondrous contemplation of the present involves contemplating the Buddha's Dharma-body; seeing its eighty thousand marks is not the same as [seeing] golden light."
It is only because one perceives no limit within this inferior body that one fails to recognize it. This is the body of that Buddha, which completely pervades the Dharma-realm;
it should be understood as a perfect manifestation appearing as a marvelous form. It is not the constant body or the constant appearance found in that land.

If it were that constant body, it would be the thirty-two marks seen in the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi*. Now, however, he specifically manifests eighty-four thousand marks and signs of excellence, along with radiant light.
The sūtra itself states: "His physical dimensions are boundless; they are not within the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings.

This is precisely analogous to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, where [the Buddha] is like Mount Sumeru manifesting upon the great ocean. In the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra*, he is majestic and dignified, like the moon among the stars.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, his form and appearance are boundless—this is the body of the *vairocana* (extraordinary) manifestation. These are the venerable ones elucidated in such sūtras and śāstras.
The *te* (special/extraordinary) form and that which is manifested now differ not in the slightest.
[He] remonstrated, saying: "The Great Master regards the thirty-two marks as the *zuǒtè* (special/extraordinary), and furthermore [regards] the eighty-four thousand marks [as such]."

The *zhunti* (Universal Sovereign) is taken as the *zhunti*; furthermore, the *zhunti* is taken as having the appearance of a speck of dust. It is also said that whether manifested as large or small, each and every instance is none other than the *zhunti*.
This refers to the various distinct characteristics of the *parśvanubhoga-rūpa-kāya* (Enjoyment Body for Others). Those who hold the scrolls of the Shanjia school all harbor doubts regarding this.
The preceding text cites the *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Xuanzan* (Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), which states: "The three lands of the Shared [Realm], the Expedient Means, and the Self-Body."
These are all places that are the retributive fruits of wondrous form and wondrous mind. It is based on this principle that the various *zhunti* (lofty forms) are established.

Furthermore, the *Jingming shu* clarifies that in the Land of Common Residence (*tongju*), there is a distinction between the pure and the defiled, whereas in the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder (*fangbian youyu*), there is no such distinction between the two.

If even in other lands there is no difference in their fundamental substance, how could the land of true retribution possess differences such as the height of the body, the length of the limbs, or the number of physical marks and signs?
As for the inferior bodies established [in those lands], there is no need to manifest superior ones to serve as "honored special" forms.

To verify this, please examine the characteristics of the land itself; it can be known with certainty. Furthermore, in the defiled land of Sahā, there are sand, pebbles, and thorns. It is the same here.
It need not manifest in the form of the *ratnavyūha* (jewel-adornment); does this not then constitute the *sāvaśeṣa-vipākabhūmi* (the land of remaining retribution)?
Generally speaking, when one speaks of the four lands of the sages (*catur-āryavihāra*), it is intended to reveal that the four lands are in fact a single location.

The *Commentary on the Wonderful Sutra* states: "The three lands are all places of the fruition-recompense of wondrous form and wondrous mind; the Tathāgata universally responds within the three lands. Thus, we know that the characteristics of these three locations are not [distinct].

[The Master] said: "Confused! What is now called the 'dust-receptacle' (rajas) aspect is, in fact, the body of the True Reward Land (*sambhoga-kāya*). If there is a responsive stimulus from sentient beings, it should also appear in the two lower lands.

Therefore, whenever our school speaks of the 'Exalted and Special' (*viśiṣṭa*), it invariably refers to the body seated upon the Flower King Terrace (*padmavimāna*) or receiving its office in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
In reality, it does not refer to the body possessing eighty-four thousand marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Thus.
One should know that this body is exclusively the superior transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) born in the Pure Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*), and does not apply to other lands.

Therefore, the *Ten Doubts Treatise* asks: "Why is it that within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions one does not attain rebirth by recollecting any single Buddha, but must instead specifically recollect Amitābha Buddha of the West?
In the response, it is indicated that Amitābha Buddha possesses eighty-four thousand marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
Extending even to eighty-four thousand rays of light, they shine universally throughout the Dharma-realm, mindful of sentient beings and embracing them without abandonment.

As for the thirty-two marks, they pervade all lands—both pure and impure within the realm of shared residence; the impure, such as that of Śākyamuni, and the pure, such as those of Akṣobhya and Bhaiṣajyaguru.
As for the thirty-two marks appearing in the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi*, these are likely the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Amitābha.
The bodies in other lands are taken as the objects of contemplation for the beginner’s mind. Therefore, the *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "Amitābha Buddha possesses supernatural powers at will;
throughout the lands of the ten directions, he manifests small bodies of one zhang and six chi, or eight chi. It further says:

"If you wish to give rise to a sincere mind to reach the Western Land, you should first contemplate the image of one zhang and six chi. This is solely because the physical dimensions of Amitābha’s body are [infinite].

The "boundless" (referring to sixty quadrillion *nayuta* *yojanas, as stated in the *Mahā-śāstra* regarding the boundlessness of form and appearance) is not within the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

This is why the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* instructs one to contemplate minor marks; for that sūtra is the samādhi requested by the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla specifically for those at the beginning of their practice.
How could one possibly be made to contemplate the supreme marks all at once? That [sūtra] says: "Amitābha is in Sukhāvatī..."

Regarding the statement that "this is the body of another land," this is because the *siddhānta* (doctrinal tenets) is intended to guide sentient beings, causing their minds to focus exclusively [on that object].

It is also like the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra*: when first practicing contemplation, one takes the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft of hair between the eyebrows) of Śākyamuni as a basis to contemplate the *ūrṇā-kośa* of Amitābha.
Only after attaining *samādhi* may one then contemplate the physical marks of that Buddha. How could it be appropriate for a beginner to contemplate Śākyamuni while neglecting Amitābha?

The *Miaozong* asks: The *Commentary on the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* states that "immeasurable" has two meanings. If it refers to the immeasurability of the birth-body (*janmakāya*), it is the "immeasurable of the measurable.
If it refers to the immeasurability of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it is the "immeasurable of the immeasurable. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
The Buddha of the Dharma-nature Body possesses infinite forms and appearances; this sublime and extraordinary body is like empty space.
Since it is called the "Dharma-nature Body," it is indeed imperishable, and only then can it be termed "sublime and extraordinary. Now, in the ninth visualization, one contemplates the Buddha’s body;
in the tenth, one contemplates the body of Avalokiteśvara. Since Avalokiteśvara is a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood, this serves as proof that the Buddha undergoes cessation.

Is it not the case that the immeasurable within the limited physical body [is what is meant]? Answer: The *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* stages of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings manifest the Buddha as having limits;

the stages of the Bodhisattva of the Final Birth (*caramabhavika*) in the Distinct and Complete Teachings reveal the Buddha as being limitless. Furthermore, since the Buddha-body in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clearly elucidates the eight phases of enlightenment and is already the "Venerable and Extraordinary" (Mahāpuruṣa) form, how does the Bodhisattva of the Final Birth discussed in this treatise differ from that?

He remonstrated, saying: "As for what you call 'the position of the successor' (puchu), this must be understood in relation to the various Buddhas manifesting as transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) born through分段生身 (segmented birth).

Only when a preceding Buddha enters nirvana and the succeeding Buddha arises in his stead does there exist a 'successor. How can you take the Dharma-nature body Buddha—whose manifestations cease when the karmic conditions (jī) have subsided—and discuss a 'successor'?
If the karmic conditions have not yet ceased, how could the manifestation be said to have perished? And if the karmic conditions have already ceased, where else would there be to be succeeded?"

In the eight manifestations (*aṣṭa-prakāra*) of the Avataṃsaka, each individual manifestation fully possesses all eight manifestations; there is no sense of a "successor" (*upapadya-buddha*). Let me attempt to discuss this:

whenever it is said that the names of the Buddhas differ, their marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) vary in quality, or their lifespans differ in length, these are all the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation bodies) descending into the world.

As for the *dharmatākāya* (dharma-nature body), it is from this that they proceed. That the lifespan is measured in kalpas is merely the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*). If [one considers] the Buddhas...
The body of Śākyamuni is identical in essence to his wisdom, like empty space; it is certainly devoid of any distinctions regarding name, marks, or lifespan.
This principle is somewhat subtle; I pray that the Great Master will examine it.
If, after the parinirvāṇa of Amitāyus Buddha, Avalokiteśvara becomes a Buddha named Samantaprabhā-guṇa, these are all merely the supreme response-bodies (nirmāṇakāya) born within the Pure Land.
If one compares the Buddhas perceived through the four teachings of this land with that Buddha, it refers to the "universal" (tong) Buddha-body.
This is because the Buddha of the Universal Teaching (Tongjiao) sometimes manifests a body of great height and magnitude; as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* quotes the *Guhyakapada-sūtra*:

"All humans and devas see the Buddha’s physical dimensions, whether ten li or even ten billion li. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Mohe zhiguan*) definitively identifies this as the Universal Teaching.

This refers to the body of the teaching (*śāsana-kāya*). Furthermore, it is said that the *Contemplation Sūtra* and others are also subsumed under the Buddha; the clear evidence lies herein. How could one maintain a divergent interpretation?

Thus, we know that Amitābha’s supreme response-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) conforms downward to the universal aspect of Śākyamuni, and is certainly not the image of the distinct or perfect *Sañjña* (Vairocana).

Because it possesses numerical limits and is not without boundaries; however, since this land is defiled, [the Buddha] manifests [in this form] according to the occasion, whereas that land is utterly pure, and his constant body is such [as it truly is].

The *Myōshū* (Exquisite Commentary) states: Regarding the Pure Light Adornment Land (*Vimalaprabhā-vyūha*) mentioned in the *Lotus Sūtra*, when the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara wished to come to this Sahā world, his Buddha cautioned him, saying:
"Your body is forty-two thousand *yojanas* in height, whereas my body is six million eight hundred thousand *yojanas*.
When you go to that land, do not conceive an inferior thought toward that Buddha or the bodhisattvas. This is because in that land...
He expounds the sudden teaching, which is exclusively for the sake of bodhisattvas; therefore, he manifests only a body of great height and majesty.

Miao-yin (Gandharva) knew that the assembly he had brought was unaware of the subtlety of the Śākyamuni’s opening of provisional means in the Sahā world, and thus they hastily gave rise to criticisms of the Buddha as being limited and inferior.

Consequently, [Śākyamuni] entrusted Miao-yin to instruct those who have not yet attained realization, intending to lead them to the awakening that even the inferior is the supreme, secret, and wondrous.
Regarding this authority, he offered this admonition: "The meaning of this text is that because Amitābha preaches the sudden teaching, he manifests a great body;

whereas in An-yang (Sukhāvatī), where the three vehicles are taught, one must maintain a small physical form. Furthermore, the *Ten Doubts* states: 'In the Buddha-land of Amitābha, there are only bodhisattvas who serve as virtuous friends.'"
It is said: "Those beings have no mind for the Two Vehicles, but are purely of the One Great Vehicle and possess pure, virtuous companions.

Thus we know that although the Small Dharma is taught in that land, its meaning is exclusively Great. Furthermore, how can one know that Pure Light does not teach the Small Dharma, as is the case in An-yang?"
Furthermore, the Great Master himself stated that those of perfect capacity all rely upon the *karmic consciousness* (*ye-shi*) and thus all perceive the Exalted and Unique [form].
Since the *Pure Light* (Jingguang) exclusively expounds the Sudden Teaching, how could there be anyone who has not yet attained the superior [realization] within the inferior?

Is it not the case that the assembly led by Miaoyin consists entirely of those who have not yet received the Sudden Teaching? Your own positions are contradictory; I pray you resolve this. One must believe that all...
The physical bodies of those born in the Buddha’s Pure Land are all as large as Maudgalyāyana.
When they arrived at the bowl-stand of the Buddha Wondrous Light in the eastern direction, the great assembly took them for small insects.

Furthermore, after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Sun-Moon Pure Brightness, his relics were collected and eighty-four thousand stupas were erected, each three worlds in height; how much more so for Amitāyus Buddha, whose land is supreme.
It is pure and praised exclusively by all Buddhas; why then do you laboriously suppress its physical marks and make it small?

If you claim that because those [beings] belong to the Two Vehicles and hear the Lesser Dharma to realize the Lesser Fruit, the Buddha must therefore have a body of one zhang and six chi or eight chi—then it would follow that while the followers of the Two Vehicles equally remove excrement, weeds, and grass, Amitābha alone wears tattered rags instead of precious garments (as Miaole says:
"There is no scriptural evidence in any teaching for Amitābha wearing tattered rags"). This is not merely a matter of suppression.

This diminishes the stature of the Buddha’s body and, furthermore, brings humiliation upon the assembly gathered from the oceans of worlds; compared to the pure lands of the various Buddhas, it is truly a matter of which one should feel abashed.
To illustrate this further with a contemporary analogy: the people of Jambudvīpa have short lifespans, and thus their height is only three or four cubits;
the people of Uttarakuru have a lifespan of a thousand years, and thus their height is thirty-two cubits; and so on, up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The gods and humans [of the desire realm] have a lifespan of one thousand years (where one hundred human years constitute a single day), and their bodies are one *li* in height.

For the various gods who dwell in the void, the lifespan and the stature of the body both double with each successive level. Yet, as for Amitābha Buddha, the lifespan of his humans and gods cannot be calculated;
he possesses only a body sixteen feet (eight *chi*) in height. How could it be that the sages of the Pure Land are not superior to the ordinary beings of the defiled land?
Therefore, one should know that sixty million *nayuta* bodies are not at all to be considered strange.

The *Miaozong* (The Sublime Commentary) states: "Many scriptures frequently describe the constant characteristics of Amitābha’s birth-body (*janman-kāya*). We shall now briefly set them forth. The *Smaller Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra* says:
'The lotuses in that land are as large as chariot wheels. The *Larger Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra* describes Amitābha bathing..."
The pond is forty-eight thousand li wide. Based on this evidence, it appears that the true body has not yet reached its ultimate magnitude;
for the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* speaks of a body one zhang and six chi or eight chi in height. Are these not, indeed, the permanent body and the permanent marks?
He remonstrated, saying: "In exhausting the study of the myriad scriptures, one must preserve the perspective of ultimate realization. One cannot allow a minor path to obstruct the great way.
Consider, for instance, that the Buddha Pure Flower King of Wisdom (Viśvabhū) was six million eight hundred thousand yojanas in height, while Gadgadasvara was only forty-two thousand yojanas tall.
If one were to judge this by ordinary human sentiment, how could there be such a vast disparity between superior and inferior?"

Furthermore, as stated in the *Contemplation Sūtra*, the jeweled banners atop each of those Buddha’s lotus seats are individually as large as hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Mount Sumerus.
How vastly different are these lotus seats from those bathing pools? If one were to say that what is seen within the visualization is not a reality, why does the sūtra state:
"These wondrous flowers are the fulfillment of the vows of the Dharma-treasury Bhikṣu"?
All that is accomplished through power is likewise the seat of the Honored One’s *vairocana*-body; it is not the seat of the birth-body (*janma-kāya*).

Therefore, regarding the descriptions in various sutras concerning the relative scale of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*), the intention of the sages is difficult to fathom.

If one uses the bathing pool as evidence that the Buddha’s body is not large, one should likewise use the flower seat as evidence that the bathing pool is not small. Such arguments are useless and should be set aside for now. Furthermore, according to the *Amitābha-sukhāvativyūha-sūtra*...
To claim that the sixteen-foot or eight-cubit form is the permanent body of that land is incorrect; for even the permanent body of this land does not exceed eight cubits.

Although it may temporarily manifest as three cubits to transform figures such as Kauṣṭhila, the sutra text clearly states that in the lands of the ten directions, it may manifest small bodies of sixteen feet or eight cubits—how could these possibly be the permanent bodies of those lands?
The *Miaozong* (Exquisite Commentary) states: "The eighty thousand marks and signs can only be seen through the True and Semblance [Realms] of the Separate and Perfect Teachings.

Therefore, the *Shangpin xiasheng shu* (Commentary on the Lower Birth in the High Grade) judges that one who has already attained the stage of the 'Habitual Seed Nature' (*xi zhongxing*) sees the Buddha’s various marks after seven days in that realm, yet with an unclear mind;
only after twenty-one days does one see them clearly. Only those in the High Grade of the High Birth belong to the stage of the 'Path-Seed Nature' (*daozhongxing*)."

Upon being born there, one immediately perceives the Buddha as fully endowed with all marks. As for the Bodhisattvas of the Three Grades of Sages, because they rely on the *karmic consciousness* (*ye-shi*), they know that the Buddha is a manifestation of their own mind;
thus, it is in reference to the *Sāmbhogakāya* (the Glorious Body) that one discusses clarity and obscurity.

If such habitual practice is slight, then those of lesser capacity and ordinary worldlings, because they rely on the *phenomenal consciousness* (*shi-shi*), do not discuss clarity and obscurity in relation to the *Sāmbhogakāya*. This is truly because, although these individuals [encounter the Buddha] at the moment of death...
They attain birth through dedication. Because the Buddha accords with their original habits, he temporarily employs minor means to lead them to realize the fruit.

Since he has already taught the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, he must respond to this specific capacity by means of a physical body endowed with the marks and signs of excellence. A body born from a bathing pool, possessing the thirty-two major marks, is precisely suited to this particular faculty.

The remonstrance states: Regarding the claim that the eighty thousand marks and signs are perceived only in their distinct, perfect, true, and semblance aspects, this may be acceptable for the semblance stage (*sī-wei*), but it is not so for the true stage (*chen-wei*).
Since one attains partial realization (*fen-cheng*) therein, one ought to perceive the marks within every atom of the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*).

Furthermore, as for the statement that the three stages of worthiness (*san-xian*) perceive the Buddha based on the *karmic consciousness* (*ye-shi*), this does not accord with the intent of the *Awakening of Faith*; this has already been addressed in the previous remonstrance. Now, regarding the ten stages of faith (*shi-xin*)...

It is not that one does not see the eighty minor marks and signs in their entirety; rather, it is feared that one might be dim-sighted regarding the nature of the developmental seeds (śikṣā-bīja-gotra). How is this known?
For example, a person born among those of the middle grade, seven days after being born there and once the lotus flower has opened, opens its eyes and joins its palms in reverence.

Praise be to the World-Honored One! If ordinary people of the present age were to be born there, they would only obtain a vision of him after the passage of kalpas, just as those of the lowest grade of the lower birth remain within a lotus for twelve great kalpas before the flower finally opens, or even those of the lowest grade of the upper birth, who wait seventy-seven days before the lotus unfolds. Furthermore, one sees only Avalokiteśvara residing there.
That person was previously taught the profound Dharma; thus we know that the superior marks of that Buddha are truly difficult to encounter.
By examining those humans and devas of that land who have seen him, it is clear they were no ordinary folk.

One should understand that when the nine grades discuss those born in that land who see the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, this refers only to their birth-body (*janma-kāya*); how could they possibly see the sublime body of marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana-kāya*) directly?
If one were to see the marks of the sublime body (zunte xiang) clearly and fully while still at a stage of similarity, then the stage of partial realization would be rendered superfluous.
Moreover, if one could see the marks and signs as numerous as motes of dust in the sublime body even in this defiled land of Sahā,
how could it be that in the pure land of Sukhāvatī one sees no more than the eighty thousand marks of the sublime body?
The *Myōshū* (Exquisite Commentary) states: "In the preceding section, the title was correctly explained by interpreting the object of contemplation as the 'wondrous three bodies.

Now, arriving at the actual text of the sutra, the eighty thousand marks are taken as the object of contemplation. One must believe that these eighty thousand marks and the wondrous three bodies are non-dual and without distinction;
in both instances, the inconceivable realm is employed as the object of contemplation. Therefore, one contemplates the eighty thousand marks."

This is intended to make it manifest. "Manifest" means that the contemplation has been perfected; there is nothing else to be manifested. Furthermore, this is not the object of contemplation for a beginner's mind, but rather the object contemplated by those who have reached the seventh stage of faith in the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).

How could one, having already perfected the perfect contemplation (*yuanguan*) regarding the seated image, then rely upon the physical body (*shengshen*) of the *zang* and *tong* [teachings] to practice contemplation?
Moreover, contemplating the physical body to manifest the subtle marks of the *zang*—this is the way a person of the *tong* [teaching] is led toward the *bie* and *yuan* [teachings].
[The opponent] replies: "This is entirely not the perfect contemplation from beginning to end of the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao).
[I] remonstrate: In the commentary on the title of the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, it is clearly stated that it discourses upon the 'immeasurability of the measurable.

Furthermore, it specifically shows: 'Amitābha is the immeasurability of the measurable. If this present sūtra does not contemplate this body, what then is the point of the instruction provided by the Wise One?"

Is this not to delude the masses? If one follows the Great Master’s interpretation, which maintains that one directly contemplates the "immeasurable within the immeasurable," and further asserts that those of perfect capacity all perceive based on their *karmic consciousness* (*ye-shi*), then this present sutra would consist solely of contemplation upon the environment and inhabitants of the Real Reward Land (*shibao*), entirely lacking the environment and inhabitants of the Land of Common Residence (*tongju*).

Consequently, the principle of relying upon that [common] environment and inhabitants to cultivate contemplation would be untenable. Now, it is said that the *Contemplation Sutra* proceeds from the water...

Once the visualization is complete, one sees that the lands of those realms have already departed; these are all the marks of the environment and inhabitants of the Pure Land of Co-residence (*sahabāsa*).

Those of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanren*) rely upon them to cultivate the Three Contemplations: in Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), all marks vanish; in the Provisional (*upāya*), every mark is clearly illuminated;

and in the Middle (*madhyama*), both vanishing and illumination are simultaneously transcended. If one wishes to distinguish how the Three Bodies (*trikāya*) are realized therein: Emptiness is the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*); the Provisional is the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The "Middle" is precisely the Dharma. Furthermore, one must know that within the contemplation of the provisional (假觀) there are two different levels. In some cases, one merely perceives the eighty thousand marks and signs;
in other cases, one further perceives marks and signs as numerous as the motes of dust in a sunbeam. Because this contemplation is perfected, the stage of attainment is high.
Furthermore, it is said: "Contemplating the birth-body (janma-kāya) reveals the marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) as numerous as motes of dust.

This refers to those of the Shared Teaching who are being grafted onto the Distinct and Complete Teachings; why then is this so restrictive? Could it be that the Distinct and Complete Teachings have no birth-body?

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha has a birth-body which, like that of humans and dharmas, possesses ailments and the like. As seen in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this applies to the four great bodhisattvas and the Buddha Śubhavyūharāja.
Inquiring after Śākyamuni, one says: "Are you free from illness and affliction? Is this not your birth-body (*janmakāya*)?

If it is argued that the Dragon Girl praised the Buddha as having a "subtle, pure Dharma-body endowed with the thirty-two marks," since it is called the "Dharma-body," the Dharma-body is precisely the most sublime of all forms (this interpretation appears in the preceding text of the *Miaozong*).
The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "He has profoundly attained the principle of the Dharma-body, and thus is fully endowed with the marks and signs. The *Ji* (Sub-commentary) [explains this].
Regarding the thirty-two marks: the various teachings list them with differing accounts of how they are attained through cultivation; these mostly pertain to the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*).

As for the true path (*bhūta-mārga*), they are simply manifested through the arousal of the aspiration [for enlightenment]. This is the intent of the *Shuji* (Commentary): it means that while the principle of the Dharma-body is inherently complete, the thirty-two marks of the birth-body manifest fully as that principle.
These are not like the marks attained through cultivation in the various teachings; how could they ever be pointed to as such?

This is precisely the *viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa* (extraordinary mark). It should be said that because the person of the *pariniṣpanna-kāya* (perfect body) realizes that the *janma-deha* (birth-body) is itself the Dharma, every mark is quiescent and equal to empty space.
This is like the moist nature of waves pervading the great ocean; because the Dharma-body is identical to the birth-body, the body shares in illness, and the thirty-two marks appear.
This is like the movement of waves within the moist nature, whose characteristics are not extinguished. If one follows the profound meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*...

The *Yi* (義) states: "Within the soiled garment is the true body, which is the body adorned with necklaces" (*Miaozong* cites this as proof). This reveals that the *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras refer solely to the body of Śākyamuni Buddha alone;
it was formerly clothed in necklaces, and now wears tattered rags—it does not mean that the tattered rags themselves [are the true body].
This is precisely what constitutes the *ratnāvalī* (necklace). If it were not so, would the body upon the lotus pedestal be that of an old bhikṣu? The *Miaozong* asks:
"If this is the *zhunti* (special/extraordinary) form, it ought to be a permanent body. Why, then, does the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) judge the *Guan wuliangshoufo jing* by stating:
'It is actually finite, yet is spoken of as infinite'? The answer is: This is for the purpose of rectifying [the text].
In the commentary, there is an erroneous citation from that sub-commentary. That sub-commentary states in both instances: "It is truly finite, yet it is called infinite.

This is consistent with the commentaries on the *Amitābha-sūtra* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, as well as this very commentary. This is because [the term] refers to both the Large and Small *Amitābha-sūtras*.
It is not exclusively for those of special capacity or for those of sudden enlightenment; therefore, that Buddha manifests the thirty-two marks to universally accommodate all capacities.
He cautioned:
"In all sutras, whenever the term 'Amitābha' appears, it refers only to his birth-body (*janma-kāya*). This is especially true for both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna versions."
There is no mention of the thirty-two marks [in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*]. Why, then, do you suddenly point to it?

Even if the two versions were not exclusively intended for the Sudden Teaching, since we now see that they are indeed exclusively intended for the Sudden Teaching, why does the commentary instead point to the birth-body (*janma-kāya*)?

One must not use the meaning of the two versions to explain the title of the present sutra; this is merely like hanging a signboard over a prefecture—it only confuses practitioners. This is what has been cited for correction.

The meaning is not incorrect; however, Master Yuan should not take the body with mountain-like brows and ocean-like eyes and immediately identify it as the body perceived by those dwelling on the stages (bhūmi).
For he does not likewise take the sixteen-foot body and so forth to be the *sambhogakāya* (honored special body). The *Amitābha Sūtra* asks: [What is the nature of this body?]

Regarding the visualization of Amitābha Buddha, one enters through a single mark or excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). One should simply visualize the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) between his eyebrows until it is extremely clear and distinct.

When the white tuft between the eyebrows is seen, the eighty thousand marks and excellences will naturally manifest. The commentary instructs that one should take the *ūrṇā* mark of Śākyamuni as the object;
whether large or small, it should be clearly visualized. Only when samādhi is attained and the visualization-mind is perfected can one then invoke that Buddha.

One contemplates by means of the marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Quoting the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is said that the *Prajñāpāramitā* is taught for the sake of increasing the Bodhisattva’s *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*;
thus, one contemplates by manifesting the extraordinary physical marks (*kāyalakṣaṇa*). Now, as for these "extraordinary bodies," are they not the *vairocana-kāya* (the Body of Universal Radiance)?

Since that [text] is cited to prove this, it is verified that the eighty thousand marks and signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) are precisely the *vairocana-kāya*. Answer: This is merely a general citation of analogous examples; it is not...
It may be said that the supreme body of Amitābha must be accomplished through *samādhi* before it can be visualized.

For example, the extraordinary physical marks of Śākyamuni were likewise accomplished through *samādhi*. One should take this as the basis for visualization, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"For the purpose of increasing the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* of all bodhisattvas, [this practice] is mostly for those dwelling on the stages of the Distinct and Perfect [Teachings]."
[Sa]. In the treatise, it is clarified that the Buddha with a distinct body (zunte-shin) preaches the Dharma for Bodhisattvas of the Dharmakāya outside the realms.

As for the *Guanjing shu* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra), it states: "If one attains samādhi and achieves the contemplation of the mind, such a person belongs solely to the stage of contemplative practice within the Perfect Teaching."

In the *Vyākhyā* (the *Śū*), the stages of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) are clarified. First, one contemplates the marks of the Buddha, like casting a golden image, until the contemplation is perfected and the Buddha is seen.
His major and minor marks are vast and expansive, like the waters at the end of a great kalpa.

Thus, one knows that the samādhis in these two locations differ in depth, and the Buddha-bodies contemplated—whether as a body born of karma or as a reward body—differ accordingly. One must determine this through the underlying meaning; do not be constrained by the literal text. (Rén)
Ren’ō) respectfully addresses the Great Master once more. Regarding the ten admonitions above, I have cited only the general outline of the *Myōshū* (The Wondrous Commentary);
I do not dare to enumerate all its miscellaneous details. Ren’ō has heard that skillful artifice is not equal to simple sincerity;
therefore, the words from my pen cannot help but be harsh to the ear. If you hold the Buddha-dharma in mind, I pray that you view them with a compassionate heart. Formerly, when I was born...
Gongli Chengtian attained Buddhahood, yet those of the old school regarded this as heterodox teaching. He was once expelled from the assembly and sent away;
however, while standing before the multitude, he assumed a solemn countenance and vowed: "If what I have taught contradicts the meaning of the scriptures, may I [suffer] in this very body."

This immediately manifested as leprosy. Had his words not been in contradiction with the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), he would have wished that at the time of his passing, while seated upon the lion throne and having finished his discourse, he might shake out his robes and depart;
thus the signs of his future repose would have been clearly evident. (Ren’ue) Although my words are unworthy, I have nonetheless imitated the living master.
If what I have discussed regarding the Buddha-body should happen to contradict the purport of the teachings, I pray that I may incur the calamity of white leprosy in this very life.
If one accords with the sacred mind, they will surely vow that at the moment of death they shall depart for the Pure Land. How could one dare not believe in the retribution of fortune and misfortune?
I prostrate myself and request that the Great Master burn incense to bear witness to this. With humble regards, the disciple (Ren’aku) writes.
The Ten Letters of Admonition from Master Yue (Concluded).

The Bhikṣu Zongxian of the White Lotus Society in Taizhou, intending to sell the teachings of the Vehicle, has prepared woodblocks for the circulation of the *Fazhi Yibian* (The Compilation of Bequeathed Teachings by Fazhi) and the *Jiebang Shu* (Treatise on Dispelling Slander).
The Dharma-grandson (Jizhong) has compiled the *Zhizhe Zongcheng* (The Essential Vehicle of the Wise One). Since I began my studies under his instruction, more than forty years have passed.

Whenever I have explained a single passage or expounded a single meaning, I have never failed to rely upon the various sections, flavors, teachings, and contemplations as my standard of judgment. Recently, I have compiled my private notes, entitled the *Miaozong* (The Sublime Commentary).
In the *Jie shi liu guan jing shu* (Commentary on the Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations), regarding the "Contemplation of the True Dharmakāya," it states:

"However, these physical marks are the true recompense-body (*sambhogakāya*) that responds to the Shared Land; they are also called the 'Venerable and Extraordinary' (*zunte*) and the 'Supreme Response' (*shengying*). Yet the commentary says:

"'Dharmakāya' refers to cultivation being identical to the nature, thereby accomplishing the non-active contemplation (*wu zuo guan*). A certain group of scholars has hastily produced the *Yizhang* (Treatise on Meaning), openly contradicting this explanation. Regarding...

Outside the main body of the treatise, he extensively constructs difficult arguments, establishing that the hundreds of thousands of marks and signs of the Avataṃsaka’s treasury constitute the *vairocana-kāya* (the sublime body),
whereas the eighty thousand marks and signs of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, as well as the thirty-two marks of the Lotus Sūtra, must certainly be the *janma-deha* (the physical body).

I then cited those difficult arguments and explained each one in detail. He, however, remained stubbornly attached to his own established position and composed ten letters of admonition (*daśa-vinodana-patra*).
These were criticized for their extreme contradictions and censured for their reversal of meaning and violation of the text, compelling me to revise and edit my notes to conform to his views.
Yet, as for these ten admonitions, they did not follow the correct path of scriptural teaching and contemplation, but merely relied on [his own] body...
The [opponent’s] various arguments are numerous, yet they constitute a "special feature" (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa) that deviates from the perfect intent; not a single point among them is acceptable.
Now, when examined through correct reasoning, those views result in two kinds of slander against our school. Why is this?

Because they determine the marks manifested by the sudden contemplation of this sutra to be the birth-body (janma-kāya), and they determine the foremost body resulting from the revelation of the provisional in the *Lotus Sūtra* to be the inferior response-body (hīna-nirmāṇa-kāya). This...

This is to diminish slander. To claim that the *Avataṃsaka*, with its nature of encompassing both the Separate and the Perfect Teachings, is merely "venerable and supreme," while the two *Prajñāpāramitā* sutras (*Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* and *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*), with their appearance of being "mixed" [with other teachings], are uniquely "transcendent and exquisite"—this increases slander. Because of this destruction of the present commentary, I have incurred this profound resentment.

Fearing that if it is not clarified, it will frequently delude the masses, I have been compelled to compose this "Treatise on Dispelling Slander. My fellow practitioners of the same school must surely understand my intent.
Such is the nature of striving with diligent effort for the Way.
In the *Miaozongchao*, the Dharma-body of the Lotus Sūtra is established as the *zunte* (lofty and distinguished) Buddha; therefore, it cites the *Miaoxuan*:
"The body within the soiled rags is in reality that of the jeweled-necklace elder," as its authentic proof.
The slanderer says: "The *Miaojing xuanyi* states that 'the body within the soiled garments is in reality a body adorned with necklaces.
This is intended to show that the *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras refer only to the body of the single Buddha Śākyamuni; that he formerly wore necklaces and now wears tattered rags.
It does not mean that the tattered rags themselves are the necklaces. If it were not so, then the body upon the lotus pedestal would be..."
"Is it an old bhikṣu?
[The interlocutor] explained: "Our patriarch, the Wise One (Zhiyi), descended to this land of Zhendan solely to proclaim the two subtleties of the *Dai* (Provisional) and *Jue* (Ultimate).
Those who study our own school should restrain themselves and say: 'In the past we wore jeweled necklaces; now we wear tattered robes,' so that the subtle One Vehicle may return to its source."
The Threefold Canon (Tripiṭaka) represents the wondrous teaching of our own school; that it has suddenly sunk into oblivion—how can it be propagated to benefit all living beings?

By wearing soiled garments upon his body, he is in truth a "Garland-Wearer" (Mālākāra) elder, precisely demonstrating the essence of the opening of provisional means and the cessation of the ultimate.

Thus, the *Miaoxuan* says: "The essence of this present sutra is the essence of the provisional and the real of transforming others, which is identical to the provisional and the real of one's own practice. As it is said:

"The soiled garment within is actually the jeweled necklace of the elder. The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) states: "This refers to the opening [of the truth] regarding the soiled garment of the six-foot body.
The soiled garment is precisely the provisional and real [teachings] manifested for the sake of others through the Hīnayāna.

Now, this 'opening' is the identical-in-essence provisional and real [teachings], the jeweled necklace of the elder" (end of passage). This is the definitive resolution of the Śrāvaka Dharma; it is the king among all sūtras. Opening the coarse [is...]
Sublime! Outside of the sublime, there is nothing coarse; therefore, one may speak of the "Gems-Adorned (Mālādhara) Elder. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-vyākhyā* states:

"If one preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one merely manifests the honored and supreme [form]. It further states: "Gathering the kings and great ministers, he establishes the natural bond of father and son, saying:

'You are truly my son; I am truly your father. This is precisely the manifestation of the Honored Extraordinary Body (*vairocana-kāya*) in the *Lotus Sūtra* when bestowing predictions upon the śrāvakas."

Furthermore, within a single cycle of transformation, there have been four instances in which the *viśeṣa-kāya* (the body of supreme excellence) was manifested. Among these, the body [revealed] in the *Lotus Sūtra* is the foremost.
Yet some slanderously claim: "In the past he wore necklaces and ornaments; now he wears tattered robes. This does not mean that the tattered robes are themselves the necklaces and ornaments.

Jingxi [Zhiyi] clearly demonstrated that the opening of the meaning—that the six-foot *dust-robe* is itself the necklaces and ornaments—is not a matter of bestowal (*pradāna*), nor is it different from that.

Regarding the *Fayi*, my ancestor spoke of the "wondrous" precisely in the context of "opening. Since the teachings clearly manifest this opening, you instead claim they are "attached. This slander is even more egregious.

If one follows your interpretation, it would mean that in the past, the provisional and the real were of the same essence (*tongti*), whereas now, the provisional and the real are merely for the sake of transforming others (*huata*).
To slander and insult such a sublime sutra, and to bury the unique teachings extracted by the wise—when I heard these words, it was as if three hundred spears were piercing my heart.
How can one turn one's back on the ancestors and deviate from the lineage to such an extent? Alas, how painful!
And yet you further slander it, saying: "The dragon girl praised the Buddha’s subtle and wondrous Dharma-body, endowed with the thirty-two marks; this is the Dharma-body."
The thirty-two marks are possessed by the birth-body (*janma-kāya*). When has this [birth-body] ever been pointed out as being the "exalted special body" (*vairocana-kāya*)?

This would be in immediate contradiction with your own words. In your explanation regarding the lifespan of the three bodies, you state: "That which arises from the Dharma is called the 'Responsive Body with a Basis';
it is not the birth-body, and must be named the Dharma-body. Now, if the Dharma-body possesses these marks, for what reason do you instead say [the birth-body does]?

This refers to the birth-body (*janma-kāya*). Herein, the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*) is inherently pervasive, whereas the physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are inherently localized. Since their bodily characteristics are mutually contradictory, this is not the meaning of non-duality (*advaya*).
As stated in the *Advaya-mukha*: "The defiled body and the Dharma-body are equal in measure; the defiled lands and the Land of Quiescent Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*) are no different."
