This means that within every single atom and every land there are all lands, and within every single atom-body there are all bodies.
This is precisely the peerless subtlety of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the correct principle and authentic text regarding resonance and response.

To destroy the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*) and establish my own biased views—unless one immediately reforms and repents, calamity will not be far off. Know this, know this! The Dragon Girl wished to manifest the wondrous aspect of the revelation of provisional means; therefore she said:
The Dharma-body is endowed with the thirty-two marks. Each of these marks manifests as the entirety of principle (*li*), because the Dharma-body is all-pervasive.

Since the thirty-two marks are each universally pervasive, the Dharma-body possesses ten thousand virtues; the marks must likewise possess this wondrous body. If it were not so, it could not be called the "Exalted and Special" (Vairocana).
What other body, then, could be designated as the Exalted and Special? Since Śākyamuni has entered within the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna, [this serves as] verification.

It is not a manifestation of the physical form; only when it is majestic and sublime can it be called the "Exalted and Distinct" (zūntè). This refers specifically to the resonance of the Middle Way, whereby even within the body of one *zhànglù* (sixteen feet), there appears an ocean of marks.
This explains the "Exalted and Distinct" by revealing the superiority [of the ultimate] while opening the provisional [teachings] to show that which was inferior.

Therefore, one must understand this: the body seated upon the lotus pedestal in the *Dunbu* (Sudden Section) is the "Exalted and Distinct," for as the provisional has not yet been opened, it still involves cultivation based on conditions (*yuánxiū*). If compared to the [body of the] Elder...

The Venerable Kū (Śākyamuni) opened [the teaching] as the secret and wondrous. Outside of the wondrous, there is no coarse; that which is called the "Exalted" (*viśiṣṭa*) serves to forever eliminate the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Whether the teachings belong to the shared or the distinct categories, they do not at all weigh upon the mind. How could one possibly attain realization through the provisional opening of physical marks?

To erroneously judge the Exalted as being the birth-body (*janmakāya*) is to destroy the fundamental school and obstruct the wondrous understanding. This opening and revealing of the wondrous is precisely the teaching and contemplation of our Patriarch.

Hongzong: If this principle were clarified, the body-teachings throughout the one lifetime [of the Buddha] would be as clear as pointing at one's own palm. Therefore, I shall first resolve this single point of censure.
The *Miaozong* states:
"The 'one-fathom-six-inch' and 'venerable special' bodies established by our school are not fixed; they are distinguished according to the degree of their manifested characteristics."
This is distinguished through the response and stimulus within the ultimate reality (*tathatā*). As explained in the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*) regarding the meaning of the "combined body":

those who perceive only emptiness see only the *zhàngliù* (sixteen-foot) form; those who perceive non-emptiness see the *zūntè* (lofty and special) form. The birth-body (*janma-kāya*) is fundamentally intended for those with the capacities of the *xiàng* (Vaipulya/Shared) and *tōng* (Shared) teachings, while the *zūntè* body responds to the assemblies of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings.

The slanderer says: "In the explanation of the lifespan of the three bodies, it was established that the *janma-kāya* (birth-body) is manifested specifically for the capacities of the *Hīnayāna* and *Triyāna-śrāvaka-pratyekabuddha* vehicles, while the *vairocana-kāya* (exalted special body) is manifested specifically for the great capacities of the *Vaipulya* and *Pratyaksa-bodhi* [Mahāyāna] vehicles. This, then, already distinguishes them based on the responsive manifestations within the realm of reality (*tathatā*)."

The commentary states: You establish that the birth-body (nirmāṇakāya) accords with the capacities of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings, while the Honored Distinct Body (saṃbhogakāya) accords with the capacities of the Separate and Perfect Teachings.

At this juncture, how could you know of the response and stimulus within the True [Middle Way]? If you already knew this, why, upon hearing my words, would you claim that I am merely making up these explanations and that they do not accord with the scriptural texts?
If you know that the Perfect capacity receives the Perfect Teaching, then this is the response and stimulus of the Middle Way.
Why do you slander [this teaching]? Now, observing the Buddha manifested here, it is certainly the *janmakāya* (birth-body). The Sūtra says:

"The Buddhas are the Dharma-realm body (*dharmadhātu-kāya*), which enters into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings, just as when the sun rises in the sky its reflection appears in a hundred rivers. Is it not the case that the entry of the Dharma-realm body is the response of the Middle Way?
Is it not the case that the purity of the sentient beings' minds is the invocation of the Middle Way? This is the resonance and response of the Middle Way; such is the Sūtra.
The Commentary explains this, clarifying it as being like a thousand suns. Why then suppress it and treat it as the response of the True Truth (*satyasaṃvṛti*)? This is the scriptural text;

it first demonstrates the essence of contemplation, so that the practitioner may, by means of this wondrous contemplation, evoke the wondrous response of the Buddha. Therefore, there are eighty thousand marks.

This clarifies the meaning of the *zhuntè* (distinctive majesty) and refutes the slander that [the Buddha] possesses only a birth-body (*janmakāya*); thus, it collapses by itself without need for further attack.

Regarding the *Miaozong*’s specific treatment of the *tongjiao* (common teaching) by dividing the body into two types of response (*yìng*), this is because at this stage, the two principles of the provisional and the real intersect, the two contemplations of emptiness and the middle diverge, and the two consciousnesses of activity and karma arise and cease;
thus, the distinction between the birth-body and the *zhuntè* body becomes clear, allowing for the removal of erroneous interpretations and the manifestation of the fundamental.

Thesis: If one maintains that only by abiding in the [Buddha] Ground (*bhūmi*) and relying upon the *karmavijñāna* can one perceive the *vairocana-kāya* (the Honored Special Body), then those who attempt to have the three faculties enter the semblance stage according to their respective positions would be entirely devoid of the capacity to behold the *vairocana-kāya*.

If this were the case, this teaching would lack the principle of the *saṃbhoga-kāya*. However, while the resonance of the Middle Way is easy to speak of, it is difficult to comprehend. Now, let us attempt...
This is stated briefly to clarify the meaning of "perfect" (yuan). That which is called the "Middle" (zhong) takes non-bias as its significance and transcendence of all dependencies as its function.

If there were a "Venerable and Extraordinary" (zunte) body existing outside of the "Six-Foot" (zhangliu) body, they would be in a state of blazing opposition, and the meaning of the Middle would not be established. It is the same for sentient beings:

if they have a thought that evokes [the Buddha] while being directed toward something external, and further oppose it with another dharma, they do not possess the capacity (ji) for the Middle Way. Since there is no response to what is external, how could there be two responses to a single stimulus? How could this be?
I, Zhang, am of the school that holds that within the "Good," one must certainly not grasp at difference. I dare not fail to rely upon the extensive explanations of Jingxi [Zhiyi].
Therefore, in the *Ten Gates of Non-duality*, from "Defilement and Purity are Non-dual" up to "Receiving Moistening is Non-dual," all are the wondrous responsive resonance of the Middle Way.

The "Gate of Establishing the Dependent and the Proper" states: Within every single atom and every single land, there are all lands; within every single atom-body and every single body, there are all bodies.

Their vastness and narrowness, their excellence and inferiority, are difficult to conceive; their pure and impure locations are inexhaustible. If it were not for the Three Thousandfold World as Emptiness, Provisionality, and the Middle, [this would not be possible].
How could such sovereign function as this be accomplished? Only then does one come to know that birth and Buddhahood are equal, and that self and other are identical;

that phenomena and principle mutually encompass one another. In the section on "Self and Other," it says: "Sentient beings, because they are endowed with the three thousand [realms] by principle, are able to evoke a response;

the Buddhas, because the three thousand are perfected as the fruit, are able to respond. The response is universal and the capacity is universal; their joyful meeting is never mistaken. Furthermore, in the section on "Receiving Moistening," it says: "Things..."

The capacity of the faculty and the response of the teaching are in perfect accord; body and land are without partiality, identical to the eternally quiescent light, the unconditioned Dharma-realm. The four subtle elements share the same essence, and provisional and ultimate benefits are equal.

If the response and resonance of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are considered within the Perfect Teaching, because it reveals and manifests [the truth] according to the timing, there is no faculty that does not attain penetration.

Regarding milk and the two types of cream, those of the three vehicles do not know them; only the person of the Perfect Teaching understands them. The manifestations of the response and stimulus of the Middle Way are roughly as described above.

How can one slanderously claim that the Buddha-body in the *Lotus Sūtra* is necessarily an inferior response-body, or that the marks of the Buddha revealed by the sudden contemplation of the present sūtra are necessarily a birth-body?

Furthermore, you yourself have established that the "Exalted Special Body" (zuntèshēn) responds to the capacities of those of the Separate and Perfect teachings—this was the judgment of the Great Master Zhiyi.
Since this teaching belongs to the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun), it properly corresponds to the attainment of the vision of the Buddha of the Honored Special Body (zunte shen).

Even if there were matters regarding the birth and death of one in the stage of "near-attainment" (buchu), these would not differ at all from the *Avataṃsaka*’s response to sentient beings. How can you suddenly level the slander that there is a difference between heavens?

This [teaching] is disparaged as the "body born of life," while that [other teaching] is praised as the "Honored Special Body. Moreover, you yourself have established that the Mahāyāna "body born of life" is identical in meaning [to the Honored Special Body].
The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The Dharma-body of the Hīnayāna is identical in meaning to the birth-body (*janmakāya*). Is the sudden teaching of the present sutra that of the Hīnayāna?

If it were Mahāyāna, it would necessarily be the Dharma-body. If it were the Dharma-body, it would not be the same as the "exalted special body" (*vairocanakāya*). Discussing them in terms of concession, illusory existence is identical to emptiness;
yet speaking in terms of negation, this is the nihilistic view of the non-Buddhists.

The detractor says: "The *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* clarifies that the primary marks and secondary signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) and the radiance of that Buddha each number eighty-four thousand.

However, the 'Chapter on the Ocean of Marks' and the 'Chapter on the Radiance of the Secondary Signs' in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* state that Vairocana is endowed with primary marks and secondary signs as numerous as the atoms within ten oceans of Lotus Treasury worlds. Thus, what is taught in these two sūtras [is contradictory]."

The distinction between the *utpannakāya* (birth-body) and the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation-body) is profound. Therefore, one should know that beyond the eighty thousand marks and signs of the *utpannakāya* of Amitābha, there exist further marks and signs as numerous as atoms (*paramāṇu*) belonging to his *vairocanakāya* (honored and extraordinary body).
For now, we shall judge it to be finite based on his *utpannakāya*.

Although he possesses a lifespan as vast as the weight of mountains and the drops of the ocean, he nonetheless manifests in accordance with the birth and death of the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) realm. (This passage is from the "Explanation of the Lifespan of the Three Bodies" by the Opponent.)

The commentary states: To study the Tiantai school without relying on its teachings and contemplations, yet to claim that a Buddha with few marks and signs must belong to the *janman-kāya* (birth-body) while one with many marks and signs must be the *sambhoga-kāya*, is a vague assertion entirely devoid of meaning. This is merely a name for a collection of marks numbering as many as motes of dust.

In the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata" in the *Avataṃsaka*, it is now asked: among the various ten bodies in the *Avataṃsaka*, which of these ten bodies' marks is this?
Furthermore, since it is called the "Ocean of Marks," there is nothing about it that does not carry the meaning of the *vairocana-kāya* (the majestic, transcendent body).

To claim that the Buddha of Immeasurable Life has eighty thousand marks and signs is certainly [to refer to] the *janma-kāya* (the birth-body); it lacks any basis whatsoever and contradicts both the text and the principle.

This is because of the underlying meaning (*artha*). As for "contradicting the text," first, it contradicts the original sūtra, which states that the body of Amitābha Buddha is boundless in size and is not within the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings;
this is because its boundlessness constitutes the measure of the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward-body). The *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says:

Because that which is manifested is itself without limit, it contradicts the cited scriptural evidence. The *Śāstra* (Treatise) cited in the commentary uses the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to prove that the dimensions of the body are limitless, stating:
"The *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* was taught in order to increase the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* of all bodhisattvas.
Now, in teaching the *Prajñā*, he manifests the marks of the *vairocana-kāya* (body of supreme excellence), such that its radiance and physical form pervade the ten directions.
This constitutes contemplation. By means of a wondrous and extraordinary body, one realizes the present vision of the Buddha;

this is the mark of the *guǎngpútíxiàng* (Universal Extraordinary Body), which increases the contemplation of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo guān*) and leads to the realization of the stage of semblance (*sìxiāng wèi*) and the stage of partial truth (*fēnzhēn wèi*). For all Bodhisattvas practicing the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, to deviate from this manifest text [would be an error].
To establish this as the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) contradicts the commentaries in three ways: First, the sutras describe its physical dimensions and eighty thousand marks and signs;

these are manifest as the marks of retributive fruition within the *sahā-loka* (the shared world). Therefore, these bodily characteristics are both retributive and responsive (*nirmāṇa*). Yet the commentary specifically states that one contemplates the true *dharmakāya*.

This causes one to know that the two types of cultivation—retribution and practice—are manifested as the very nature [of reality]. Now, the Buddha of Retribution is distinct from the Buddha of Separate Practice;

this is the subtle and wondrous mark of the *tūn-yuán* (dull-perfect) *zhùntè* (special) body. It certainly contradicts this commentary to claim that it is the *shēngshēn* (birth-body). Fourth, it contradicts the text of the *Shíyí lùn* (Treatise on the Ten Doubts), which says:
"Regarding the Buddha Amitābha, whether it be the *dharmakāya* or the *saṃbhogakāya*, there is golden radiance and eighty-four thousand marks."

Within each of the primary marks, there are eighty-four thousand secondary signs. From each secondary sign, eighty-four thousand rays of light are emitted, constantly illuminating the dharma-realm and gathering in those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha (as stated in that text).
Since both the dharma-body and the reward-body have been mentioned, it immediately says that the light of the marks and signs illuminates the dharma-realm;
this is a single thought-moment that suddenly illumines the three bodies. The perfect interfusion of the three and the one accords with the textual meaning of the current explanation of the title.

The *fuchi* (seal of correspondence) states: "Observing the characteristics of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Only then does one see that our own school elucidates the *guṇaviśeṣa-kāya* (body of special qualities).

All texts are of one accord on this point. Next, as for the contradiction in meaning: it is because [the opponent] fails to rely at all upon the reasons for the two bodies of the *niśraya* (basis) and the *pratipakṣa* (response).
Why is this so? It is because the wondrous function of True Suchness (*tathatā*) manifests based upon the two consciousnesses. Therefore, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says: "Function is of two kinds."
First, that which is based on the *shishi* (active consciousness): this refers to what is perceived by the minds of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles; it is called the *saṃbhogakāya*.

Because they do not understand the transformation of consciousness (*pariṇāma-vijñāna*), they perceive [the Buddha] as coming from outside and grasp at the boundaries of form, being unable to know him exhaustively.
Second, that which is based on the *ye-shi* (karmic consciousness): this refers to all bodhisattvas, from their first aspiration until the ultimate stage of a bodhisattva.
That which is perceived by the mind is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body). This body possesses immeasurable colors; these colors possess immeasurable marks (*lakṣaṇa*);
and these marks possess immeasurable secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*). The supporting fruits upon which it dwells are likewise immeasurable.

Its various adornments are boundless according to what is manifested. It is free from the characteristics of limitation; according to what is appropriate, it is always able to maintain itself, neither decaying nor being lost. As it is said:
These merits are all accomplished through the perfuming of the untainted practices of the various pāramitās and through inconceivable perfuming;

they are fully endowed with immeasurable marks of bliss, and are therefore called the *saṃbhogakāya*. Furthermore, it is said [in that text]: "They manifest solely in dependence upon the mind, not departing from *tathatā*.
The reason these two points clarify what is essential lies in the fact that [the former] is "mind-only" while [the latter] is "coming from without. This...
This precisely and analytically distinguishes the two types of causes for retribution and response. This sutra repeatedly demonstrates that the Buddha’s marks appear as manifestations of the mind.
The sutra states: "The Buddha's Dharma-realm body enters into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings.

Therefore, when you contemplate the Buddha with your mind, this very mind is endowed with the thirty-two marks and so forth. It further states: "This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha."

The ocean of the Buddhas' perfect and universal knowledge arises from the mind and its perceptions. Since the sutra has already revealed that the Buddha is a manifestation of mind-only, he is eternally distinct from the objective consciousness that comes from the outside.
Since the Buddha is mind-only, and because the nature of the mind is all-pervasive, the Buddha’s form is boundless and free from the marks of limitation.
The Buddha reveals to the practitioner the method of observing mind-only, so that they may come to see his sublime and wondrous body. For what reason?

For this reason, the eighty thousand oceans of marks are certainly the *janma-kāya* (birth-body). In the commentary on the phrase "the Buddha’s Dharma-realm body entering the mind and thoughts," there are two meanings.
The first states: "As for the entry of the Buddha’s retributive Dharma-nature body, it should enter the perceiving mind.
The Buddha is fundamentally non-existent; he exists because the mind is pure. The second states: "The Dharma-realm is the Buddha’s body; there is nowhere it does not pervade. The Dharma...

The *dhātu* (realms) constitute the essence. As for the *āyatana* (entrances), they refer to the entrance through principle, which is the contemplation of the mind. Furthermore, the retribution of the Buddha-nature and the Buddha-dharmadhātu have an essence that is omnipresent;

this consists of the hundred realms and three thousand worlds, which are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Into such a wondrous essence, one enters the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi).
According to what is manifested, there may appear either the thirty-two marks or eighty-four thousand marks—how could there be only one?
Regarding the marks: if they do not possess the three thousand [attributes], are they not then emptiness, the provisional, and the middle?
If these marks are not themselves the "Venerable and Extraordinary" (zūn-tè), what other marks could be pointed to as the Venerable and Extraordinary? This contradicts the meaning [of the teaching].

To claim that these Buddha-marks are definitely the birth-body (janma-kāya) is to suppress the purely perfect marks of this fundamental sūtra and to exalt the combined and distinct bodies of other sections—effectively taking the feet for the head and elevating the heavens.
This is a particularly grave slander. By cultivating the sublime contemplation of the mind, one reveals the perfect true reality; thus the merit of the school’s essence is established.
Yet, when one looks back upon the discourse on the inverted views regarding the segmented birth-body of the Shared Teaching, it is something that should not even be heard or seen.
The critic says: "In wishing to explain a meaning, one must first rectify the terminology. If the terminology is not correct, the meaning will be distorted and erroneous.
Now, regarding what is called the 'Six-Foot' and the 'Venerable Extraordinary' (zūntè): is the Six-Foot not small? Is the Venerable Extraordinary not large?

If you say otherwise, I do not know whether the Venerable Extraordinary is established based on principle (lǐ) or established based on phenomena (shì). If it is established based on phenomena, how could it..."
Is this not the mark of the uniquely exalted and honored? Although the text is extensive, its intent is concise; the principle is fixed as one, yet the manifestations are fixed as diverse.
It even states: "If the Great [Manifestation] does not appear, it is then the Honored and Exalted.
Thus, for those of the Separate and Complete Teachings, seeing monkeys, deer, or horses is none other than the *paranirmita-vashavartin* (other-receiving) reward-body, for all are the Middle Way.
This is due to the principle of resonance (ganying).

The commentary states: To define the names and explain their meanings, the principle is indeed as it should be; however, these names and phrases must be established according to the Four Reliances (*catur-apāśraya*).
In the *Fahua wenju*, it is said that all thirty-two marks are oceans of marks; in the *Mohe zhiguan*, it speaks of the three types of Buddha-marks.

All are called "oceans. How can one fail to rely upon the perfect and true teaching to correctly explain the meaning of the name "Ocean of Marks" as being honored, supreme, and particularly excellent?

How could one slander the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and this present sutra by asserting that their perfect and wondrous marks are definitively those of an inferior, segmented response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*)?
To whom should such perverse and inverted views be attributed? If it is the Middle Way that is perceived...

Regarding the term "Exalted and Distinct" (zuntè): this name occurs most frequently in reference to the Buddha. Sometimes he manifests a body of great height and majesty to display the marks of the exalted and distinct;
at other times, he displays the marks of the exalted and distinct through his ordinary body alone by manifesting its boundless limits.

If he manifests forms differentiated according to the nine realms, he does not necessarily establish the title "Exalted and Distinct. Although the name is not established, its meaning is nonetheless present. As it is said:
The *Avataṃsaka* clarifies the ten bodies of Vairocana. Does his body of karmic retribution not include [the forms of] monkeys, deer, and horses?
Since he is called Śākyamuni, this signifies the meaning of purity and perfection. Being both pure and perfect, how could he not be the Honored One of Extraordinary Marks?

This is what is manifested according to conditions in the *Awakening of Faith*; it is indeed boundless, free from the marks of limitation, and is able to perpetually maintain itself according to what is appropriate.
That it is neither destroyed nor lost is entirely accomplished through the permeation of the untainted practices of the various pāramitās;
therefore, it is called "retribution" (vipāka). Since it is called "retribution," is this not precisely the meaning of the "Exalted and Distinctive" (vairocana)?

The *Miaozong liaojian* states: "The fundamental basis for the manifestation of the Buddha-bodies of the four teachings is none other than the two principles of the provisional and the real, the two contemplations of emptiness and the middle, and the two consciousnesses of activity and function.
When analyzed according to these categories, the distinction between the birth-body and the honored special body is as clear as pointing at one's own palm."
The critic says: "It is true in principle that the basis for the arising of marks is such; how then could the marks that arise fundamentally be confused?

Now, in discussing the Buddha-body, we are strictly relying on the manifested marks (nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa). How can one turn one's back on these marks and speak only of their underlying principle? I now reply:
If one discusses the fundamental Buddha, then the marks are remote and the principle is intimate. If one discusses the manifested Buddha, then the principle is remote and the marks are intimate.

The principles established by the *Miaozong* (Sublime Commentary) are, in fact, mutually contradictory. To trace them back to the source: the Dharma-body is without marks; marks must belong to the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The response-body possesses both provisional and real aspects, and its marks possess degrees of excellence. When the response-body cohabits with defilement and purity, it properly employs the birth-body (*janmakāya*);

when the response-body manifests as the expedient, the true reward, or the sublime special body (*vairocanakāya*), it properly employs the honored and distinguished body. Those of perfect enlightenment understand that there is but a single Dharma-substance which gives rise to two functional applications. As for these applications...
Because it is identical to the essence (*tattva*), a single characteristic cannot be apprehended; because the essence is identical to its function (*vṛtti*), all characteristics are vividly present.

The commentary states: This appears to be a discussion of principle (*li*) that does not rely on the fundamental school [of the Avataṃsaka], which results in the Buddha’s marks and the ultimate principle being as far apart as heaven and earth. Why is this so?

Now, to clarify the principle of perfect interfusion: it is inherently endowed with the three thousand realms. Whether as principle or fruition, whether as essence or function, there has never been even a moment’s deficiency.

As for the dharma of the three thousand realms, when manifested in the form of a Buddha for the sake of ordinary beings and those of the *zàng* and *tōng* capacities, it appears as if coming from the outside.

Since there is a fixed limit to its scope, it is called "corresponding" (*yīng*). If, for the sake of specific capacities, one manifests the form of a Buddha, although it appears from the mind and arises based on the Truth (*tathatā*), it must still rely on conditions and cultivation;
thus, it does not fully accord with the nature (*dharmatā*) and is merely termed "retribution" (*pāpa*). This applies only to the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.

The Buddha-body is manifested; each and every mark is itself the nature, the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. Since the Buddha has thoroughly exhausted this, his entire being gives rise to its function, such that all things mutually interpenetrate.
Thus, even the marks of the Buddha in the *Avataṃsaka* still involve distinct cultivation, whereas the fruition of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) is entirely the path of teaching.

Therefore, Miaole said: "Only upon reaching the present sutra does one finally know that [the previous teachings] were pointing back to the past; only the Buddha has fully exhausted this"—these words are indeed true.

Therefore, we know that only when one has thoroughly exhausted the thousand suchnesses of the hundred realms is there "one achievement which is the achievement of all. This is the ultimate subtlety of the discourse on the perfection of marks (*lakṣaṇa*) regarding the attainment of Buddhahood.
Among these various scriptures, many aspects are discussed at length, and the manifestation of the Great Body (*mahākāya*) is shown;

yet these are all termed "taking and giving according to the head" (i.e., partial or provisional). Only the *Lotus Sūtra* exhaustively investigates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, and only then can it be called the "pore of calculation" (the ultimate point of reckoning).

Therefore, although both the Separate (Bie) and Perfect (Yuan) Buddhas possess the *zhuntè* (extraordinary physical form), the Separate must rely on conditioned cultivation (*yuánxiū*), and is thus termed "retribution" (*bào*).

Because the Perfect is identical to the intrinsic nature (*xìng*), it receives its designation from the Dharma. Thus, one body is all bodies, and one land is all lands; these characteristics are inherently present in principle (*lǐjù*).

Through contemplation they are perfected, and through manifestation they arise. One should distinguish their intimacy or distance according to the two teachings: in the Separate, the characteristics are intimate while the principle is distant; in the Perfect...
That which is identical to principle is intimately related, while that which contradicts the Buddha’s perfect marks is distantly related to principle; the fault of the latter is none too great.

Therefore, although the ocean of eighty thousand marks in this present sutra constitutes the *vairocana* (exalted) body, they are named the *dharmakāya*. Although these marks have not yet been fully revealed, the teaching already belongs to the Sudden.

This is because for those of the Perfect Teaching in the past, all four [aspects] were secret and subtle. Since the marks are identical to principle, how could one definitively distinguish them as "great"?
Regarding the relative size [of the bodies]: if the *dharmakāya* (body of reality) of the Lotus Sūtra were definitively small, why would it be called "Exalted and Distinct" (*zuntè*)?

The slanderers say: "If even the *Miaozong* (The Subtle Commentary) speaks of the 'name and appearance' of a dung beetle, then upon reaching the ultimate state, for what reason must the name and appearance of the *saṃbhogakāya* (birth-body) be definitively changed to that of the 'Exalted and Distinct'?
This is because the two functions of the permanent and the impermanent are like the pair of birds [in the same branch].
[Question: How are they distinguished? [Answer: The explanation says:
"When one is enlightened, a thousand follow; when one is deluded, ten thousand afflictions arise. Now I shall briefly explain this so that you may discern its general direction.

Regarding the name and characteristics of the dung beetle (*gongqiāng*) up to its ultimate state: this clarifies that the rational nature (*lǐxìng*) is replete with the ten realms (*shíjiè*). Since all are inherently complete within the nature, the nature must necessarily...

Eternally abiding—these ten are all the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). The Dharma-realm has no exterior; every realm universally encompasses all others. Every phenomenon (dharma) is lofty and vast. At the stage of the ordinary person (pṛthagjana), there is only principle (li);

upon first hearing the names, the five grades of practitioners achieve contemplation, and the six faculties begin to manifest their semblance. Through the forty-one stages, the true essence and function are distinguished;

at the wondrous enlightenment of non-duality, one reaches the ultimate equality of nature. Since phenomena and response are perfectly interfused, even creatures such as dung beetles may, by means of provisional [conditions], [attain realization].

If it is true that, whether real or provisional, each and every thing associated with the Buddha—including the five aggregates—is none other than permanence, bliss, self, and purity, then these are the supreme sentient beings and the supreme five aggregates.
Since both possess these four virtues and are further designated as "supreme," how could a single person or a single dharma not be the Honored One of Extraordinary Marks?

Therefore, when the fruit of the three thousandfold world-system is realized, all are said to possess permanence and bliss; thus both name and meaning are manifest and clear. Yet scholars remain deluded of their own accord.

Thus, they take the dung beetle as a metaphor for the perfect fusion of name and reality, desiring to establish the *vairocana-kāya* (the sublime body) as eternally distinct from the *janma-deha* (the physical birth-body).

Examining this, it is evident they are deluded regarding the name and entirely ignorant of the meaning. Furthermore, the six stages of the dung beetle are discussed in terms of vertical progression; these correspond to the two bodies of the Buddha, wherein the provisional is established based upon the ultimate.
To "reveal the real by opening the provisional" is discussed in terms of the horizontal; thus, the nine provisional and one real are also a horizontal discussion of non-duality.

If there is first the bestowal [of the provisional] and later the assembly [at the real], this is also a vertical discussion of non-duality. Although the horizontal and vertical differ, both are simultaneously non-dual.
Therefore, Master Jingxi used the ten non-dualities to reveal the meaning of the ten dharmas. Since one is deluded regarding this principle, one has not yet entered the gate at all.
If one enters this gate, then the two functions of permanence and impermanence can be discerned. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* states:

"What is now called 'wandering in both' means that saṃsāra is both permanent and impermanent; nirvāṇa is likewise so. Whether dwelling below or above, they wander in both and are simultaneously stilled."

Phenomena are identical with principle; principle is identical with phenomena. The two truths are identical with the Middle; the Middle is identical with the two truths. It is not that there are two middles, yet there are two middles.

Thus, the meaning of "traversing both" is established, and the "male and female" are likewise established. Once the meaning of traversing both phenomena and principle is established, [the path is complete].

From the contemplative practice of names and words up to the ultimate realization, both [aspects] are accomplished through simultaneous cultivation; they are fully endowed both horizontally and vertically, without deficiency (as stated in that text).

Regarding phenomena and principle, or the middle and the extremes—though not three, they are three. These three cycles exhaustively encompass the two functions, whether concerning the body or the land.
Whether it be persons or dharmas, each and every one is fully endowed with these two functions. These two functions are non-dual; they mutually pervade and mutually encompass one another.

In the fifth period, this non-duality is revealed and made manifest. For those of perfect capacity regarding all the flavors [of the teachings], all four are non-dual. Therefore, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says:
Although one may cultivate all the meditative concentrations of the various sūtras, until one hears the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, one will always say that everything is impermanent.
Once this sūtra has been heard, even though afflictions still exist, they are as if non-existent; one is then able to benefit all humans and devas.
Why is this? Because one clearly understands that one’s own body possesses the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu). This is what is called "permanence. Furthermore,
The end of this chapter states: "Wherever there are sentient beings who should be transformed, the Tathāgata manifests birth therein.
Although he manifests birth, in reality there is no birth. For this reason, the Tathāgata is called the Permanently Abiding Dharma. It is like the kalaviṅka and ruddy sheldrake birds;
students should know that if one attains only impermanence, one loses the constant function. One who attains the constant function [attains both]. II.

This is accomplished through their mutual integration. If one does not clarify this by relying on the temporal teachings, but instead merely pursues the manifest arising of bodily forms to make distinctions, then the meaning of the two functions—perfect and wondrous—will forever remain submerged.
The slanderer says: "In the *Awakening of Faith*, it is stated that the karmic consciousness (karma-vijñāna) sees the Buddha.

According to the judgment of our own school, this refers precisely to those from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*) and above. Why? Because they see True Suchness (*tathatā*) to a limited degree.
The text below clarifies that these Bodhisattvas, seeing the Dharma-body to a limited degree, are able to manifest the eight phases [of a Buddha]. Thus, it is by means of the karmic consciousness..."
One must see the marks as numerous as the atoms within the Flower Treasury World (*kusumagarbha-lokadhātu*), the body of the truly retributive land of non-obstruction (*samyak-vipāka-asaṅga-bhūmi*).

How could there be the marks of the six-foot [body] with thirty-two major and eighty minor characteristics? Furthermore, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* clearly demonstrates the marks of the reward-body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*), stating: "The body is immeasurable."

Each form is immeasurable; each characteristic is immeasurable. If you claim that a small body which does not manifest as large is the *saṃbhogakāya*, would this not be entirely contrary to the teachings of Aśvaghoṣa?

Furthermore, in the treatise, although ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles are contrasted with the various bodhisattvas, they are distinguished according to the two types of consciousness, which must be categorized as either *vyavasthita* (separate) or *pariniṣpanna* (perfect). Only at the stages of the *bhūmis* and *vihāras* [is this fully realized].
Previously, this also belonged to the *saviṣaya-vijñāna* (consciousness of objects).

Although one knows that all phenomena arise from *tathatā* (suchness) and manifest through *karmavijñāna* (the consciousness of karma), because ignorance (*avidyā*) has not yet been destroyed, there still remain aspects of conceptualization according to specific objects.

The commentary states: *Qixin lun* (The Awakening of Faith) is a treatise that provides a general exposition of the Mahāyāna. Its title designates "Mahāyāna," which implies it should encompass the three teachings of the Vaipulya (Ekayāna) regarding both severance (*prahāṇa*) and realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).

Thus, the *Weimo jing xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) says: "The *She lun*, the *Foxing lun*, the *Weishi lun*, and other such treatises provide a general exposition of the three teachings of the Mahāyāna.

If this is the case, then *Qixin lun* cannot be understood as elucidating only the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) in isolation. If one were to argue that the text speaks of the "accomplishment of faith" (*xin cheng*), [it would still not be restricted to the Perfect Teaching alone].
This refers to the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), which is precisely the first stage, the Dwelling of Initial Arousing of the Mind (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*).

Since it states that one "partially perceives the Dharma-body and is able to manifest the eight phases [of a Buddha]," this is identical to the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s teaching that "at the moment of initial arousing of the mind, one immediately attains perfect enlightenment. Therefore, Jingxi [Zhiyi] judged this to belong to the stage of "partial truth" (*bhūtārtha*) within the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*).

If one discusses it in terms of the contemplative wisdom of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it is equivalent to the Bodhisattva at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) who has first aroused the intention. At...

The mindfulness of difference and the mindfulness of non-difference have no distinct characteristics. Because one abandons coarse discriminative attachment, it is called "similar awakening" (*sādṛśa-bodha*).

Since it is termed "similar," how could it be "partial realization" (*vibhāga-satya*)? There is indeed the stage of entering the *bhūmis*, which is named "partial awakening" (*anurūpa-bodha*). Therefore, these three stages of worthiness (*pṛthagjana*) and the ten stages of sainthood (*ārya*) are clearly distinguished as "true" and "similar";
they cannot be judged categorically according to the positions of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanwei*). The treatise explains "karmic consciousness" (*karma-vijñāna*), stating: "That is to say—"
From the bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment up to the bodhisattva in the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), that which is perceived by the mind is called the *saṃbhoga-kāya*.
The treatise clearly explains that because of profound faith in the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma, one perceives it only partially;

yet one knows that its physical marks, adornments, and so forth, neither come nor go, are free from spatial limitations, appear solely in dependence upon the mind, and do not depart from *tathatā*. Thus...
It says: "If one has deep faith in *tathatā*, one can then see a small portion of the *saṃbhogakāya*. Therefore, it further states that one 'knows its color-forms and so forth.
An-hui takes this "deep faith" as a partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*) and omits the term "deep faith," stating instead that one sees a small portion of *tathatā* itself.
His intention is to align this with the subsequent passage which speaks of seeing a small portion of the *dharmakāya*. One must understand the *saṃbhogakāya*.
The body is its supreme manifestation. Through deep faith in *tathatā*, one is able to see it slightly; it cannot be compared to inferior states.
Because one sees only a small portion of the *dharmakāya*, the deep faith is said to be hidden. Is it not a deception of the mind to claim that one sees only a small portion of *tathatā*?

If one says that the *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*) must perceive the marks of the *ālayavijñāna* as actual retributive fruits (*vipākaphala*), this would openly contradict the two types of retributive meanings established in the treatise.
For the treatise first states: "The body has immeasurable forms; forms have immeasurable marks;

and marks have immeasurable secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). It further states that whatever is manifested is itself boundless and free from the marks of limitation, according to its [manifestation].
It should be understood that these two meanings—being able to constantly maintain and uphold [the Dharma] without defiling or losing it—are summarized as "retribution.
Why, then, do you say that the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) only perceives the marks of the true retribution-body (*vipākaphala*)?

If one does not discuss the meaning of these two kinds of retribution, then one cannot explain the thirty-two marks and the sublime, distinguished body (*vishesharūpakāya*) described in such sutras as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and the *Sātrāntika-sañcaya*. Thus, it would not be so named.

In this general exposition, one should understand that the teachings of Aśvaghoṣa and the Master Zhiyi regarding the meanings of "manifestation" (*shì*) and "opening" (*kāi*) are in profound accord. Why is this?

The *Śāstra* clarifies that regarding the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), ordinary beings with small minds do not know that the manifestation of the Buddha’s marks arises from the transformation of consciousness;

they perceive it as coming from without and grasp at its physical dimensions, thus designating it as the "response body. When it comes to clarifying the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body), it states: "It accords with what is manifested."

It is thus without limit and free from the characteristics of boundaries; according to what is appropriate, it can constantly maintain and sustain itself without being destroyed or lost, and this is termed "retribution" (*vipāka*).
Is this not because one must rely on the provisional (*upāya*) to show the wearing of soiled garments, thereby manifesting the provisional and the real for the sake of transforming others?

Therefore, [the retribution] comes from the outside and takes on the boundaries of form. As for retribution in terms of opening up the provisional, this refers to the transformation of others, which is identical to the single-substance (*ekasvabhāva*) of the provisional and the real.
The *Ratnavyūha* (瓔珞) *Śreṣṭhin* [Sūtra] states that what is manifested according to conditions is itself boundless, free from the marks of limitation, eternally abiding and indestructible;
thus, the meaning of "opening through giving" perfectly accords with the function of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Who, then, has publicly contravened the teachings of Aśvaghoṣa?

Furthermore, it says: "As long as ignorance is not yet destroyed, there still remains the establishment of conceptual discrimination according to phenomena," prior to the stages of the *bhūmis* and *vihāras*.
To claim that all [consciousnesses] depend on the *vastu-vijñāna* (object-consciousness) and that one sees the physical body would further contradict the treatise.

For the treatise clearly states that the *vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative object-consciousness) is reckoned by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) as "I" and "mine," and that it grasps the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

Since this consciousness is produced through the perfuming of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), and because the delusions of view (*darśana-heya-kleśa*) are severed at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), the *vastu-vijñāna* is extremely subtle; for the delusions of view are like forty *li*.

Water. Because the delusions of thought are like a single drop of water. Therefore, in the treatise, from the very first aspiration, one relies on the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) to perceive the physical marks of the Buddha’s body, which is free from all limitations.
As for this karmic consciousness, it arises through the perfuming of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
The treatise explains this clearly; how can you slander it by claiming that the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) still persists as long as ignorance (*avidyā*) has not been destroyed?

Such a view contradicts the Wise Ones and further opposes Asaṅga; it is entirely false speech. Furthermore, you say: "The current school’s assignment of the seven, eight, or nine consciousnesses to the four sages is merely a provisional approach.
You should know that there are those who, relying on the *ālayavijñāna*, also perceive the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body), and there are those who rely on the *karmavijñāna*.

Regarding the statement that "consciousness also sees the Inferior Response-body (*hīna-nirmāṇa-kāya*) and so forth," this intends to apply the analogy of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses to the [first] five consciousnesses (*karma-jñāna*).

This, however, completely fails to understand the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of consciousness and the persistence or cessation of delusions (*kleśa*). Why is this? It is because the sixth consciousness arises through the perfuming of pervasive delusions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) and is severed by those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
The seventh and eighth consciousnesses originate from the Mahāyāna and arise through the perfuming of specific delusions (*viśeṣa-kleśa*), which combine and merge with the ninth consciousness.

The matter is only fully exhausted upon reaching Buddhahood. Although the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) employ the seventh consciousness, they do not know its fundamental nature of joy and aversion;

thus, this discussion is based on the Mahāyāna and distinguishes the three types of persons according to the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*). If explained according to ultimate reality (*tattva*), it is like dyeing gold with earth.

Therefore, both the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are the functional domains (*śakti-bhāga*) arising from the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*); they must not be confused with the phenomenal consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*), because of ignorance (*avidyā*).
The perfuming of ignorance and the perfuming of views and attachments constitute two distinct categories of consciousness, differing in both their general and specific characteristics.

To perceive the Buddha according to principle, yet claim that there is a distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles, is to turn away from truth and give rise to delusion; it is to cling to the roots and branches while completely failing to rely on the teachings, acting entirely according to one's own whims.

If those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) have already eliminated views and attachments, they do not perfume the *saviṣaya-vijñāna* (empirical consciousness); thus, the majestic and sublime forms they perceive are due to [the power of]...
Regarding the *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*): because the teaching has not yet been opened, one merely dwells in a thatched hut.

If, within the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, those at the stage of external ordinary beings (*bālapṛthagjana*) of the Perfect or Distinctive Teachings have suddenly suppressed the five abodes (*pañca-vāsa*), they are able to discern the *karmic consciousness*. Although they know it, because they are practicing emptiness with a mind of central correctness, they are necessarily unable to see it.

It is through the Buddha’s power being added that they see; this addition occurs where it can be added. If the *phenomenal consciousness* (*vastuvijñāna*) is blazing, the Middle Way observation is completely obstructed. Thus it is said:

To claim that this is not the case is to see what is not its proper portion; in truth, there is no such principle. If one distinguishes between the Separate (Bian) and Perfect (Yuan) [teachings], those in the stages prior to the Grounds (di-zhu-qian-wei) perceive the "exalted special" (zunte) form because they rely upon the *karmic consciousness* (*ye-shi*).
Therefore, the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "For the sake of Bodhisattvas prior to the Grounds, the Reward Body (*baoshen*) is manifested; it is not the Self-enjoyment Body (*zishouyong*)."

How much more so regarding the scriptural texts of our own school: the Perfect, the Distinct, and the positions of semblance [of the Distinct] all involve seeing the Body of Enjoyment for Others, which does not reside in just one place.
If one were to use the "true" and "semblance" visions of these two teachings to distinguish between the Ordinary Birth-body and the Honored Special-body (Zhunti), it would be absolutely impossible.

This is because from the stages of the Ten Abodes upward, vision is discussed in terms of the "True," while prior to the Ten Abodes, vision is discussed in terms of the "Semblance. Furthermore, this concerns the vision of the Perfect contemplative practice; how much more so when he himself says:

In the *Avataṃsaka*, ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles of the *Sūtra* and *Prajñāpāramitā* stages are said to be able to see the Buddha’s sublime and extraordinary body (*zunte*), yet it is not appropriate to say that they see it based on the sense-consciousness (*shishi*).
This was originally intended as a reprimand [for their limited capacity]. Now, in this sutra, the Buddha’s contemplation belongs to the birth-body (*shengshen*);
yet you claim that ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles can see the sublime and extraordinary body. How can such a position be established?
The slanderer says: "What the Dragon Honored One (Nāgarāja) praised was not restricted to a small body; why then do you say it merely lists the thirty-two marks?

Moreover, the sūtras do not have a fixed number [of marks]. Since the marks of great height and majesty are resplendent, how can one claim they praise only the *zhànglù* (sixteen-foot) body simply because some of their names are identical to those among the thirty-two marks?
Furthermore, how can one know that the *zàngchén* (dust-mote) body does not possess these?"
[Question: Is it so? [Answer:

The explanation is as follows: If one has thoroughly understood the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* such that the inferior is pointed out as being identical to the superior and constitutes the "honored special" (zuñtè), then this is a slander against one's own understanding;

why need it be stated again? However, fearing that those with biased attachments might mistake what is wrong for what is right, I have briefly provided this response. Since the Sūtra clearly states that there is a "perfect halo" (yuánguāng)...

"One *xun*—is this not sixteen *zhang*? Although this chapter does not explicitly state a fixed measurement, following the previous chapter on Repentance, which praises the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics as taught by the Golden Drum, and after praising the Buddha who was honored in the past, he makes a vow that in the future he may encounter Śākyamuni Buddha;
at night he sees him in dreams, and during the day he describes him as he truly is, enabling his two sons to attain the same realization."
They received their predictions together. The fruit [of this] was realized in this very life. He dreamed of a golden drum; he was taught to repent and taught to praise.

If, in the past, he had praised the golden drum with its myriads of marks and signs, he would have merely been taught to praise the thirty-two marks, which would not have fulfilled his prior aspiration.

This already includes the two sons; for it was because they did not receive a prediction [of enlightenment] that they were excluded. We know that regarding the past and the present, the praise of the Dharma is no different.

Furthermore, in the commentary on the "Chapter on Praise," the four virtues are clarified in relation to the body endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. Since these four virtues are fully possessed, [the body is perfected].
It has been verified that these are not the marks of a physical body; how much more so is this the case for the present major and minor marks?

Their names and meanings correspond exactly with those in the *Dharmadhātu-krama* and the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics. Yet, when compared to the ninety-seven types [of marks] in the *Avataṃsaka*, they do not resemble them at all.

Why must one contort and twist [the evidence] to force them into the marks described in that sūtra? To deviate from the spirit and the principle is to bring retribution upon oneself before long. As the verse of the sūtra praises:
[The] text states: Never has there been a single word [to the contrary]. As for the height and magnitude of the body, by what cause is it so?

It simply takes the extent of the area illuminated by the light as the measure of the Buddha’s bodily stature. Thus it says: "The halo extends one fathom (*vyāma*) and can illuminate immeasurable [realms], like the gathering together of hundreds of thousands of suns and moons.
It further says: "The body emits a great radiance, universally illuminating immeasurable lands throughout the ten directions. It also says: "The Buddha..."

The light is majestic and sublime; its brilliant flames are fiercely intense, capable of completely eclipsing the immeasurable suns and moons. Furthermore, the three instances of the term "immeasurable" (apramāṇa) and the half-verse concerning its majesty all describe this light.
Is it not correct to interpret this as referring to the dimensions of the body? It is like the solar disk illuminating the four continents;
how could one claim that the substance of the sun itself is as vast as a single world-system, while asserting that [the Buddha's light] can only be restricted to a single fathom (vyāma)?
This text [claims] that it harms immeasurable meanings. Since the Sūtra does not state that the physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are immeasurable, how could it have harmed anything?
This is merely your own construction. You correctly praise the *Sambhogakāya* (Honored Unique Body) while simultaneously subsuming the meaning of the *Nirmāṇakāya* (Birth Body), stating:

"The towering height refers to the *Sambhogakāya*; the one fathom refers to the *Nirmāṇakāya*; and the purity of all Buddhas, their subtle wonder and quiescence, refers to the *Dharmatākāya* (Dharma-nature Body)."
The three bodies are a single essence, yet they do not intermingle. How could they possibly be a single, undifferentiated, chaotic unity?
To interpret and explain it in such a manner violates both the text and the meaning beyond measure. To violate the text is to take "light" as the "body. To violate the meaning is...
The two bodies are superimposed. The halo extends one *xun* (approximately eight feet), which, by the standard of the sixteen-foot body, constitutes the *nirmāṇakāya* (birth-body).

Its radiance is majestic and lofty, yet it is also the *vairocanakāya* (body of supreme excellence). This is the birth-body upon which the body of supreme excellence rests; this too is the birth-body.

To emit and manifest the body of supreme excellence is like a theatrical performance. Furthermore, taking the general praise—“subtle, wondrous, and quiescent”—completes the three bodies. Thus, all aspects are fully seen without deficiency.

[Text missing]. Provisionally borrowed [from other systems] to be established. If one follows our own school (the Tiantai), the three bodies are explained based on a single body; they are neither conjoined nor dispersed.

This has already been demonstrated in the *Miaozong chao* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning); now I shall briefly state it further. The three bodies of the Perfect Teaching have as their essence the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*).

The three do not depart from the one; to raise the one is to manifest the three. The hymn of praise by the Dragon King skillfully demonstrates this, even while praising the individual marks and signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*).
Previously, in the general summary of matters and principles, we praised the three bodies and all threefold dharmas, thereby manifesting that one Buddha is all Buddhas;
that the many and the one are inconceivable. This is truly because the Buddhas have never for a moment departed from the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*):
the secret treasury of one Buddha is not diminished, and the secret treasury of all Buddhas is not increased. Thus, there is both the single aspect and the manifold aspects.
It is likewise so. The Secret Treasury is the ocean of the Dharma-realm; there is nothing it does not encompass, and all things are mutually interfused within it.
Since it constitutes the entirety of the Dharma-realm manifested as the thirty-two marks, each and every mark is fully commensurate with the ocean. If one were outside of the six-foot [form],...
If there were dharmas not subsumed [within these marks], how could they be entitled to the name "ocean of marks"?

If one can have deep faith in the words of our patriarch and, relying on the present commentary, explain the thirty-two marks by means of the various oceans of marks, then the meaning of the *zunte* (the exalted special body) will naturally be established.

Thus, the meaning of the three bodies is perfectly realized; it is not necessary to point to a separate "dust-receptacle" (rajas-kośa) form as the *vairocana* or *vairocanābhisambodhi* body, nor is it necessary to project a *vairocana* body from atop the birth-body (*janma-kāya*).
To discuss the one as being the three, it is simply the halo extending one fathom.
Regarding the thirty-two marks: when the Tathāgata’s wondrous power acts for those of the Tripiṭaka vehicle, he manifests them with limitations; this is called the "birth-body" (janma-kāya).
When the Tathāgata’s wondrous power acts for those of the vehicle that enters the particular from the general, he manifests them without limitations;
this is called the "exalted special body" (vairocana-kāya). When the Tathāgata’s wondrous power acts for those of the Perfect Teaching (Vimalakīrti), he manifests each and every mark individually.

This is precisely the fundamental nature; the dharma-gates it possesses are called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Due to three types of spiritual capacities, beings evoke the Tathāgata, who then manifests three kinds of appearances within a single body.
Regarding the depth and shallowness of these three appearances, those who perceive the preceding do not perceive the succeeding.

Regarding the principle that seeing each subsequent [body] necessarily entails seeing each preceding one: once the Honored King Golden Dragon has seen the Dharma-body, he is not lacking the former two.

It is not merely that they are seen together; rather, they are mutually fused and realized as such. This is because all three bodies are secret and wondrous. Although each is individually wondrous, [they are so in their interpenetration].

The manifestations differ according to the objects, yet where they differ, they are constantly fused; where they are fused, they are constantly distinct. Since this is the case for both the characteristics and their essence, it is likewise so for the karmic activities of those characteristics.

This is truly because the person of perfect capacity cultivates the karmic activities of the three characteristics within a single thought-moment and establishes three kinds of conditions; thus, other sentient beings perceive them differently according to their own capacities.
The self-nature is eternally fused. Now, regarding this fusion of the three, we specifically praise the *zhuntè* (the sublime physical form). This *zhuntè* is the *bào* (retribution body);

it is sublimely in accord with the *dharmatā*, yet it responds appropriately to the capacities of sentient beings. To speak of its essential points, the *Zhùnzètèshū* states: "The *zhuntè* is majestic, grand, and magnificent, unlike the ordinary body.
Since [the Buddha] manifests no limitations even within the *zhàngliù* (six-foot) form, what aspect would not be complete? What place would not be reached?
It is not like the ordinary, limited bodies commonly seen by the mundane and the small; therefore, it is called "lofty" (*weiwei*). Its true appearance is distinct from common characteristics;
thus, the commentary explains these marks as being, one by one, "inconceivable oceans," just like the thirty-two marks of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
For this reason, they are named the "marks of the Honored and Extraordinary. Since the Perfect [Teaching] has no separate marks, how could there be anything that is not sublime?
This is the name of the ocean. How could it clarify that the essence of the marks is the primary name?

The merit of this exegesis is truly great. Critics say: "Regarding the body under discussion, whether it is the Dharma-body or not the *zunte* (exalted special) body—this surely has its intended meaning.

Now, principle (*li*) has no fixed location; it is omnipresent within phenomena (*shi*). Since phenomena must be identical with principle, how could the arising [of the body] not be merely the Dharma? It is indeed the essence of principle.

The formless is such that its functional activity possesses form; these characteristics cannot be conflated. How could one take the *saṃbhogakāya* (the body of enjoyment) and indiscriminately equate it with the *vairocana-kāya* (the body of supreme manifestation)?

Furthermore, because the provisional is identical to the real, within the emptiness of the three thousand realms, there is difference without difference. Because the real is identical to the provisional, the three thousand realms appear vividly;
there is non-difference within difference. Thus we know that the characteristics of the provisional function do not err by even a hair’s breadth. It resides in...
The principle may indeed be correct; I hope you will follow it. The commentary states:

If one understands both principle and phenomena, as well as the provisional and the real, they will never be treated as separate. It is because of a failure to understand that the "ordinary body" (*shēngshēn*) and the "exalted special body" (*zūntè*) lead to slander wherever one encounters them.
[One might say: "The three thousand realms are perfectly manifest, not erring by even a hair's breadth," yet [in truth] this refers to the "intentionally formed body" (*yìchéng shēngshēn*) and...
That Honored One and these two [the provisional and the real] are not mutually unrelated; yet one must not fail to contemplate that the provisional is itself the real.

The three thousand worlds are manifestly present; this is the wondrous provisional. This provisional arises because a single realm possesses the ten realms, and these ten become a hundred. This, then, is the Buddha-realm.

It encompasses nine realms; the same applies to the other nine. If the six-foot body does not include the Honored Unique Body (zuntè), then these two bodies within their respective realms would be as far apart as Hu and Yue;
how then could they harmoniously encompass the other nine realms? If they do not harmoniously encompass them, then the three thousand [realms] do not exist.
This constitutes the hundred realms and the three thousand worlds; there is not a single thought-moment or a single speck of dust that is not universally encompassed.

Even the physical retribution-body of an ordinary person is thus; how much more so the response-body of a fruition Buddha—how could it possibly allow for division? Therefore it is said: "The response is universal and the capacity is universal; the joyful meeting is never mistaken.

It is identical to the Constantly Quiescent Light, wherein there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm. This is the resonance and response of the *Lotus Sūtra* and those of the previous Perfect Teaching.

Therefore, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and the *Sāṃkhyāyana* speak of thirty-two marks, this present sutra speaks of eighty-four thousand marks and excellences (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
The wise all say that the ocean of marks in the Great and Small Vehicles is not inconceivable; how could the marks of mutual fusion and inclusion not be called an "ocean"?
Why then take the perfected fruit of ultimate fulfillment and, based on the divisions of deluded sentiment, create a separation and distinction?

If one perceives that the luminous and wondrous provisional [truth] is such that the one is the all, then the provisional and the real are naturally integrated, and there is no separation from the emptiness of *ākāśa*.

Birth is merely identical to the Dharma, yet not identical to the *viśeṣalakṣaṇa* (exalted special marks). This is simply the *tongjiao* (Shared Teaching), wherein the illusory birth-body is identical to the *dharmakāya* of mere emptiness.

If it were identical to the perfect emptiness (*yuan kong*), there would be no sense at all of it not being identical to the exalted special marks. One should seek the principles of the teachings to dispel delusion.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of two birds flying together. You also believe in this principle of the two bodies (*dvikāya*).
It says: The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "All things have causes and conditions. Wherever there are sentient beings who should be transformed, the Tathāgata manifests birth therein.
Although he manifests birth, in reality there is no birth. For this reason, the Tathāgata is called the eternally abiding Dharma. As it is said:
Regarding the *kalaviṅka* and the ruddy sheldrake, the intent of the sūtra is simply that birth is itself non-birth and non-birth is itself birth;

this constitutes the meaning of the two birds being inseparable. Now, considering their cohabitation: manifest birth is the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), and non-birth is the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*).
If this birth-body (*janma-kāya*) were itself the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*), it would constitute the "Exalted Special Form" (*bimbadhātu*). This chapter, however, entirely lacks such a "great body.

It is the multiplicity of marks that constitutes the Exalted Special Form; within the textual sections, it merely indicates that the response-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) is itself the dharma-body, as in the statement: "This body of mine is itself the dharma-body.
Because these two functions—wandering in tandem—are inconceivable, the *Pumen pusa qingwen jing shu* (Commentary on the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra) mentions only the birth-body and the dharma-body.
It is verified that the dharmas themselves are not few; there is no need for the "exalted special" (zunte) form to manifest separately, as its meaning is already perfectly established.

Those who slander [this teaching] say: "The *Miaozong* (Subtle Commentary) takes the thirty-two marks as the exalted special, and also takes the eighty-four thousand marks as the exalted special, and also takes the marks numbering as many as the motes of dust as the exalted special; it further says that they manifest according to whether they are large or small. Regarding this...
That which is not "non-supreme" is precisely the *parabhogika* (other-enjoyment) recompense, which possesses various distinct characteristics.
Those who hold the scrolls at Mount [Tiantai] all harbor doubts regarding this. Previously, the *Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra* cited the statement:

"The three lands—the land of common dwelling, the land of skillful means, and the land of self-nature—are all of wondrous form and the locus of the fruit-recompense of the wondrous mind. It is based on this meaning that [the classification of the lands] was established.
Regarding the "Exalted Form" (zūntè): according to the *Jìngmíng shū* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra), in the Land of Common Residence, there is a distinction between the pure and the defiled;

however, in the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder, there is no such distinction. If even the land of "Remainder" lacks such distinctions, how could the Land of True Reward possess differences in the dimensions of the body or the number of its marks and signs?
Therefore, the inferior bodies established [in that context] need not be manifested here.
"Victorious! As for those who are 'Distinguished and Preeminent' (Zhunti), I request that you verify their bodies by means of the characteristics of the earth;

then it can be known with certainty. The commentary says: Since you do not yet know that principle and phenomena are non-dual, this is not the perfect understanding (*yuanjie*). How then could you believe in this discourse on profound fusion?

The *Miaozong Liaojian* has already demonstrated that the entire substance of the Dharma-realm manifests as the three marks and the ocean-like marks of the Buddha-body. This is the fundamental [nature].
Since these are manifestations of the entire reality of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the eighty thousand and thirty-two [marks] are further called the "ocean of marks" (*lakṣaṇasāgara*).
Because an ocean must be deep and vast, each individual mark is immeasurable and profoundly deep. If the marks perceived did not accord with principle, then principle and phenomena would be divided;

such a state would be unfit for discourse on the Way—how, then, could one be called a person of perfect realization? Therefore, the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) explains the Distinct and Perfect teachings in full detail.
The two types of factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are the dharmas characterized by cultivation. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"Profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, he universally illumines the subtle, wondrous, and pure Dharma-body throughout the ten directions, endowed with the thirty-two marks and immeasurable life.

The *Amitābha-sūtra* says: "Amitābha Buddha possesses eighty-four thousand marks; each mark has eighty-four thousand secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*). Both the *Satyaka-parivarta* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* state the same.

The primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) constitute the ocean of great marks, and the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*) constitute the ocean of minor marks. Since they are called "oceans of marks," how could they be restricted to merely thirty-two?
In the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), this passage is explained by extensively clarifying that there are as many marks as there are atoms in ten lotus-treasury oceans.

This is precisely our school’s clarification that the three kinds of marks are all termed the true marks of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and are collectively called oceans of marks. This serves to refute the [limited] views of other schools.

Regarding the "Universal Mark" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*): it is not the thirty-two marks elucidated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. That which is called the "Exalted and Distinct" (*viśiṣṭa*) is so named because it is identical to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Therefore, this sutra clarifies that the Buddha’s Dharma-realm body enters into the thoughts and mind; "this mind makes the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha.

This precisely accords with the *Aśrayamati-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith), as all things manifest based upon the mind and do not depart from True Suchness (*tathatā*); thus they are called the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Since its three... [text fragment ends].
These chapters are all the true marks of the Dharmakāya. Why then should these two chapters on the *Zhuntè* (Exalted Form) alone not be so?
To slander that which is non-different from the Dharma as being distinct—what kind of transgression is this? If you truly do not understand, you merely incur the fault of ignorance.

But if, after hearing and knowing [the truth], you persist in holding the false to be true, deceiving your own mind and resisting with defiance, you will inevitably invite an evil retribution. O Divine Spirits!

This is clearly manifest; it is truly difficult to escape [this truth]. Now, within the two lands of the pure and the impure, the distinct marks of the Honored One (zūntè xiàng) appear because both the eternal and the non-eternal functions are simultaneously manifested.
Thus, while the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of the Honored One’s imminent *nirvāṇa*, it is only at the conclusion of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* that his eternal abiding (*chángzhù*) is fully revealed.
This is because the two birds rest together and fly as a pair. Furthermore, in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, the four Buddhas descend into the chamber. (From the Commentary).
It is said: "The 'Exalted Unique Body and Unique Wisdom' does not mean that four Buddhas are merged into one Buddha to be called a 'single body.

It is simply designated as 'one' in accordance with the capacity and understanding of sentient beings. [This refers to] the Buddha of the Flower Adornment Treasury, whose physical marks and signs are as numerous as motes of dust, appearing successively as one passes away and another arises."
If one does not clarify these scriptural passages through the two inconceivable functions of resonance and response by means of the Middle Way, they will create obstacles at every turn.
As for those who "cling to their scrolls" and all harbor doubts—observe how firm and unyielding your attachment is; if you follow along with my words, you will surely cease to doubt.
Regarding the statement that "the three lands are all places of the retributive fruition of wondrous form and wondrous mind," if one is able...

The names "wondrous form" (*miao-se*), "wondrous mind" (*miao-xin*), and "fruition-retribution" (*guobao*) are correctly established; their meaning is self-evident. It is precisely because they are inconceivable that they are termed "wondrous.
As for this wondrous form and mind being "fruition-retribution," it is that which is obtained through long-term cultivation of karmic practice.
That this fruition-retribution pervades the three lands (*san-tu*) means that, as stated in the *Qixin lun* (Awakening of Faith), whatever is manifested is itself boundless and free from division.
The sovereign power of the state is always able to maintain itself, neither being destroyed nor lost, according to what is appropriate.

All such things are accomplished through the permeation of the untainted practices of the various *pāramitās* and the permeation of the inconceivable; therefore, they are called "retribution" (*vipāka*).
If it does not pervade the three lands, how can it be called "according to what is appropriate"?

If it is not formed by the permeation of the principle of practice, how can its wondrous form and wondrous mind be considered anything other than the retribution of the *vairocana* (Universal Illumination) body? Since even the six-foot form in soiled robes is termed "exalted and special" (*zunte*), one can verify that there are no few among the various responsive and transformational bodies.
This is precisely what is meant by the name "the ten-body *vairocana*. If one were to stubbornly insist on [limiting] the lands...
