Regarding the superiority or inferiority of the upper and lower bodies, both the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras do not refer to the *viśvabhaumika-rūpa* (the majestic,
transcendent body). Critics claim that whenever this school speaks of the *viśvabhaumika-rūpa*,

it invariably refers to the body seated upon the Lotus King Pedestal or receiving its office in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, and does not actually refer to the body endowed with eighty-four thousand marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
Therefore, it is known that this body is exclusively the supreme transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) born in the Pure Land of Sukhāvatī, and does not extend to other lands (and so forth).
The commentary states:

Regarding the sublime and extraordinary transformation-body, one must determine right and wrong based on the capacity of the recipient and the teaching; it specifically refers to receiving office upon the lotus throne.
Regarding this body as the *vairocana-kāya* (the Universal Body), it would cause those in other places to see only the *janma-kāya* (the birth-body).

The "tattered robes" of the *Lotus Sūtra* would never receive the revelation [of their true nature] and would instead become mere necklaces of jewels. If the practitioners of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanren*) had previously spoken of the four bodies, they would not have established the secret and wondrous [teachings].

How could this only obstruct the various other sections [of the canon]? It would also suppress the *Avataṃsaka*, for by specializing in the Lotus pedestal as the site of *nirvāṇa*, it would only then be... [complete].

Regarding the *zhuntè* (extraordinary body): if there were a thousand billion [bodies], yet they did not realize the principle of quiescence, they would all be *shēngshēn* (birth-bodies). You maintain that the *zhùchén* (dust-motes) constitute the marks of the *zhuntè*;
does the body beneath the tree possess these marks? Therefore, the "Chapter on Ascending to the Summit of Mount Sumeru" states:
"At that time, by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, throughout all worlds in the ten directions, in all four continents, and in Jambudvīpa..."
In the midst [of each tree], they all saw the Tathāgata sitting beneath it, with a Bodhisattva by his side;

through the Buddha’s spiritual power, each preached the Dharma, none of whom failed to think, "I am always in the presence of the Buddha. At that time, the World-Honored One did not leave any of the bodhi trees, yet ascended Mount Sumeru toward the palace of Śakra.
Is this not proof that the *Avataṃsaka* is the manifestation of hundreds of thousands of millions of response-bodies?

As for what has been said: since this body is perceived as the *viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa* (exalted and distinctive) form by those of both the distinct and perfect capacities (*bhedaka-vartula-avakāśa*), why must one point exclusively to the body that receives its office upon the lotus pedestal?
It is like the four Buddhas of the four directions descending into the chamber of Śraddhālakṣaṇa. The commentary states:

"If one sees the four Buddhas as identical to the *viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa* body—wherein a single body is a single wisdom—this is precisely the eternal body (*nitya-kāya*). This is because the assembly of disciples is one. If one sees the four...

The Buddha. The Buddha’s bodies are not the same; these are the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-transformation bodies). Because his disciples are numerous, it is known that [the term "disciples"] refers specifically to the assembly of distinct and perfect bodhisattvas.

When it says "disciples are few," it refers to the *Hīnayāna* (Tripitaka) and *Śrāvaka* (Shared) vehicles of the three vehicles. When it says "disciples are many," it refers to those who have the fundamental response [of the Buddha].

If its body were eternal, it would be called the *viśiṣṭa-kāya* (Distinguished Body). As a response to that which has no fundamental basis, the body is impermanent; thus, it is not the *viśiṣṭa-kāya*.

Regarding the capacity of the audience and the definitive teaching, the categories of the *janma-kāya* (Birth Body) and the *viśiṣṭa-kāya* exhaust all meanings. It is definitively established that this refers to those on the lotus pedestal and those who have received their office.
The meanings [of these positions] are largely contradictory. This is because the *Lotus Sūtra* states that the thirty-two marks constitute the "exalted" (or "special") body (*zunte*).

The Commentary says: "The response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) also enters the many-jeweled stupa of Śāriputra; its body is not truly majestic, but it is only because the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) possesses the marks that sentient beings with perfect faculties perceive it as such.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* repeatedly identifies this as the exalted mark. Furthermore, if one stubbornly insists that the Buddha...
The claim that the manifestation of the Great Responsive Vision (da-jijian zunte) constitutes a failure of resonance between the stimulus and the response is incorrect.

For example, when the four Buddhas descended into the chamber to encounter the distinct capacities of the Separate and Perfect vehicles, it was necessary to unify the four into a single Buddha before the disciples could perceive the wisdom of the one body.
If this were the case, why does the sutra state: "At that time, Xinxiang heard these four Buddhas proclaim..."?

It is taught that the lifespan of the Tathāgata is immeasurable; one should have deep faith and understanding in this, even to the point where it says: "At that time, the four Tathāgatas suddenly disappeared.

One must know that this was a response to the specific capacity and conditions [of the practitioner]. Having seen the One within the four, this is the Buddha’s miraculous manifestation. Regarding the realization that there is no limit to the small body, it is not that the Buddha is incapable of responding.
Since the resonance between the response and the stimulus has already been established in seeing the One within the four, how could it be otherwise when the inferior perceives the superior?
The principle of resonance (ganying) is manifest; there is no need for confusion regarding it.

Critics claim that the thirty-two marks [of the Buddha] within the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* are merely the body of Amitābha as he responds to other lands, used here as the object of contemplation for beginners.

The commentary states: Since you have already firmly maintained that what is revealed by sudden contemplation—the sixty trillion nayutas of yojanas and the eighty-four thousand marks and signs of radiance—is the true Dharmakāya Buddha, this is merely the appearance commonly seen by ordinary beings and followers of the Hīnayāna.
This would be diametrically opposed to what is taught in the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra* regarding ordinary and inferior beings constantly seeing their own bodies;

as it would obstruct my doctrine, it must be moved elsewhere to another land. One should not contemplate such a teaching, for it contradicts the text and subverts the meaning, slandering the Buddha and misleading others.
That sutra states that Amitābha Buddha possesses the thirty-two marks and resides within the Jewel Hall of Sukhāvatī, preaching the sutra for the bhikṣus.
This sutra clearly explains: "Those who wish to direct their resolve toward rebirth in the Western Land should contemplate a sixteen-foot image upon the waters of the pond.
The *Mahāvaipulya* [Sukhāvatīvyūha] Sutra further states that in the land of An-yang (Sukhāvatī), there is a bathing pool belonging to the Buddha.

It is forty-eight thousand *li* in width. A small lotus flower is as large as a chariot wheel; how much more so for the King Drum-Sound (*Duṇḍubhisvara*) and other sutras, which all describe the environment and inhabitants of Sukhāvatī.
Although that land is pure and superior, it merely distinguishes the relative weight of the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya*) compared to this Sahā world.

How could it be compared to this sutra, which exclusively elucidates the Dharma-realm revealed through the wondrous contemplation of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*), and the majestic proportions of the *Vairocana* body?

The marks and embellishments (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana) are transcendent and extraordinary. If one takes the contemplative instructions of the wise as the standard, this sutra is purely and perfectly complete.
In contrast, the *Avataṃsaka* combines the distinct and the inclusive; their superiority and inferiority are thus evident.

To suppress the exalted and distinctive Dharmakāya and instead present it as the segmented birth-body perceived by the Hīnayāna is merely to follow one's own arbitrary whims; such a shift even applies to the thirty-two marks of the Pratyutpanna Samādhi.

They shall be transferred to other lands. If the Buddha-bodies in the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* must be moved, whether small or large versions, then the sixteen-foot image by the pond described in this sutra, as well as the Buddha-bodies seen in the middle three grades [of the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*], must all likewise be relocated.

How could it be that only the environments and inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*) mentioned in various expositions are moved? Aside from the bodies and thrones of the Three Holy Ones, all the environments and inhabitants discussed in the Sixteen Contemplations must also be transferred.
All must be moved to other lands, for none of them accord with the Buddha’s true reward-body (*dharmakāya*). This is the error of contradicting the texts and背离ing the meaning.

Now, when one sets the mind and establishes practice based on the holy words of the Buddha, one should contemplate the thirty-two marks with utmost sincerity and discernment as they exist in *Sukhāvatī*.
How could it be expected that these marks would reside in another land? Thus, all the practices and methods of the various sutras [would be rendered inconsistent].

This results in error and deviation. One directs the visualization toward the West while the object resides in the East; since both the objective realm and the subjective mind are thus distorted, rebirth there becomes impossible.
This is because the sutras do not state that one may borrow the marks of another Buddha as the object of contemplation, nor is there any instruction from the Four Reliances to do so.

If one were to follow the present sutra’s description of the *ūrnā-kośa* (the white tuft between the eyebrows), it would be difficult for those at the initial stage of practice to visualize. Therefore, the wise clearly recognize that one should borrow the *ūrnā-kośa* of Śākyamuni Buddha [as the object].
Small. A practitioner of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), having understood that the inferior is employed to manifest the superior, avoids the error of a discrepancy between mind and object.
This [otherwise] would be the fault of slandering the Buddha and misleading others; it is surely no trivial matter.
The slanderer says: "In the eight phases [of a Buddha] in the *Avataṃsaka*, each individual phase contains all eight phases; thus, there is no meaning of 'Successor' (*upapadya*).

As for what is called a 'Successor,' it must refer to the various Buddhas manifesting in a body born of分段生身 (*bheda-janman*)—only when a preceding Buddha enters extinction and the succeeding Buddha arises does a 'Successor' exist. The bodies in the *Avataṃsaka* are a single body and wisdom, just like..."
"Space has no name, nor does it possess distinctions such as marks, signs, or lifespan. The commentary states:
When one wishes to refute or establish a point, one must seek the meaning of the text. Why then do you employ false speech to slander the Honored Scripture?

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* begins by stating that [the Buddha] was in the kingdom of Magadha, at the site of the Aranya practice, beneath the Bodhi tree, having first attained perfect enlightenment. If...
It is not a stage for those in their final birth (abhisambodhi-bhūmi), so how could it be called "just newly accomplished"? Furthermore, the "Chapter on Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru" states:
"Kāśyapa Tathāgata, endowed with great compassion, was the most supreme among all auspicious ones; that Buddha once came to dwell in this hall, and therefore this place is most auspicious.
Kanakamuni, possessing unobstructed vision, was the most supreme among all auspicious ones; that Buddha once..."
"Come and enter this hall; therefore, this place is most auspicious. With these ten verses, he praised the ten Buddhas who had previously passed away.
The gods of the Yāma heaven likewise praised ten Buddhas with verses; those of Tuṣita and Paranirmita-vaśavartin did the same, each praising ten Buddhas.
If it were not the case that former Buddhas have already passed away and subsequent Buddhas arise in succession, how could there have been forty Buddhas prior to Śākyamuni,
whom Sudhana encounters in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter and from whom Maitreya Bodhisattva fully describes his future birth in this Jambudvīpa realm?
In the kingdom of Magadha, at the village of Kuṭa, in a brahmin household, I dwell here within this great multi-storied pavilion.
This is for the purpose of bringing to maturity those gods who were my companions in Tuṣita Heaven, and also to instruct Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Those whom I have sent forth have been made to attain full awakening; therefore, they pass away from this life and are reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.

My vow fulfilled, I shall attain Bodhi. Since you and Mañjuśrī have both clearly seen me as described in these texts, how can you slanderously claim that there is no meaning of the "Successor" (Upapadya)?
The passage concerning the "Assistant in the Flower Ornament" (*Avataṃsaka*) is already thus; such being the case, [the Buddha] possesses the marks and signs as numerous as motes of dust.

The Buddha must be a body subject to the arising and ceasing of the segmented [existence], a response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) that dwells together with all Mahāyāna practitioners, and there is not the slightest difference between them.

One should know that when those of the Separate and Perfect Teachings perceive the Buddha through their *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*), although it is indeed a response-body, it is in no way different from this: one body and one wisdom.

This is because, having fulfilled the fruit of one's own practice, the *karmic consciousness* has already perished; thus, they share the same essence as the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) with all Tathāgatas, reaching ultimate perfection.

It is eternally abiding, with no distinction between self and other. Furthermore, it is identical to the Buddhas in arising for the sake of benefiting others; when the conditions for establishing karmic affinity have matured, it universally responds to all sentient beings.

Appearing at the nine assemblies according to their capacities, it manifests the ten bodies. Through the five periods and four teachings, it displays the appropriate dignified deportment for each stage.

Whether in this world or other realms, it proclaims the Dharma with a single voice. Therefore, the ocean of marks of the *Avataṃsaka* and the ocean of marks of the present Buddha are merely manifestations of retributive fruition.

To what extent does this differ from that manifestation? The merits of the ten realms are inexhaustible; therefore, the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana) are numbered according to the atoms of the ten Flower Treasury worlds (*kusumagarbha*).
Now, because afflictions (*kleśa*) are purified within the causal stage, the Buddha’s primary and secondary marks are numbered at eighty-four thousand.
Thus, the *Mahā-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Mohe zhiguan) unifies the thirty-two marks with the eighty-four thousand atoms of the Flower Treasury. III.
The quality of these [images] is excellent; they are all produced through the cultivation and realization of the stages of the path of the Distinct, Perfect, and Single Reality (yuan-shi).

They are collectively termed "Ocean of Marks" (*xianghai*). In contrast to and in opposition of the *zang* and *tong* [teachings], these marks are not merely extraordinary; one must distinguish the Buddha-body through both teaching and contemplation.

To claim that the difference between them is merely a matter of degree—denigrating the fewer marks as the "birth-body" (*shengshen*) and the more numerous as the "exalted body" (*zunte*)—is to slander the Dharma and harm sentient beings; no fault is greater than this.
As for those who slander [this teaching], they say: "If one compares the Buddhas perceived through the four teachings of this land with that Buddha, he is indeed a 'Universal Buddha' (Sambhogakāya).
This is because the Buddhas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) sometimes manifest bodies of great height. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites...
The *Guhyakapada-sutra* states: "All humans and devas perceive the physical dimensions of the Buddha as being either ten *li* or even up to ten billion *li*.

The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Vimalakirti-nirdesa*) definitively identifies this as the body of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*). It further states: "The *Amitabha Sutra* and others are likewise subsumed under the Buddha [of the Shared Teaching].

The clear evidence is found here; how could one possibly maintain a different interpretation? Thus, we know that Amitābha’s supreme response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) accords with the shared characteristics of Śākyamuni.
It is certainly not the image of the Samantabhadra-śānta (Universal Wondrous Tranquility) of the Separate or Perfect [Teachings], because it possesses numerical limits and is not without boundaries.
However, since this land is defiled, [the Buddha] manifests only in accordance with the times; whereas in that land, which is utterly pure, the eternal body is thus.

The commentary states: The scriptures and their commentaries are clear and manifest; the teachings and contemplations are explicit and well-known. Yet, you openly contravene them, suppressing the Perfect [Teaching] to reduce it to the Partial.

This cuts off the life-force of the wondrous contemplation of those who practice according to the path—how tragic, how tragic! The scriptural text reveals that the Buddha-dharma realm-body enters into the thoughts and mind.
It further says, "This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. These are the words of the scripture, demonstrating the essence of perfect contemplation.

The eighty thousand marks and signs manifested therein—on what basis are they instead identified as the Buddha-body of the Shared Teaching? Furthermore, the Commentary clearly judges this to be the Sudden Teaching;
yet it is not the Sudden teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* flavor, but is in fact the Sudden teaching of the Vaipulya (*Brahmajāla*) contemplation. To claim otherwise is erroneous.

The *Miaozong* (Exquisite Commentary) contradicts both the teachings and the contemplative practice; therefore, I specifically offer this admonition and clarification. If you follow this advice, then I shall establish [this work], for one who slanders the Buddha and reviles the Patriarchs is an extremely evil person.

Can such words of admonition be trusted? Furthermore, the *Fuxing* (Subsidiary Records) of the *Zhi guan* explicitly states that the eighty thousand marks and signs of the Contemplation of Immeasurable Life are identical to the marks and signs of the Flower Garland Sūtra (*Avataṃsaka-sūtra*), which number as many as the motes of dust in the ocean of the Dharma-realm. This is a distinct [point].
The Dharma-body accomplished through the *Yuandao pin* (Chapter on the Perfect Path) is the true reality that refutes the characteristics of the *Zang* and *Tong* [teachings].
Since these are not extraordinary, how can you arbitrarily claim they are certainly not the image of the *prajñā* of the *Bie* and *Yuan* [teachings]?

What the sutra text demonstrates—that it is sixty million billion nayutas of yojanas—is for the purpose of establishing the contemplative method of the "semblance stage" (*sidi*). However, this is the mind-activity of the *dharmadhātu*-mind; this is the verification.
It is not that the objects seen by the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (active consciousness) come from outside; they are, in reality, the bodies perceived by the *karma-vijñāna* (karmic consciousness).
Whether large or small, they are all without limit. Even a body sixteen feet tall is itself without limit, let alone that great body.

Although the sutra indicates the dimensions of the body in terms of *yojana*, it also states that the body of Amitābha Buddha is boundless in measure; this perfectly accords with the *Awakening of Faith*, which says that [the manifestation] follows what is appropriate.

To manifest [the Buddha] as having no boundaries is what is called the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya). The Commentary (*Śāstra*) cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, stating that the radiance, color, and form pervade the ten directions;

this is taken as the object of contemplation for the "increasing mindfulness of the Buddha. To suppress the "Exalted and Special" (Vairocana) body and treat it as the "Birth Body" (Nirmāṇakāya) because one’s concentration is rooted in the view of self is to contradict the sutras, contradict the commentaries, and contradict the cited evidence. If you do not reform your mind, you will incur an evil retribution. Regarding this...

Regarding the statement that the *Contemplation Sūtra* is also subsumed under the Buddha [teaching], the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) repeatedly identifies the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* with its forty-eight vows as being the *Contemplation Sūtra*, because in that sūtra the Buddhas are seen equally by those of the Three Vehicles.
Master Jingxi would certainly not have specifically contradicted this. Now, this commentary takes the Buddha-body of the Sudden Teaching and subsumes it within the Shared Teaching;
furthermore, it is not content with viewing the Shared Teaching as merely the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), but rather reveals it as the Honored and Special Body (*viśiṣṭa-kāya*).

This refers to the meaning of being "received. It was not that the spiritual consciousness was unaware; rather, it has now voluntarily submitted. How much more so for a distance of ten billion *li*, where the cognitive consciousness (*shishi*) can perceive the matter?
As for sixty million billion *nayuta* *yojanas*, this is the realm of the karmic consciousness (*yeshi*), which is beyond reach.
Even when one perceives the various distinctions among the heavens, they remain obscure; as for the measure of their boundless extent, it is simply beyond the reach of faith.

The *Myōshū* (Exquisite Commentary) states: In the *Lotus Sūtra*, when the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara was about to come to this Sahā world from the Land of Pure Light Adornment, that Buddha cautioned him, saying:
"Your body is forty-two thousand yojanas in height, while my body is six million eight hundred thousand yojanas.
When you go to that land, do not conceive an inferior notion regarding that Buddha or the bodhisattvas; for that buddha-land..."
He expounds only the sudden teaching and exclusively benefits bodhisattvas; therefore, he manifests only a lofty and great body.

Miao-yin (Ghoṣadatta) knows the assembly led by the Buddha, yet they do not understand the subtlety of the opening of the provisional means in this Sahā world. Consequently, they hastily disparage the Buddha as being definitively small.
Thus, [the Buddha] entrusts Miao-yin to guide those who have not yet attained realization, intending to lead them to the insight that what appears inferior is in fact supreme. This is the secret.
This is merely the skillful means of the Wondrous One.

Those who slander [this teaching] say: "If it is stated that all those of the Perfect Teaching (yuan-jen) rely on the karmic consciousness (ye-shih) and all perceive the Honored One with his distinctive marks (zun-te), and if the Pure Light were purely expounding the Sudden Teaching (dun-jiao), how could there be anyone who has not yet attained the superior state within the inferior? They further cite the *Ten Doubts Treatise* (Shi-yi lun).
In the Land of Amitābha Buddha, there are exclusively bodhisattvas who serve as excellent companions. Furthermore, it is said that there is no mind of the two vehicles there;
it is purely the One Great Vehicle. This means that since the Triple Vehicle is not taught in An-yang (Sukhāvatī), the Buddha-body therein is entirely devoid of any inferior qualities.

The commentary states: In the Land of Pure Light, the assembly consists solely of bodhisattvas; it is known that [the Buddha] there expounds only the Sudden teaching. This is appropriate for manifesting his supreme body.
However, the capacities of those to whom he addresses himself vary in their levels. Those of high station are thoroughly conversant with both the Sudden and the Gradual from beginning to end.

As for those of lower station, their contemplation of the Sudden is not yet profound. Their mastery of the skillful means employed in other lands—such as the Bodhisattva of the Fragrant Multitude—is not so.
I recognize those of inferior capacity who do not understand the provisional application of skillful means; therefore, they come to this land to study the practice of the two wheels [of Dharma].

How could it be that in that land they do not receive the Sudden Teaching? Furthermore, just as those who enter the *Avataṃsaka* in this land are inferior to those who enter the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is because they have not yet undergone the process of refinement and maturation.
Moreover, even those who previously received the Perfect Teaching may still regard the Perfect as something distant at the initial stage of their practice.

Because it is partial, one must clarify and reveal [the full meaning] and so forth. How can you claim that [the teaching] was received as sudden? Is there anyone who does not understand that what is inferior here is actually superior?

This is merely using a narrow perspective to challenge a universal principle. According to the *Ten Doubts Treatise*, the statement that "Pure Land is purely great" is due to a failure to recognize the pedagogical methods established by the Four Reliances.
Furthermore, the *Ten Doubts* is an explanation of the Sixteen Contemplations provided by the Great Master (Zhiyi); how could it be anything else?

Regarding the remoteness of people, it is frequently said that because those Buddhas were accustomed to those of small capacity, they manifested the Dharma of the Śrāvakas so that they might achieve small fruits.
Thus, the *Miaoxuan* states: "If the precepts are lax, the vehicle is also lax; if they are urgent, it is a defiled land.

This is because Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas together constitute the Saṃgha. Because the precepts are lax, the land is defiled by the five turbidities; because the vehicle is also lax, this is the opening of the three [vehicles].

Because the vehicle is also urgent, this reveals the One Vehicle; this refers to the Sahā world. Regarding "the precepts are urgent while the vehicle is both slow and urgent," this refers to the Pure Land.
Because the precepts are urgent, it is free from the five turbidities. Because the vehicle is slow, it opens up the three vehicles; yet because it is also urgent, [it leads to liberation].

This reveals the One Vehicle; it is the realm of An-yang (Sukhāvatī). Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-ṭīkā* states: "In the realm of An-yang, the trees preach suffering and emptiness, and the people attain arhatship.
Since it does not mention 'vows,' one can verify that this land is not [a land of] high [aspiration].

Although the land of Flower-Light Buddha is not an evil age, because of his original vows, he preaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles. The Three Vehicles in An-yang are not preached as a fulfillment of a vow, but rather for..."
This treats of turbidity; however, while the turbidity is slight, it is not entirely absent. Therefore, it is said that it is "not high.
How could those who are habituated to suffering and emptiness see the ocean-like marks of the dharma-realm, sixty million billion nayutas of yojanas in extent, upon reaching that place?

It should be known that the rank of the one who perceives is not low; this refers to the stages of the nature-seed (*prakṛti-bīja*) and the path-seed (*mārga-bīja*), which are seen by the eye of wisdom.

Even if one employs the perfect contemplation (*pariniṣpanna-vipaśyanā*) at the initial stage, though it may suddenly suppress and suddenly perceive [the object], because the contemplation is shallow, the majestic and extraordinary body (*vairocana-kāya*) [is not fully revealed].
Although it has not yet reached greatness, one is nonetheless able to understand that there are no boundaries.

Therefore, in explaining the title and clarifying the contemplative practice (*guanxing*), even though many things are seen wherever one encounters them, these are discussed from the perspective of the Buddha-body in the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi*. Thus it is said: "To survey everywhere, there is nothing that is not the realm of the Buddha."
In the *Ten Doubts Treatise*, it is stated that those in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*) consist exclusively of bodhisattvas who lack the minds of the two vehicles.

This is based on the fact that they have already dedicated their roots of goodness and do not stubbornly cling to the Lesser Vehicle, unlike those in this land who definitively seek eternal cessation.

Furthermore, if one follows the teachings of the Great Master Zhiyi and cultivates the Perfect Contemplation (*yuan-guan*), upon reaching that land, one will always have the great bodhisattvas as virtuous companions. Its...

These words are not false. The frequent mention of the eighty thousand marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) within the treatises is for the purpose of encouraging the cultivation of Mahāyāna contemplative practices.
Furthermore, one must not hold the view that because there are no such texts in other teachings, Amitābha is clad in tattered rags, or that his land does not employ the Hīnayāna at all.

In brief, tattered robes represent two kinds of patience: patience toward sentient beings and patience toward phenomena. Patience toward the affliction caused by sentient beings is called "patience toward beings" (*sattva-kṣānti*);

patience toward the affliction caused by non-sentient things is called "patience toward phenomena" (*dharma-kṣānti*). Since there are no wicked people or predatory beasts there, and because of the absence of cold, heat, wind, or rain, these two kinds of "robes of patience" are not required.
Furthermore, as the five turbidities have become light and both views and afflictions have been subdued, the vessel used for clearing away filth is no longer employed exclusively.

However, to achieve the lesser fruits [of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha], one must preach the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness. This sutra repeatedly demonstrates that it teaches the "lesser" based on both the primary and secondary [teachings].

Furthermore, all other sutras state this as well. If these dharmas were absent, the lesser fruits could not be achieved; therefore, for the sake of such practitioners (*kaiki*), he manifested a physical body (*janma-kāya*).

Regarding the *Píngguān shū* (Commentary on the Avalokiteśvara Sutra), its definition of the "physical body" in terms of being "limited" or "unlimited" refers to those who are the objects of this specific capacity. This clarifies the point.

Immeasurable, immeasurable! That this mind creates the Buddha and that this mind is the Buddha is what is revealed in the present sutra; it concerns those of the "exalted and special" capacity (*viśiṣṭa-adhimukti*).

Even if there were those in the stage of "near-attainment" (*upapatti-bhūmi*), their cessation would not be a true cessation, being identical to what is taught in the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*:
the unchanging nirvana, where the two birds fly together as one.

The *Miaozong* states: "Many scriptures frequently describe the constant characteristics of Amitābha’s birth-body (*janma-kāya*). Now, I shall briefly cite them. As the *Smaller Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra* says:
'The lotus flowers in that land are as large as chariot wheels. The *Larger Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra* says: 'Amitābha’s bathing pools are forty-eight thousand li in extent.
Based on these [scriptural] evidences, it is clear that his physical body is not yet ultimate. The *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* speaks of the Buddha Amitābha..."
The Buddha, endowed with the thirty-two marks, was within the Sūmadhi Jewel Hall, preaching a sutra for the assembly of bhikṣus.
In this sutra it is said: those who have practiced the lesser [vehicle] will, upon being born there, immediately see the Buddha and hear the Dharma, and shall then realize the lesser fruit.
It further says: "If one wishes to give rise to a sincere resolve to be born in the Western Land, one should contemplate the sixteen-foot image as being upon the waters of the pond.
Furthermore, there are bodies of sixteen feet and eight feet; are these not the permanent body and the permanent marks?

As for what is contemplated now—the eighty thousand auspicious signs and marks—only through the Separate and Perfect [Teachings], in their true and semblance aspects, can they be seen" (and so forth).
The slanderer says: "As this sutra states, each of those Buddhas' lotus seats and the jeweled banners upon them are each like hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Mount Sumerus.
How vastly different are these lotus seats from those bathing pools?
If it is claimed that what is seen within meditative visualization is not a real thing, why does the sutra say that such lotus seats are the fundamental reality?"
The lotus thrones of the exalted and special marks are all accomplished through the power of the vows of the Bhikṣu Dharmākara; are they not, therefore, the thrones of his birth-body?

Thus, regarding the large and small dimensions of the environment and the inhabitants as described in various sutras, the holy intention is difficult to fathom. Perhaps, by means of the bathing pools...
If one examines the Buddha’s body, it is not large; likewise, it would logically follow that the flower seat is not small. To continue such arguments is useless;
it is best to set them aside for now. Furthermore, as for the claim that this sutra describes a body of sixteen feet or eight chi as the ordinary body in that land:
Moreover, the constant body in this land is not even eight chi in height; although it manifests as three chi, this is merely a temporary transformation for the sake of Kauṣṭhila.
The sutra text clearly states that in the lands of the ten directions, it may manifest a small body of one zhang, six chi, or eight chi—how could these be its constant body in those lands?
The commentary states: "Words that accord with one's inclinations" refers to those that are leisurely and relaxed; "texts that accord with reason" refers to those that are essential and pertinent.

If one were to rigidly discard such mental practices based on these views, one would understand that what is discussed throughout the various sutras concerns the practice of rebirth [in the Pure Land].

This pertains to the four teachings and encompasses the six classes of ordinary beings. Whether it be the cause for repenting of offenses, the relinquishing of the Small Vehicle and turning [the merit] toward enlightenment, whether in a state of concentration or distraction, or whether the attachment is heavy or subtle—the capacity of the audience is already broad, and thus the manifested land should be lowly.

Therefore, in both the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Small Version) and the *Mahā-saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Large Version), the lotus flower and bathing pool are used to compare with the Buddha’s body;
they do not yet reach the height and greatness [of the Pure Lands]. Furthermore, King Drum-Resounding speaks of a city of ten thousand yojanas.
In one *daśāha* (ten days), the Buddha has parents, he has a son, and he has Māra, as well as Devadatta; these serve to verify that land when contrasted with this Sahā world.
One may merely distinguish between the lightness and heaviness of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).

Although the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* discusses perfect contemplation and manifests the *vairocana-kāya* (the sublime body), since it is intended for beginners, it relies upon the thirty-two marks of the Pure Land. Because these are manifestations of the mind alone, they are not [actual] births.

Although his physical body is present, his jeweled hall and its various environments and supports have not yet reached the state of supreme excellence. The sutra merely states clearly that he resides in *Sukhāvatī*;
one must not arbitrarily move him to another land, as such an act would mislead people and slander the Buddha—a transgression no light.

Since the "exalted special" (*zunte*) environments and supports are termed "retribution," how could they be accomplished without the power of past practices and vows? Based on this text, it is certain that he has been born [there].
Regarding the seat upon which the body sits: the person of perfect enlightenment (yuanren) performs a single practice that is able to adorn the four lands and gather the four types of capacities.
Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* says: "Whatever is manifested is all accomplished through the permeation of the untainted practices of the various pāramitās."

Therefore, it is called the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). To say that if one examines the Buddha’s body by means of the bathing pool, it is not large, and likewise if one examines the bathing pool by means of the flower seat, it is not small—is this such a proponent mad or deluded? Is it mere jesting?

It is simply because they clearly see that the bathing pool and its environment correspond to the ordinary and inferior [realms], being the constant body and constant marks; whereas the flower seat and its environment correspond to the distinct [Buddha-lands].

The "Perfectly True" and "Resembling" [images] possess extraordinary physical characteristics that defy conventional logic; they even subvert ordinary language to deceive the sight and hearing of deluded people.
I am well aware that this deviates from reason, and for this reason, I shall simply set it aside. The Sūtra states:

"If one wishes with a sincere heart to be reborn in the Western Land, one should contemplate an image one zhang six chi tall standing upon the waters of a pond. Since it says, "if one wishes to be reborn in the West," one should...
Observing the sixteen-foot image, we verify that this statue represents the body of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

The subsequent passage mentions both the sixteen-foot and the eight-foot [images], only then stating that they manifest with sovereign freedom throughout the lands of the ten directions. Since there is already a sixteen-foot image in that land, what prevents there also being an eight-foot body?
For the Buddha of that land accommodates the capacities of the nine grades of beings; therefore, the Buddha’s body cannot be said to be of only one size.

Those who slander [the teachings] are stubbornly attached to these views: they insist that the eighty thousand marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are necessarily the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), and that the marks and signs filling the universe are necessarily the honored special body (*vairocana-kāya*).

Furthermore, they maintain that the honored special body is only seen at the stages of partial and complete truth (*viśeṣa-bhūmi* and *pariniṣpanna-bhūmi*) within the Separate and Complete Teachings, whereas at the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*), one sees only [the birth-body].
"Born body. Explanation:

It has already been explained previously that the three types of bodies—the marks, the signs, and the ocean-like [body]—are all called "exalted and distinguished" (*viśiṣṭa*). To claim they exist solely within the "dust-receptacle" (the physical eye) is to undermine their meaning.

If they were truly exalted and distinguished, they would not be seen as merely occupying a single position; such a view would actually contradict the scriptural texts. Therefore, the *Pumen* Commentary states: "There is..."
As for the people of other lands, those at the stages of semblance, partial, and full [of the Separate Teaching] suppress and break the delusions of the Separate Teaching;

their vision of the ocean of marks is identical to that of the true recompense body. Those who have not yet suppressed or broken [these delusions] see less than the former. Is this not indeed the "semblance" ability to see the body of special characteristics?

If, in this land, those of the three faculties of the Shared Teaching who receive the transition according to their respective stages do not see the body of special characteristics, how can it be called the "unified body"?

Regarding the "Fourfold Faith" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, how could one behold the Buddha’s marks of true recompense (*vipākaphala*) found in the *Avataṃsaka*? How could one enter the stage of partial truth (*bhūta-tattva*) and only then perceive them?

If one were to judge based on the Perfect and Distinctive [Teachings], since they are seen at the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*), they would be categorized as belonging to the body of birth (*janma-kāya*). This would be entirely inconsistent with the teachings and contemplations of our own school.

Therefore, one must understand that within the ocean of the three types of bodies, both the high and the low are observed; it is merely distinguished according to the stages of contemplative practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) and semblance.

The distinction between true clarity and obscurity depends on the dimensions of one's body, which must correspond to the depth of one's meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*). At the shallow stages, what is seen is small;
at the profound stages, what is seen is vast. Those in preceding stages do not see those in succeeding stages, whereas those in succeeding stages necessarily see those in preceding stages.
This is the universal principle for discussing the marks and characteristics of the Buddha-body (*buddhakāya*); be careful not to be partial or narrow-minded, lest you harm yourself and others.
Those who slander [this teaching] stubbornly maintain that the body of Amitāyus Buddha, measuring six million *koṭi-nayuta* *yojanas*,

is the body constantly seen by ordinary beings and followers of the two vehicles in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*), and that it is definitively a "birth-body" (*jāti-kāya*) composed of the five aggregates of the segmented realm (*prādeśika-skandha*).
The commentary states: If one applies oneself to the teachings and contemplations of a single school, one must certainly not take this [limited perspective] as one's permanent state.

This is surely due to failing to rely on the sacred words as the standard of authority and failing to take mental contemplation as one's merit, thereby resulting in such erroneous attachments. Now, regarding this Sudden Teaching:

Establishing the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha, one counts up to sixteen. This is because one takes as the object of contemplation the environment and inhabitants of that land, as well as the nine grades of practice of sentient beings, and cultivates meditation upon them.
As the meditation gradually deepens and becomes focused, the objects of contemplation gradually become more sublime and superior; the practitioner's stage follows these objects of contemplation.
Only when the merit of subduing and severing [afflictions] is accomplished can one behold this lofty and great form of the True Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

What are these stages? They are like first contemplating the sun. The Commentary states: "Performing contemplation eliminates the five heinous crimes; this is discussed in the section on the lower grade. Thus, it is the contemplation of the sun.

The level of inferior-inferior (adhamādhamā) corresponds to the stage of verifying the visualization of ice. Reaching the stage of provisional visualization of the earth, one belongs to the lower three grades and is a person of the name-stage (*nāma-manuṣya*).
Next, having attained samādhi, one sees that actual earth and enters into contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*). For the first two grades, one next contemplates the jeweled trees.
As for the ponds and towers, their completion corresponds to the third and fourth chapters. The completion of the visualization of the precious throne corresponds to the fifth chapter.

By comparing the jeweled banners atop the throne—which are as numerous as hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Mount Sumerus—to the throne itself, one knows that its magnitude is inconceivable;

it is not something attainable through the third visualization alone. When the merit of the three visualizations is perfected, ordinary minor matters of dhyāna cannot compare to the vision [attained here]. This is the visualization.

Although [the visualization] is accomplished, the sutra text does not permit one to immediately contemplate the Buddha’s body; rather, it requires one first to visualize a great precious image seated upon its throne.

How much more so when the entire practice consists of this non-dual wondrous contemplation—contemplating it until the mind’s flow of observation becomes sharp and proficient before one is permitted to contemplate the Buddha.

Students should know that from the "Contemplation of the Sun" onwards, the three contemplations thus cultivated are shared with the meditative concentration on objective phenomena (*vastu-dhyāna*). This is indeed the case.

Because one must contemplate both the primary and secondary aspects of that [Buddha], once meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) has become superior, the afflictions of the three realms (*tridhātu-kleśa*) are entirely subdued.

When the subtle contemplation observes the image and the perception of it is shattered, one immediately ascends to the seventh stage, the stage of faith (*śraddhā*). Having attained this stage, one is then able to contemplate the Buddha’s true Dharma-body;
as the vast and sublime body manifests, it is then termed "Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi" (the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha), which immediately evokes the presence of all Buddhas.
The prediction is bestowed in their very presence. Such is this samādhi: one then beholds the physical marks of a body sixty trillion nayutas of yojanas in height.

Upon being born there, one immediately realizes the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The Great Master’s classification of the stages holds that upon reaching that land, one attains the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

Examining this, it is the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); this chapter corresponds to the highest of the high. This is the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*). It is the body seen by those whose six sense faculties have been purified.

What is its appearance? It is said that for those of the common and small vehicles who have constantly perceived the Buddha since the time of the Contemplation of the Sun, all who have cast off their bodies shall be born in that land.
Upon being born, they must see the Buddha; yet how could they all behold such a vast and lofty body?

Just as when one has completed the visualization of the earth, one then visualizes the trees, which stop at a height of eight thousand *yojanas*—this is because the eye of contemplative wisdom reaches only this far. This...
The trees look toward the seats like stars compared to the moon; the jeweled banners between the seats are as large as hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Mount Sumerus.
Those who are born there as soon as the visualization of the trees is completed—by what eyes and mind could they see the flower-seats?

One must know that these are the seats of the Buddha-image; when the true visualization of the Buddha is perfected, these seats will surely follow the visualization of the Buddha and become even more sublime. To slander this supreme body [is a grave error].

This is the Buddha as commonly seen by ordinary, inferior persons; it is because they do not fully contemplate with their eyes following meditative observation that they see the Buddha’s size [in this way].

If one first achieves success in the "Contemplation of the Sun" (*sūrya-vipaśyanā*) and is born there through scattered wholesome roots, then seeing this great body is receiving a reward without prior merit.

If the "Nine Contemplations" (*navavipaśyanā*) are achieved, one sees him as those who constantly see him do; otherwise, the three contemplations would have been practiced in vain and laboriously, whereas the suppression and subduing [of afflictions] would have been effective.
There is no reward for this.
The slanderers say: "The commentary on the title of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* clearly discusses the 'immeasurable' within the measurable. Furthermore, it specifically states:
"Amitābha is the immeasurable within the measurable. If one does not contemplate this body in the present sutra, [it is] that which the wise..."

This demonstrates: how could it be intended to confuse the masses? If one were to simply observe the "immeasurable within the immeasurable," and further claim that all "perfect persons" (yuanren) perceive solely through the karmic consciousness (*ye-shi*), then this present sutra would consist only of the observation of the *shibao* (real-retribution) environment and inhabitants, entirely lacking the *tongju* (co-resident) environment and inhabitants.

In that case, the principle of relying upon those [co-resident] environments and inhabitants to cultivate contemplation would be untenable. Now, I maintain that the *Guanjing* proceeds from the visualization of ice to its completion.

Having seen this, one perceives that the lands of those realms have already departed; they are all the marks of the environment and the inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu* and *adhiṣṭhāna*) of a Pure Land of Common Abode.

Those of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanren*) rely upon these to cultivate the Three Contemplations (*san guan*). In the contemplation of emptiness (*kong*), all phenomena vanish. In the contemplation of the provisional (*jia*), every mark is clearly illuminated.

In the contemplation of the Middle (*zhong*), both vanishing and illumination are simultaneously transcended. If one wishes to identify these with the three bodies (*trikāya*), emptiness corresponds to the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). The provisional corresponds to...
This is appropriate. "The Middle" is precisely the Dharma (and so forth). The commentary states:
The Wise One manifests the perfect and wondrous Three Bodies to explain the purport of the present title. How could he ever have used a single, limited Body alone to provide this explanation?
By means of the three wondrous contemplations, the Three Bodies that are the objects of observation must be non-dual with the Three Virtues.
There is no distinction. Therefore, after the Commentary has exhaustively demonstrated the characteristics of the three bodies (*trikāya*), it proceeds to state that they are fused and identical:

"These three bodies and the three measures (*pramāṇa*) cannot be simultaneously both distinct and identical; to do so would contradict the essence of the Dharma. Being three while being one, and being one while being three, is precisely what accords with the profound text.

Since the three bodies are thus fused and identical, they constitute the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*). Thus, the two bodies of Dharma and Reward, as well as the two types of Response—superior and inferior—are perfectly [integrated]."
It is wondrous and illuminating; how could it be excluded from the finite birth-body? Although it is not excluded, it is truly not the same as the two teachings' view of the person.

For the two functions of permanence and impermanence are mutually identical; thus, these three bodies together constitute the wondrous realm. This is because for those of the Perfect Teaching in the past, there was nothing that was not secret and wondrous.

Therefore, one should know that although the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* speaks of the birth-body as being like the sickness of ordinary people, [it does so while maintaining its ultimate wondrous nature].

Regarding illness and affliction: when a Bodhisattva inquires after one’s health, a person of perfect realization (yuanren) knows that these matters of illness and affliction are entirely the Dharma-realm manifesting as a response.
How could illness and affliction ever be separate from the Dharma-realm? Is there not a single thing that is not profound and mysterious?

Furthermore, regarding the lifespan of the three bodies, it is explained that the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) of the Mahāyāna is the Dharma-body manifesting as a response. Since the response has its source, so too does the birth.

They share the same dharma; therefore, all receive the designation of "Dharmakāya. However, because they do not realize that the three bodies are one essence—whereby taking up one is immediately the three—they equate it only with the Dharmakāya and not with the *Sambhogakāya* (the Honored Special Body).
To claim there is only one and no two, or only two and no one, is in neither case called "Perfect" (*yuan*).
For a practitioner of the Perfect Teaching, this is a fatal malady. Since the explanation of the subject is thus, when we now interpret the sutras and contemplate the Buddha...

Main Text: If there were only a single kind of measurable birth-body (*janma-kāya*), it would immediately contradict the meaning of the introductory commentary (*pūrvapīṭhikā*). Could those who possess discernment accept this?

Thus we know that the eighty thousand marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) explained here perfectly coincide with the meaning of the three perfect and wondrous bodies (*trikāya*) in the introductory commentary;

their meanings merge as one. For this reason, the Wise One (*Jñānabhadra*) points to these physical characteristics as being the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); this is his intended meaning. If one were to insist...

To hold that these eighty thousand marks and signs constitute the birth-body (janma-kāya) is an extreme perversion and confusion; it shows a complete failure to understand the perfect subtlety of our Patriarch.
As for the statement that one takes those environments and beings as objects to cultivate the three contemplations—is this not so now?

One must simply know the distinctions between the coarse and subtle, and the high and low stages of the environment and beings. By means of this, the practitioner’s seat and image are brought to completion through visualization.
The stage [of this practitioner] is already deeply established; it should correspond to the conclusion of the seventh and eighth stages of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

It does not take the physical body (*janmakāya*) as its object according to the Tripitaka or Shared Teachings, but rather takes the sublime and extraordinary marks of the Buddha’s Pure Land body as the object, contemplating it through the three contemplations (*sanguan*).
This causes the mind’s eye to see it. Therefore, the commentary states: "One contemplates the Buddha’s Dharma-body. To provide scriptural proof for this, it says:

"The radiance and physical forms pervade the ten directions; take this as the object of contemplation. Thus, the Sūtra clearly reveals that the Buddha’s Dharma-realm body enters into the thoughts of the mind.

Furthermore, it is said: "This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. This meaning is entirely identical to the "karmic consciousness perceiving the Buddha" (*karmavijñāna-dṛṣṭa-buddha*) described in the *Awakening of Faith*.
It is simply that [the Buddha] manifests based on the mind and does not depart from True Suchness (*tathatā*). However, this Bodhisattva is not yet termed a Dharmakāya;

this is precisely the meaning of perceiving the Buddha through karmic consciousness at the stage of semblance (*sādṛśyabhūmi*). There is no discrepancy here. One must know that there are eighty thousand marks.

The "Excellent Radiance" (Sukhāvatī), though it is a body of *viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa* (extraordinary marks), is nonetheless a body within the Land of Shared Purity (*sahā-śuddha-kṣetra*), because Avalokiteśvara serves as the successor there.
Within that *Avataṃsaka*, the body with "dust-mote" marks is likewise a body within the defiled land of shared existence, because after the extinction of Kāśyapa Buddha, Śākyamuni succeeded him;
and after the extinction of Śākyamuni, Maitreya will serve as the successor. Furthermore...

Since you yourself have stated that the three contemplations correspond to the three bodies (*trikāya*), and that the provisional contemplation encompasses the two kinds of marks—the eighty thousand minor marks and the [major] signs—then since these three contemplations exist within a single mind, they function as the three bodies.
In principle, they are unified within a single object, thereby manifesting the three bodies within a single object;

this is the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*). Why do you stubbornly insist that the eighty thousand marks and signs belong exclusively to the birth-body (*janmakāya*)? You will obtain only this [limited view].
The phrase "three views of the mind" completely obscures the principle that the three bodies (trikāya) are one essence, resulting in a contradiction between what is said and its own meaning.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, and the commentaries on this very sutra all state that while [the Buddha] actually possesses a measurable [body], he speaks of it as immeasurable.
"Amitābha. The *Kanjōshō* (Notes on Revision) erroneously cites this, saying: "That which is actually finite yet spoken of as infinite refers to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*."
The slanderer maintains that whenever any sutra refers to Amitābha, it is always referring to his birth-body (*janmakāya*).
Furthermore, since neither of the two versions of the *Mahāyāna* [Amitābha] Sūtra contains any mention of the thirty-two marks, how could one suddenly point to them?

Even if those two versions were not exclusively intended for those of sudden capacity, why does the commentary, when observing that the present *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* is indeed exclusively for those of sudden capacity, nevertheless point to the birth-body? It is not so.
One may take the meanings of these two texts to explain the title of the present sutra; however, this merely hangs a signboard over the prefecture to delude practitioners.
The interpretation cited in the *Kanjōshō* (Commentary on the Revised Text) is not incorrect.

Nevertheless, Master Enchin should not equate the body with its mountain-like brow-hairs and ocean-like eyes directly with the body perceived by those dwelling on the earth. For he does not regard it as the six-foot body.
"Equal in stature" (dengshen) is itself the "Exalted Form" (zunte).

The explanation states: The textual citations provided [by the opponent] are in fact erroneous in both wording and meaning. This is because they are asserted as such out of adherence to one's own views. If you insist that they are not incorrect, then what is actually incorrect?
Regarding the citations from the three commentaries which state that although Amitābha Buddha truly has a measurable size, he is spoken of as being immeasurable—since...

The term "exclusive" does not refer to the sutras taught for the sake of sudden enlightenment; rather, you have erroneously identified it as referring to the scriptures intended exclusively for those of sudden capacity.

Furthermore, regarding the vision of one with sudden capacity: the three bodies are a single essence, and their manifestation and concealment occur simultaneously. Each body is profoundly secret and wondrous, responding to the capacity of the practitioner without fail.

This accords with the nature of reality and is without contradiction. If it were not for the fact that these teachings are specifically directed toward the Sudden Teachings, then regarding the Buddha-body shown therein:

although it is the "Venerable and Extraordinary" (zuntè) body as perceived by practitioners of the Perfect Teaching, this does not preclude the two vehicles from perceiving it according to their own limited dimensions of form. This is simply a matter of the difference between pure and mixed responses to stimuli.

To say it is not mistaken is not to be dull-witted or sycophantic. Since what was stated refers exclusively to the Sudden [teaching], why does the commentary (*shu*) instead point to the "birth-body" (*jishin*)?
Because it points to the birth-body, the Buddha is not the "Venerable and Extraordinary" (*zunte*).

This is merely seeing the mention of the birth-body within the commentary and failing to understand the reason why our Patriarch spoke thus. As for that reason: whenever one discusses the essence (*tai*), it must necessarily...
