"True Suchness follows conditions" (*tathatā-anu-ālambana*) originally appeared in the *Zangshu* (Commentary on the [Avataṃsaka] Store).

Subsequently, although Jingxi’s pen refined and edited the text, he employed that term while its meaning differed from that [of the *Zangshu*], yet both remain within the scope of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Now, Master Siming, observing the texts of the various divisions through the meaning conveyed by the name, maintains that the True Suchness of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) also possesses this meaning. He elaborates upon this at length in the *Zhiyao chao*, citing and extending the argument; therefore—
The "distinct principle" (bierli) is established because it follows conditions (*pratyaya*).

Thus, the name "following conditions" is set in contrast to "unchanging" (*avikāra*), and the designation "unchanging" is set in contrast to "following conditions. These two are mutually constitutive, like waves and water.

When one speaks of the distinct principle having the sense of following conditions, does this following conditions possess the sense of being unchanging? Indeed it does; it is the very center within the extremes.
How could this be a separate meaning? It is simply that the fruit does not exist. A name does not stand in isolation; how then can it be called "following conditions"? To analyze:
when the *Zangshu* establishes "immutable following-conditions," these are both aspects of True Suchness (*tathatā*). That [text] establishes ignorance (*avidyā*) as having two meanings of its own:
first, its lack of substance is itself emptiness; second, its functional utility accomplishes phenomena. These names and meanings constitute the very throat and collar of that single commentary.

However, regarding the two meanings of "changing according to conditions while remaining unchanging," it is not only Master Qi who finds them difficult to reconcile. Those of limited learning all consider the Separate Teaching (biejiao) to be a significant obstacle.
I shall now attempt a rough explanation so that you may understand its essential purpose, thereby clarifying the meaning of how the principle of the Separate Teaching accords with conditions.
Furthermore, the two meanings of True Suchness (*tathatā*) are precisely the Middle Way within the Separate Teaching; the two meanings of ignorance (*avidyā*) are likewise...

This refers to the two extremes of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*). That [teaching] holds that all phenomena arise from the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind; therefore, it is called "following conditions" (*suíyuán*).
Furthermore, because this single nature remains eternally pure even while dwelling in defilement, never changing from beginning to end, it is called "unchanging" (*bùbiàn*).

Is it not thus with the Middle Way of the Separate Teaching? Furthermore, the *Fahua xuanyi* states: "The *tathāgatagarbha* of the Separate Teaching serves as the support and sustainer for all phenomena."
The arising of all phenomena—is this not following conditions? The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states: "The Dharma-body of the distinct teaching is like a seed;
from beginning to end it is eternally pure—is this not unchanging? Furthermore, that which is accomplished by ignorance does not transcend the nine aspects (*kushō*).

The nine aspects do not transcend the nine realms (*kyūkai*). Are the nine realms not the two extremes? Because their essence is empty, one must extinguish the functioning of accomplished phenomena and depart from differentiation.
The characteristic of differentiation (*bhedalakṣaṇa*) is precisely the principle of conditions (*pratyaya-tattva*), which is the meaning of severing the nine [grades of delusion].

If one argues that because [the nature] follows conditions it is not immutable, thereby challenging [the doctrine] as being neither of the two extremes and thus not the Middle Way, this is surely due to failing to exhaust the source of the *Zangshu* (Commentary on the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*) and being utterly confused about the path of the Separate Teaching (*prthaktīrthika-śāsana*).

Furthermore, regarding the two meanings of True Suchness (*tathatā*), they are themselves discussed as mutually identical; how could the two meanings of the separate principle ever not be identical? Why then do you suddenly take the principle...

Is this not difficult to realize in practice? Furthermore, one should know that in other passages of the *Zangshu* (Commentary on the Treasury), although it speaks of "the unchanging nature as dependent origination" and "not abandoning conditions while being identical to the Truth," and further states that "dependent origination is without self-nature and all things are thus," these all refer to the nature within phenomena (*dharma*) that accords with conditions.
This nature that accords with conditions and the unchanging nature are mutually identical according to our own treatise; yet, when viewed from the perspective of nature toward phenomena...

In the end, they become separated. One must sever the nine realms and return to the single nature. Therefore, Xuánzàng’s commentary on the *Śāstra* explains that the non-arising and non-ceasing [nature] is in harmony with arising and ceasing;
being neither identical nor different, it is called the *ālayavijñāna*, which is termed the "intrinsically pure mind.

Because its activity of arising and ceasing is inseparable from it, it is said to be "in harmony" (*saṃprayukta*). This does not mean that there is a separate arising and ceasing that comes into being.

"Union with the True" refers to the mind of arising and ceasing. Because the arising and ceasing of the mind have no two distinct characteristics, they lack two distinct essences and do not separate from one another.
These various passages are as clear as the sun; how could they not be "immediate"? [The opponent] says:

"Xuan [the author of the *Jingangxianlun*] claims that this 'immediacy' is identical to the present Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), and that it is absent in the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), which must be discarded according to conditions. Now I shall question him in return: regarding the Separate Teaching...

Regarding what is explained: must there not be a separate arising and ceasing that comes to unite with the Truth? Or do the mind of arising and ceasing and the arising and ceasing of the mind remain mutually separated?
If one interprets it in this way, how utterly erroneous!

The wise clarify that according to the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*), all phenomena that arise are not produced from the True Nature itself, nor are they produced from other false conditions, nor are they produced by both together, nor are they produced without cause. Therefore, it is said:

This is the inconceivable cause and condition of arising and ceasing. One should know that those who receive this teaching, although they practice by means of the sequential order of the three contemplations, must eliminate views of attachment to the four natures (*catur-bhāva*).
Does such a distinct meaning not reach the discourse on the fusion and identity found in the *Zangshu*?
Since that [text] establishes the "arising and ceasing" of the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*) as its functioning, it stands as a "concomitant" [teaching].

[The opponent asks: "Regarding conditions (*pratyaya*): now, in the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*), it is held that the inconceivable true and false give rise to all phenomena; is this not also 'following conditions' (*anupratyaya*)?

Furthermore, since that [teaching] holds that *tathatā* has the sense of awakening and illumination, it establishes 'following conditions. Now, if the separate principle is itself Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), how could it lack the sense of awakening, illumination, and following conditions?
[Ying] said: "In the Separate Teaching, there is only the principle (*li*). Since its essence is not fused [with phenomena], how can it [possess such functions]?"

There is the meaning of awakening-illumination (*juezhào*). Even if one were to discuss the meaning of awakening based on *buddha-nature*, it could only be said that this refers merely to the Middle Way principle, which is fundamentally luminous and pure because it is not the non-awakening of ignorance (*avidyā*). This is merely a name established through relative designation;

how can the mere mention of the term "buddha-nature" be conflated with the teachings of the definitive doctrine (*nītārtha*) to explain the meaning of awakening-illumination functioning in accordance with conditions? To analyze this: if...
To claim that the Buddha-nature lacks the quality of awakening and illumination is a state of dull ignorance; it cannot undergo transformation through perfuming.

The arising and ceasing of the nine realms is solely due to ignorance, which precisely constitutes the fault of the "other-nature" (parabhāva) giving rise to phenomena. This arises from a mistaken understanding, wherein the principle simply fails to be integrated.
This leads to the fallacy of false refutation; I shall now provide clarification so that you may avoid persistent delusion.

Now, this teaching provisionally explains that within the Buddha-realm there is only the single True Suchness (tathatā), which does not possess the distinct natures of the nine realms. This is solely because the essence of this nature is awakening and illumination.
Yet, being stirred and perfumed by ignorance, this single principle of truth follows defiled conditions and is thereby suppressed into the differentiated minds of the nine realms.
These differentiated minds are ultimately not the originally pure and luminous essence.
Therefore, although the initial mind of an ordinary person knows that a single thought is fundamentally Buddha-nature, it is nonetheless obscured and covered by the three delusions without interval.
Being unable to immediately restore the fundamental state of fusion and purity, one must therefore cultivate contemplation through successive stages and gradually destroy delusions.

This causes the mind entangled in afflictions to follow pure conditions and accord with its original nature. Thus, there is merely a process of moving from the subtle to the manifest, severing the false and returning to the true;
for this reason, it is described as "the Middle Way that transcends extremes" and illustrated by the metaphor of the moon beyond the clouds. It is not meant to say that the Truth does not exist.
It follows after delusion; within delusion, there is no reality. How then can it be said that the Buddha-nature lacks the meaning of觉照 (awakened illumination) as it accords with conditions?
When worldly people encounter the phrase "not immediately," they interpret it by separating reality from delusion. If this were so, then the Sage would possess only reality.
If all that exists is merely delusion, why did Jingxi say that in the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the Buddha-nature is the mind capable of creating [phenomena]?

And why did he further state that within afflictions there is the Tathāgatagarbha? One should know that these statements are made possible precisely because True Suchness (tathatā) follows conditions (pratyaya).
Furthermore, Ying said: "That there is the Tathāgatagarbha within afflictions refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching."
One realizes that afflictions (*kleśa*) are provisional; yet these very afflictions are fully endowed with various supreme and wondrous merits.
Because sentient beings do not know this, the Bodhisattva resolves his mind to reveal it. This is merely according to the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Regarding the phrase "established as conforming to conditions" (*suiyuan*), an analysis asks: I have not yet ascertained from what scriptural authority the term *tathāgatagarbha* originates? Jingxi’s commentary states: "As for..."

The *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is merely another name for the true reality (*dharmatā*), which possesses both emptiness and existence according to both the Separate and Perfect Teachings.
Since even the provisional constructs of the Separate Teaching do not constitute true reality, how much less so the provisional constructs that depend on conditions?

Furthermore, regarding the claim that "these very afflictions are fully endowed with various supreme and wondrous merits," this is a meaning never found within the Separate Teaching of our own school. As for the Bodhisattvas of this teaching, from... [text continues]

Emerging from emptiness into the provisional, one practices through accumulated kalpas until the conditions and causes are fully prepared. How could it be that those of inferior capacity, whose craving and views have not yet been removed, could already possess sufficient merit?
Such a conjecture is unfit for formal expression in writing. Furthermore, one fails to realize that the Tathāgatagarbha exists within afflictions;
this is precisely the meaning of the distinct principle following conditions. Question: The Tathāgatagarbha is called "wondrous existence" (miao-you), and it is also...

Regarding the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, since it is said that this *tathāgatagarbha* already exists within the midst of afflictions (*kleśa*), does this not mean it is fully endowed with various supreme and wondrous merits?
Why then do you labor to refute others? Answer: This refers to the principle (*li*) as the "store" (*garbha*); it is the merit of the Buddha-realm (*buddhadhātu*).
That [other view] refers to the provisional (*prajñapti*) as the "store"; even if one were to establish it provisionally, it would merely be the merit of the Bodhisattva-realm.

Virtuous one, such is the vast difference between heaven and earth; how can they be equated? Thus we know that this treasury is fully present within this mind and becomes manifest upon reaching the stages (*bhūmi*).
Although delusion and awakening differ, its essential nature (*svabhāva*) does not perish. If one grasps this meaning, then it remains unchanging while following conditions (*pratyaya*);
thus, there will be no confusion regarding these two principles. Someone asked: "From which sutra or treatise is it stated that True Suchness (*tathatā*) follows conditions? He replied himself:

The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Within the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), there is the unchanging that accords with conditions; within the gate of arising and ceasing, there is the essence that is empty yet accomplishes phenomena.

It further states: "This is the teaching of ultimate reality (*siddhānta-yāna*); it is not what is discussed in the provisional teachings (*upāya-yāna*). [The author] analyzes this, saying: How could Master Aśvaghoṣa ever have made such a statement in his single treatise?
It is only in the commentaries on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (the *Zangshu*)—in their explanation of the *ālayavijñāna*—that these names and definitions were established, and so forth, at length.

He opens up the categories of truth and falsehood, establishing eight gates and so forth; yet he does not even know from where these names and meanings originate, let alone the principles of the provisional and the ultimate teachings—how could one possibly deliberate with him?

Second, the *Jianbie shiyuan men zhiyao* (Essential Guide to the Gate of Distinguishing and Revealing the Perfect) states: "The other schools clarify that a single principle follows conditions to produce differentiated phenomena.

Differentiation is the characteristic of ignorance (*avidyā*), while pure unity is the characteristic of true thusness (*tathatā*). When following conditions, there is differentiation; when not following conditions," [there is no differentiation].
There is no differentiation. Our school clarifies that the essence of the three thousand [realms] gives rise to the function of the three thousand in accordance with conditions;
yet when not following conditions, the three thousand remain perfectly distinct. Thus, the differentiated phenomena are non-dual with the essence.

Because differentiation exists upon the removal of ignorance, this is a distinction made between the two meanings of the Separate and Perfect [Teachings], thereby differentiating our own school from the other two traditions. People do not understand these subtleties and act impulsively.
[The interlocutor] asks: "Difficult. [The Master] replies: "The original possession of the three thousand [dharmas] is the principle of non-change;

this is 'non-differentiation. The various phenomena produced through conditions are matters that follow conditions; this is 'differentiation. Because they follow conditions, their provisional reckonings differ.

This is identical to the other schools' position that a single principle follows conditions to produce differentiated phenomena. Therefore, the *Yili* (Exemplars of Meaning) says: 'All things arise from the mind's discrimination. All phenomena...
How could the Dharma ever have claimed to be identical or different? Furthermore, the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) states: "The principle (*li*) is fundamentally without distinction;
distinctions pertain to phenomenal function (*shi-yong*). Moreover, the *Jinbi* (Golden Scalpel) states: "True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the myriad dharmas, because it follows conditions (*pratyaya*).

How can you openly contradict these correct words and claim that the principle is differentiated? [The opponent] analyzes, saying: "The Master once composed twenty questions directed at Master Qi, which already refuted this."

This is difficult. It is based on the principle that within the *zhong* (middle), there are both the *yuan* (provisional) and the *liao* (ultimate); that within the real, there is the provisional. This is precisely the meaning of differentiation (*bié*).
Furthermore, the *Zhiguan* quotes the *Dichijing* to clarify that there are two kinds of *dharmatā*: first, the *dharmatā* of phenomena (*shì fǎxìng*), because its nature is differentiated;

second, the *dharmatā* of reality (*shí fǎxìng*), because its nature is true. This establishes differentiation from the perspective of conventional truth (*sùdì*). Since the *dharmatā* of the Perfect Teaching is not merely the middle, how could it...?
Is this not the meaning of non-differentiation? Indeed, the ultimate truth is signless and cannot be named;
yet, in order to comply with expedient means, it is distinguished and manifested through provisional teachings. How could one then dogmatically cling to the doctrine of non-differentiation?

Furthermore, regarding the essential point, when discussing differentiation based on the substance of the three thousand realms, this is already the inconceivable conventional reality of "differentiation within non-differentiation."

How can this be explained by treating it as a mere division of melons or beans? Furthermore, to claim that there are no texts concerning the perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*) of the essential points is even more slanderous.
The following passage states: "The three thousand [realms] of all lands are without separation; they are all perfectly complete with a single thought-moment.

Since the three thousand [realms] of the Buddha-land are already interfused, they are fully present in every single response. Is this not a text concerning perfect interfusion? How can you [dismiss it]?
Upon seeing the term "distinction" (*viśeṣa*), you immediately dismiss it as being merely about self-identity and difference, failing to understand the essential purport of the Three Thousand Worlds.

How could this not deviate from the principle that, fundamentally, there is no distinction? Furthermore, if the myriad dharmas exist only by following conditions, would it not follow that the Unchanging lacks the myriad dharmas?
From the perspective of Master Jingxi’s intent, your view is more than a thousand li away. Xuán says: "The dharma of distinction resides within..."
Within the nature [of reality], is this a difference within non-difference, or is it a distinction of fixed differentiation? If one says it is a fixed differentiation, then the essence is not one;
in that case, the subject and object would be distinct, and defilement and purity would truly be different—just as various kinds of seeds are contained within a single jar.
Before emerging from the bottle, it is as if it does not follow conditions; after emerging from the bottle, it is precisely following conditions.

If one says that the essence of all phenomena is of a single flavor and cannot be differentiated, such that within this state of non-differentiation one speaks of differentiation for the sake of meaning—then what is so strange about others speaking of the principle of pure, undifferentiated unity?
To analyze this: if it is a differentiation within non-differentiation, then the three thousand [realms] are detached.
This is the essence of defilement (*saṃkleśa*). The distinction between the fixed and the differentiated is precisely the appearance of the nine realms (*navadhātu*) according to worldly sentiment.

One cannot use the appearance according to worldly sentiment to challenge the essence of defilement. Furthermore, if one wishes to equate the nature of pure unity with the principle of possessing all virtues, it would be like comparing a firefly to the light of the sun.
Why? Because that [firefly] is conventionally luminous but possesses distinctions, whereas the True [Sun] is without distinction.

They are distinct. Furthermore, by means of the two gates of the ultimate and the conventional, one breaks through the gate of arising and ceasing and returns to the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

At that time, since conventional truth has vanished and all distinctions are forever exhausted, this is merely the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), which consists of the two truths of emotion and wisdom.

Students of our own school should investigate this deeply; others will be unable to comprehend it. Now, in the fruit of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), both the ultimate and the conventional coexist. That is to say—
Because they accord with the two truths through wisdom, one can speak of the meanings of both difference and non-difference.

Thus, because the three thousand [realms] are entirely true, the essence of the Middle Way is absolute and beyond dependence; it is non-different even while being different. Because the three thousand are all conventional, the characteristics of emptiness and the provisional are vividly present;
it is different even while being non-different. Since you do not understand this profound non-difference within difference, you falsely claim that they are definitively distinct.
Regarding this distinction: who can understand the seed within the flask? Have you not seen it stated in the *Jiyao* (Essential Points):

"The three thousand [dharmas] inherent in nature are perfectly interfused, universally entering the mind of a single moment within the realm of common dwelling (*sahā-loka*). The matter and mind of this mind are such that the mind itself is the three thousand dharmas of matter and mind;
like the eight phases of a thing, they have no sequence of before or after. Is this not precisely the distinction of "fixed differentiation"? Why [is this so]?
One does not examine this carefully, but treats it with such haste. Ying said:

"If one says that there is a distinction between the removal of ignorance and the state when not following conditions—such that the principle-body itself possesses the three thousand distinct phenomena—how can this be reconciled with the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning), which states: 'The principle is fundamentally without difference;
difference pertains to phenomenal function'? Miaole replied: "The meaning of the earth possessing peaches, plums, and so forth is precisely the provisional and the real."
Using the doctrine of mutual identity (*huji*), it does not say: "Apart from the function of following conditions (*suíyuán*), the essence itself possesses differentiation;
there is differentiation apart from ignorance (*wúmíng*). Furthermore, Jingxi said: "The three thousand [dharmas] do not change; ignorance is itself enlightenment (*míng*).

How, then, could one instead say that there is differentiation apart from ignorance? To analyze this: the intention of [Fazhi] Ying is that the nature of True Suchness (*zhēnrú*) is the reality and the essence. Following...

The matter of conditions consists of the provisional and the functional. If one were to leave behind the provisional and the functional to meet with the substantial reality, there would be no distinction;

this would merely echo the views of Master Zang. Furthermore, fearing that it might obstruct the subtle and wondrous stage where the plum and peach trees both flourish—wherein the provisional exists within the real—one then speaks of the doctrine of the mutual identity of the provisional and the real, and of substance and function.
If that were so, one would necessarily have to discuss the true and the false together.

There are thus two meanings: the provisional and the real. One is truly at a loss to understand why this is so. Furthermore, Jingxi said: "The nature possesses nine aspects that are provisional and one that is real. He also said:
"Upon reaching the fruition, one accords with the fundamental provisional and real. Thus, whether in principle or in fruition, both possess the provisional and the real.

How can it be said that the essence of principle (*li-ti*) is exclusively real while phenomenal function (*shi-yong*) is exclusively provisional? Regarding the meaning of how principle is "skillfully perfected" without differentiation:

if the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) states that "the essence of principle is without differentiation, while differentiation pertains to phenomenal function," this refers to the fact that within the principle, the three dharmas mutually possess the three thousand [dharmas], and thus it is called "without differentiation.
As for the three dharmas within phenomena, since delusion and enlightenment differ, they are called "differentiated. This is not [the case for the essence of principle].
This means that, in principle, there is no discrepancy between the three thousand [dharmas] and their manifest appearance.

Furthermore, if one were to say that because the three thousand are manifest, they must all be extinguished and vanish—would this not then imply that in principle there is only emptiness, with no provisional phenomena remaining? Would this not accord with the meaning of our school’s doctrine and contemplation?

One must know that because the wondrous dharma of the three thousand is, in its very essence, both negated, it is without discrepancy throughout the day; yet because it is, in its very essence, both illuminated, it is fully manifest.
Therefore, throughout the day there is differentiation; they are neither identical nor distinct, and are inconceivable. How can one dogmatically adhere to a view that they are without difference?
Furthermore, it is said that "ignorance is itself enlightenment. How then can one speak of "removing ignorance"? This is as explained in the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra).
The three transformations of the land’s purification symbolize the removal of the sands of defilement and the removal of ignorance. Is it not a mistake to use the character "remove" (chú)?

How could one, upon merely seeing the word "remove," interpret it as a dualistic entity—removing one side while leaving the other intact? One must understand that the substance of the three thousand worlds is non-dual;
it is only through delusion and enlightenment that what is perceived differs. In delusion, that which is not limited becomes limited, and all phenomena fall into separation.
Upon awakening, that which is not pervasive becomes pervasive; every mark is eternally abiding. Therefore it is said: "Eliminate the illness, but do not eliminate the dharma.

If one knows that there is only this single trichiliocosm, from delusion to awakening, then speaking in terms of "elimination" based on such identity, there is the sense of eliminating ignorance while allowing for differentiation.
This further clarifies the profound meaning. Qi said, "The statement that the essential point does not follow conditions—wherein does this originate?

Furthermore, Ying said, "I do not yet understand at what time the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) does not follow conditions. Xi replied, "It is just as the *Zangshu* (Commentary on the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*) states:

'The Tathāgata-garbha mind possesses two meanings: that of being in combination and that of not being in combination. If it is in the stage of Buddhahood, then there is no combination. That "combination" refers to...
Regarding "conjunction" and "non-conjunction," and "following conditions" versus "not following conditions"—how far apart are they?
As for conjunction, one may also question: from which scripture does the term "non-conjunction" originate? I do not know when the Tathāgatagarbha-citta has ever been non-conjoined.
Furthermore, if True Suchness never fails to follow conditions, then sentient beings would have no means of attaining liberation, and the Buddhas would constantly [be required to act].
Regarding delusion: one should know that when speaking in terms of the phenomena of delusion and awakening, there is "following conditions" and "not following conditions.

When speaking in terms of the principle of equality, however, there is neither "harmony" nor "non-harmony. This is a minor matter, yet even here people do not understand it themselves; how much less so regarding other great principles?

What need is there to labor over such deliberations? Someone said: "If the Perfect [Truth] connects with the Shared and the Perfect connects with the Distinct, only then does the meaning of 'following conditions' (suíyuán) exist.

As it is said: 'All dharmas tend toward emptiness and tend toward existence; neither non-empty nor non-existent—there is nowhere they do not tend. The Three Truths are all real, and the Three Truths are all conventional;
they fully possess all characteristics, mutually entering and fusing with one another. Although this is called 'the Perfect connecting,' its actual nature is as follows:"

[The opponent] says: "Waiting for True Suchness (tathatā) to follow conditions" means that in the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), the Middle Way connects with the Empty-Only of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao) and connects with the Empty-Middle of the Distinct Teaching (biejiao);

this is the meaning of True Suchness following conditions. If this were so, it would imply that True Suchness does not follow the conditions of the nine realms, but follows only the single realm of the Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, after being received [into the Perfect Teaching], one has already become a person of the Perfect [Teaching]. Yet...

It belongs solely to the Buddha-realm. Furthermore, since it is said that "all dharmas tend toward" [the ultimate], where the three truths are mutually fused, what need is there for mutual dependence?

Moreover, if the Perfect Teaching connects with the Shared and Distinct Teachings and can thus be called "following conditions," then why would the Middle Way of the Distinct Teaching—which connects with the Emptiness of the Shared Teaching—not also be called "following conditions"?
If you are unwilling to accept this, your previous argument collapses. He further says: "If the Perfect connects with the Shared and Distinct..."

Thus, there is "following conditions. Because True Suchness (tathatā) does not maintain its own nature, it can follow the conditions of ignorance (avidyā); because ignorance does not maintain its own nature, it follows the conditions of True Suchness.

If one speaks of "connecting the distinct" (bie-jie), this refers to the Path of Teaching (jiao-dao). It connects only to its Truth (zhen), which is what is called "mere emptiness" (butong kong), and it does not connect to the conventional (su).
That Truth of the Shared Teaching (tong-jiao) which comes to the stage prior to the Ground (di-qian) of the Distinct Teaching still constitutes the "beyond the realms" (jie-wai).
This custom is called "returning to the mundane. When discussing the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of the Separate Teaching, it merely states that being neither empty nor existent constitutes the "True";
this is termed "Single Truth. How could this possibly constitute True Suchness conforming to conditions? Analysis states:

If True Suchness and ignorance do not maintain their own nature and thus conform to conditions, this would again be a discussion of conforming to conditions based on the phenomena and principle of delusion and enlightenment; what does it have to do with [the original point]?

Is this "being received" [into the teaching] according to conditions? Furthermore, if you claim that it is only because True Suchness (*tathatā*) does not maintain its own nature (*svabhāva*) that one is then received into the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), then we must inquire:
does the True Suchness of the Distinct Teaching maintain its own nature, or does it not maintain its own nature?

If you say it maintains it, how can it receive those of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*)? If you say it does not maintain it, then it would not be following conditions. Moreover, how could the True Suchness of the Shared Teaching come to the Distinct?

If one claims that the stage prior to the Teaching (the *śrāvaka* level) remains a mundane state outside the realm [of reality], how could it be "True Suchness following conditions"? This implies, moreover, that the mundane is not identical to the True, and therefore does not follow conditions.

If that were so, then within the Perfect Teaching itself, since the mundane is already identical to the True, why would there need to be a "connection" with the preceding stage for there to be "following conditions"?
There are many such confused arguments; I shall not refute them here at length.
Third, the section on explaining the principle according to the text:

Regarding the names and meanings used by Jingxi based on conditions (*pratyaya*), although the names belong to the Perfect [Teaching], the meanings actually encompass both the Distinct and the Common. How can one allow the name to subvert the meaning?
One must instead determine the name based on the meaning. Therefore, the *Yiyao* cites the *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Pleasure) to clarify that there is no distinct principle [independent of the others].
It abides and establishes all dharmas; True Thusness (Tathatā), when deluded, can give rise to the nine realms. Furthermore, citing the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary):

"The Tathāgata of the rational nature becomes either good or evil. These are both texts from the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao). To fail to believe in the principle of following conditions (sui-yuan) without cause is unfounded.

Is this possible? Zhiyi replied: "In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), it is held that principle alone is able to create all phenomena; thus it is said that 'from the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established.

This is the sense of establishing phenomena from principle, which represents a partial or one-sided meaning. [In contrast,] the ability to subdue and sever ignorance [is found in the Perfect Teaching]."
It is called "ignorance abiding in itself" because the *dharmatā* upon which it relies can be obscured; it is called "the *dharmatā* abiding nowhere.

Therefore, it is said that both the "obscuring agent" and the "object obscured" are equally termed "abiding nowhere. To analyze this: since it is stated that phenomena are produced solely by principle (*li*), how could they not be "following conditions" (*suiyuan*)?

How could that which is produced be separate from that which produces it? As for the statement that "phenomena are established based on principle," which implies a partiality toward one side, we know through verification that this is understood as being equal [in its application].

The principle that establishes [the teaching] exists on one side, while the phenomenon to be established exists in another place. This implies that truth exists only within the real, whereas the false is devoid of truth;

thus, the nine realms are formed, completely lacking Buddha-nature. How then should one understand Master Jingxi’s demonstration that, according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the mind that creates is itself Buddha-nature?
Furthermore, since the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) upon which they rely can be overturned, it is termed "non-existent."
Regarding "abiding": if the meaning of non-abiding is present even when things coexist, where then lies the meaning of establishing dharmas?

How could one say that the covered object is non-abiding while the covering agent establishes dharmas? What kind of statement is this! Now, we are entirely one with the True [Dharma] and thus non-abiding;

yet, we establish dharmas in accordance with the nine realms. However, because the dharmas of the nine realms must be extinguished, the name "not identical" is established. If one understands this meaning, [the truth is revealed].
One may vaguely discern the principle of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) here. Xuán said: "That which covers has no abiding place, yet it establishes all dharmas.
Since True Suchness (tathatā) is deluded by ignorance (avidyā), it becomes the basis for ignorance. Only when ignorance has a basis can it establish all phenomena (dharmas).
Thus we know that the True Principle may also be called the fundamental source of all dharmas; it is not otherwise.
The whole constitutes all phenomena; therefore, they are not identical. It is just as a seed, depending upon the great earth, gives rise to trees and the like.
To analyze this: if one were to claim that although the ultimate truth serves as the basis, phenomena are nonetheless established from the ignorance that depends upon it.
Is it not precisely the grasping of the *ālayavijñāna* of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) that gives rise to phenomena? Does this not still incur the censure of those who possess wisdom?
The *Zhili Miaole* states directly: "From the root of non-abiding, all phenomena are established. This reveals that the truth (*zhēnlǐ*) is what constructs all phenomena;

how could one then perversely add that ignorance (*wúmíng*) depends upon the truth? Furthermore, it is from ignorance that all phenomena are subsequently established. Moreover, within your own school...

The Proponent of Consciousness-Only (Vijñānavādin) himself asserts that the *ālaya-vijñāna* is the fundamental basis for the arising of all phenomena; therefore, he does not allow it to "follow conditions" (*suiyuan*).
Now, since this Distinct Teaching (the Tathāgatagarbha school) takes True Reality (*zhēnlǐ*) as the fundamental basis for the arising of all phenomena, why would it not follow conditions?
How can you claim that it is like planting a tree in the earth, providing two or three layers of interpretation? This view is laughable enough to break people's teeth. —Ying.
He said: "All dharmas are established from the root of non-abiding. Both the covering and that which is covered are termed 'non-abiding.

Is this established from the non-abiding of *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), or is it established from the non-abiding of ignorance? If you say it is established from the non-abiding of *dharmatā*, [then...]
Jingming’s *Xuanyun* states: "All the practices, stages, causes, and fruits of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) arise from ignorance and the ālayavijñāna.
How can these be eliminated? [The opponent] analyzes this by saying: "I myself have not yet understood what I am reading; how can you so shamelessly establish such a challenge and resolution?"

Since you yourself cited that "the coverer and the covered are both termed non-abiding," does this mean that the non-abiding of the covered is not the principle of establishing the meaning of the *dharmatā*?

Furthermore, regarding your objection citing the *Weimo jing xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra), that was stated because it clarifies the meaning of contemplating the mind according to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).
Thus, when contemplating the mind produced by causes and conditions, since that mind is ignorance (*avidyā*), [ignorance...]
Because it is provisional (*prajñapti*). From this provisional mind, one discriminates the immeasurable Noble Truths and gives rise to the causal stages of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
This is precisely that which can conceal non-abiding and establish all dharmas; it is also due to the power of True Suchness (*tathatā*) internally perfuming according to conditions.
Why then do you exclusively calculate this text as being solely the ignorance that gives rise to dharmas? It is just as the conclusion of the subsequent text states: "The Four Teachings."

"All [phenomena] arise from the single thought of ignorance; this should be the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). But is it merely that dharmas are established from ignorance? Please allow me to offer my humble reflections;
among a thousand considerations, there must be one insight. Qi said: "The *Zhijyao* cites the *Miaole*:

'When True Suchness is deluded, it can give rise to the nine realms,' acting as that which 'accords with conditions' (*suíyuán*). This reveals a profound understanding of the essential meaning of the character 'accord' (*suí*). Now, as for the term 'accord': it is..."
The entire substance of true thusness follows along with various conditions to produce all phenomena.

How can one establish the doctrine of "following conditions" based on the meaning of the Separate Teaching (Pṛthagdharma), which holds that subject and object are eternally distinct, and the discourse that phenomena and principle are vastly different? To explain "following" (*anuparivartin*) as "producing" (*janana*) is profoundly untenable.

Analysis states: the *Zangshu* (Commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*) correctly establishes "following" by taking the ālayavijñāna as that which is capable of producing all phenomena. Therefore, it posits [the doctrine of] following conditions.

Regarding the condition (*pratyaya*): why then do you say that it is impossible to explain "following" (*anupūrva*) by means of "arising" (*utpāda*) because the depth [of the teaching] is unfathomable?

If you claim that in the *Zangshu*, the substance of true thusness (*tathatā-svabhāva*) in its entirety undergoes transformation to produce all phenomena, and therefore "arising" can be taken as "following," yet argue that in the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna-śāsana*) it is impossible because subject and object are eternally distinct and phenomena and principle are vastly different—then I ask:
have you not considered that in the *Zangshu*, the substance of true thusness in its entirety follows conditions to give rise to the nine phases of arising and ceasing?
"Must it be severed? Or need it not be severed? If you say it must be severed, then subject and object remain eternally distinct, and phenomena and principle remain vastly different.
If you say it need not be severed, why does that consciousness possess the characteristics of arising and ceasing? Furthermore, regarding the term 'extinction':

if you claim that one merely extinguishes its phenomenal characteristics while not destroying its essential substance, this refers to the extinction of the characteristics of arising and ceasing according to the Separate Teaching."
In that case, should its substance be destroyed? If this were truly so, how would it differ from the nihilistic views of non-Buddhists?
Furthermore, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) clarifies that Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching know that the substance of the four abidings of the Two Vehicles is the Tathāgatagarbha.

If its substance were destroyed, would not the Tathāgatagarbha itself be destroyed? One must know that in the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the single principle follows conditions to give rise to the nine realms;

although the characteristics of these nine realms differ, the substance of the single principle remains without distinction. Thus, it is merely their characteristics that are extinguished, not their substance.

If this is so, then [this teaching] accords with the *Zangshu* (Commentary on the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*), which holds that the whole of the True [Nature] creates the dharmas. Why, then, should one be surprised?
In this regard, does it follow that [the Tathāgata] gives rise to the Śrāvakas? Xuán says: "When True Suchness is in a state of delusion, it can give rise to the nine realms.
This is the 'deluder' and the 'deluded,' the 'producer' and the 'produced. These are two definitive meanings, like the earth giving rise to trees, or a mother giving birth to a child.

Analysis: Regarding the "deluder" and the "deluded," these two definitive meanings may indeed be acceptable; however, as for the nature of delusion (*moha*), it is definitively established as the "deluder."

This is because it constitutes an obstruction. Regarding the two definitive meanings of "the producer" and "the produced," you have not seen any scriptural authority; it is entirely a fabrication from your own imagination.

Moreover, your previous explanation—that all phenomena are established upon the rootless foundation, with the *dharmatā* as the basis (*āśraya*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) as that which establishes—now contradicts this, as you now claim that the *dharmatā* is the producer and ignorance is the produced. This self-contradiction and confusion are insufficient [to establish your position].
This is blameworthy. Zhiying said: "Jingxi stated that True Suchness, while in a state of delusion, can produce the causes for the nine realms;

how can you specifically exclude the character 'cause' (yin) and interpret it in a forced manner as meaning that the entire substance of True Suchness produces phenomena? Zhanxi analyzed this, saying: "I suspect Zhiying may have read a corrupted version of the text, leading him to such a false statement.
Even if the character 'cause' were present, how would it contradict reason? It is like the expression 'the rational nature of the Tathāgata.'"
"Is it not the case that the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*) giving rise to phenomena is precisely what serves as the cause for both the wholesome and the unwholesome? Zhiqi replied:

"In the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*), the roots, objects, and a single moment of thought (*ekakṣaṇa*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavahāra-yāna*) are explained as the basis for delusion and awakening. It cites the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, saying: 'The Tathāgata is the cause of the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Now, the *Laṅkāvatāra* belongs to the Vaipulya (*vaipulya*) teachings; its textual intent is comprehensive and universal, yet the Master cited it to prove the Separate Teaching. [End of] *Zangshu*.

Citing this to prove the Perfect [Teaching] is like the *Zhiguan* (Mohe Zhiguan), which cites the metaphor from the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* regarding gold wrapped in cloth to prove the Distinct Teaching.

The *Shu* (Commentary) on the *Fifteen Contemplations* also cites this same passage to prove the principle of the Perfect Teaching. How could one cling to the text of the *Zhiguan* and thereby fault the *Sixteen Contemplations* for being of the Distinct Teaching?
[The opponent] analyzes, saying: "The *Zangshu* (Commentary on the Storehouse) claims that the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* cited therein proves the Perfect Teaching’s ‘following conditions’ (*suiyuan*)."

[The author] says: To criticize [the opponent] by focusing on the essential point, one should not cite the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to establish the "separate teaching" (*biejiao*) of following conditions (*suíyuán*).

That "perfect teaching" (*yuánjiao*) is identical to the present perfect teaching, so it shall be set aside for now and not discussed. Furthermore, when that [opponent] cites the *Laṅkāvatāra*, they are merely explaining the meaning of the "final teaching" (*zhōngjiào*) following conditions;

when has the perfect teaching ever been said to involve following conditions? This deeply proves that Master Qi did not read widely, yet recklessly engaged in refutation and establishment. Ying says: "Citing principle..."
The Nature Tathāgata. This explains the "single thought-moment" (ekacitta-kṣaṇa) of the Separate Teaching (biejiao).

Because this single thought-moment—the provisional mind of ignorance—covers over this rational nature (li-xing), the dharmas of the ten realms arise from this provisionally named mind. To analyze this:

if one were to take the very basis of delusion and awakening as the provisional mind of ignorance that gives rise to dharmas, not only would it expose the error in establishing the principle [of the Separate Teaching], but it would also clearly contradict the textual citations in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary).
This is an error. What grievous offense have my teacher and my ancestors committed against you? Moreover, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states explicitly: "The seven consciousnesses do not transmigrate;

they do not act as the cause of suffering or pleasure. It is the Tathāgatagarbha that serves as the cause for both the wholesome and the unwholesome, capable of universally producing all realms of rebirth.
How could Jingxi, using only the phrase "the Tathāgata as the cause," have separately interpreted it as meaning that ignorance gives rise to dharmas?
You previously came forward and stated that the Tathāgatagarbha of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) is the provisional mind of afflictions (*kleśa*).

Yet now, while you speak of the presence of the principle of nature (*li-xing*), you further claim it is covered by ignorance (*avidyā*). You thus teach that ignorance itself becomes the cause of both good and evil.
If the preceding afflictions are the Tathāgatagarbha, then what could possibly cover it? This shows that one may be brave in debate, yet lack the discipline of true learning.
This is their delusion; it is chaotic. Someone says: "The separate teaching (biejiao) holds that the arising of a single thought-moment is the basis for both delusion and awakening.

This notion of delusion and awakening can only be matched to the meanings of "awakening" (*jue*) and "non-awakening" (*bujue*) within the gate of arising and ceasing (*shengmie men*) in the *Awakening of Faith*.

It does not at all accord with True Suchness (*zhenru*). I analyze this, saying: Alas! To call "delusion" (*mi*) the meaning of "confusion" (*huo*)—how could it reach such an extreme? Within the gate of arising and ceasing, the meaning of "awakening"...

Is it not true that the *Zangshu* clarifies the two meanings of "awakening" (*jue*) and "non-awakening" (*bujue*) as the aspects of defilement and purity, and principle and phenomenon (*li-shi*), within the gate of following conditions?
Is it not the case that awakening is the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*), while non-awakening is ignorance (*avidyā*)?
Fourth, citing analogies to clarify the Dharma-gates:
When patriarchs establish metaphors, each is rooted in its own specific principle. Those [analogies] merely convey the sense of the identity between the true and the false;

here, however, one must exhaustively investigate the discourse on the differences in nature between the Separate and the Perfect Teachings. One cannot equate this present teaching with those [earlier ones] simply because the latter can be slightly harmonized through metaphor.
This is perfectly exquisite. Consequently, incense and rancid herbs were placed in the same vessel, and jade and stone were burned together;

because of this, many are deluded, and thus I shall now briefly distinguish [the teachings]. Qi said: "The other schools claim that when functioning, it surges like boiling water in a cauldron, operating while fully embodying the true essence;

when as essence, it is like a clear mirror or limpid water, where every movement according to conditions returns to stillness. Does the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) of our own school also possess such textual meanings?"
"No. The analysis says: Regarding the meaning of the metaphors used by other schools, although waves may surge or the water may be clear, they do not depart from the single water;
although functions may arise or cease, they do not depart from the single Reality. Is it not likewise so for the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) of our own school?

Furthermore, the *Fuxing* clarifies that the rational nature of the Separate Teaching serves as the cause for both good and evil, citing the metaphor of the pond water being clear or turbid from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, where an elephant enters...
It is then turbid; when the pearl enters, it becomes clear. Is this not because, although clarity and turbidity differ, there is no distinction in the water of the pond?

One must know that the characteristics of clarity and turbidity are discussed in relation to the mutual interaction of the ten realms, whereas the substance of the pond water is spoken of as the singular True Reality. If one grasps this meaning, [the principle will be understood].

How does this differ from other schools? If that were the case, the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) could also establish the metaphor of waves and water; how, then, would it be distinguished from the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao)?
One should know that in the Perfect Teaching, the inherently quiescent three thousand realms are taken as the water, while the manifested three thousand realms are taken as the waves.
Since essence and function are in harmony, movement and stillness are no different. Thus, when transformations arise, not a single wave is added, for the principle-essence is fully present;

when one returns to original quiescence, not a single wave is diminished, for the three thousand realms remain manifest. In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the single principle is taken as the water and the nine realms as the waves.
Although it is known that the moist nature of the waves and the water is not distinct, one must ultimately still cease the waves.
Only then will one see the clear water. The wise understand through analogies; you should reflect upon this. Yong said: "I have personally examined that *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*;
it merely uses the analogy of consciousness to illustrate the mind, not the true nature (*tathatā*). How can it be interpreted as 'true suchness following conditions'?

Since this passage is erroneous, all [other] explanations are false. Yi analyzed this, saying: "If one claims that the mind of consciousness gives rise to phenomena, yet does not involve true suchness in their arising..."
The *Fazhi lun* (Treatise on the Manifestation of Wisdom) agrees with the masters of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* regarding the view that the ālayavijñāna gives rise to phenomena.
You not only turn your back on Jingxi [Zhanran], but you also slander Nāgārjuna; the ancestral teachings of our own school are being destroyed by your very person.

Furthermore, in the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), Zhanran directly uses the metaphor of pond water to illustrate the Tathāgata of the principle-nature (*li-xing*). How can you brazenly distort this to mean "non-existence"?

"Clearly recognize that the mind is thus devoid of cognition; this is truly to be lamented. Furthermore, Zhiying said: "In the *Miaoxuan*, while explaining the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), it cites the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:

The commentary explains: 'The painter' refers to the mind of ignorance (*avidyā-citta*). 'All worlds' refers to the ten dharma-realms (*daśa-dharmadhātu*')."

Since it is stated that the mind of ignorance creates the dharmas of the ten dharma-realms, this is identical in meaning to the doctrine of the arising of dharmas through the karma-characteristics of *vijñapti-mātra*.

How could it be that these six [realms] arise from True Suchness (*tathatā*)? To analyze this: one must not perversely cling to a single passage and thereby cause great obstruction to the grand purport.

If that were the case, then all the various teachings of our school would be mutually contradictory in every instance. Furthermore, even the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Calming and Contemplation) cites this very analogy to clarify [the point].

In that text, it is summarized in three points: [the identity of the three thousand realms with the three truths, their mutual inclusion, and their non-obstruction]. Regarding the distinction between the "thousand" and the "three thousand," are they not identical in essence? (The meaning of their differentiation is explained in the second section. Furthermore, it is said:
"If the meaning of identity is the same as the meaning of possession, then the *Jinbi* (The Golden Needle) should have spoken only of the 'essence and magnitude' (*tǐliàng*) of the lineage (*gotra*);

it should not further include the phrase 'essence and virtue' (*tǐdé*). Now I ask: when there is the meaning of the "essence and magnitude" of the lineage, is there no meaning of "essence and virtue"? If this were the case...

I understand. How reckless you have been! Because you do not understand, I shall now explain it briefly. Furthermore, as for the three meanings of the *Jinbi* (The Golden Scalpel), they all manifest the nature that is perfectly interfused and endowed with all virtues;
they are merely explained according to the sequence of their revelation. Although the explanation follows a sequence, the meaning has no temporal priority or posteriority.
Why is this? The initial indication of the "seed-nature" (*gotra*) reveals the essence of the three paths, which possess the three virtues.
Its nature is defined by its capacity to give rise [to phenomena]; therefore, it is called a "seed" (*bīja*).

Furthermore, to reveal that this nature does not reside in a single location—being neither internal nor external—the subsequent phrase indicates its pervasive extent through its essential magnitude. Thus, one should know that this nature is like empty space.

In each and every instance there is no obstruction; the bodies and lands of ordinary beings and sages neither increase nor decrease. Once one knows that the nature is all-pervasive, one then realizes that sentient beings and Buddhas are without distinction.
This is because the third aspect demonstrates the perfection of the essence and its qualities. Therefore it is said:

"Having realized that the nature is all-pervasive, one then recognizes that the Buddha-fruit possesses the causal nature of both self and others, and that one's own mind possesses the resultant virtues of all Buddhas. If you were to act...
If one interprets it thus, then at the time of possessing the lineage (*gotra*), there would be no reality-merit; and at the time of possessing reality-merit, there would be no lineage.

In that case, sentient beings would lack the merit of the fruit, and the Buddhas would lack the nature of the cause. How can one take such a discordant, dualistic view as an analogy for the text that speaks of "immediate identity"?

We maintain that it is precisely because of the principle of inherent possession (*li-jù*) that the meaning of "immediate identity" exists. Since the three thousand realms are inherently complete within the nature, through cultivation...
Thus, not a single dharma is excluded; for this reason, the Separate Teaching (biejiao) does not speak of "inclusion" (ju) and therefore does not speak of "identity" (ji).

It possesses only the principle of the true mind transforming and creating, yet it lacks the practice of the non-diminution of the nine realms. Therefore, the *Jinbi* states: "The transformation of the mind is also pervasive, yet one should say it is 'substantially included' (ti ju).
The concluding passage of the following section says: "Transformation in meaning is only two [teachings], while identity-inclusion is only the Perfect [Teaching]. Is this not the mind?

"Transformation" refers to the principle of following conditions (*pratyaya*) in the Two Teachings; "the essence being complete" refers to the doctrine of mutual identity (*paraspara-saṃbheda*) in the Perfect Teaching.
Alas! The sun and moon adorn the sky, yet the blind do not see them; thunder and lightning shake the earth, yet the deaf do not hear them. Why not simply remain blind and deaf?

"The *Zhǐyào* quotes the *Jīngxī Jì*, stating that because the Separate Teaching lacks the nine grades of inherent virtue (*xingdé*), those who judge 'following conditions' (*suíyuán*) to be the Separate Teaching [are mistaken]; the *Qǐxìn Lùn* contains the statement regarding the possession of inherent virtue."

This is because these inherent virtues distinguish between defilement and purity, as Jingxi said: "Defilement and purity are non-dual. How then can one comprehend this through analytical discernment (*poxi*)?

He said: "Regarding what you call the *Awakening of Faith*, it contains statements concerning the possession of inherent virtues (*xingde*). Why, then, do you categorize it as belonging to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*)?

Furthermore, in the primary volume of the *Jiyao*, where is it stated that the *Awakening of Faith* represents a separate doctrine? Why do you suddenly, at every turn, slanderously claim that this work refutes the *Awakening of Faith*?
